author: Christoph Morich
title: Theodor W. Adorno – Studien zum autoritären Charakter
content:
(Teil 1): Die Entwicklung der F-Skala zur Untersuchung des potentiell faschistischen Individuums


„Die Erfahrung aber und die Geschichte lehren, ist dieses, daß Völker und Regierungen niemals etwas aus der Geschichte gelernt und nach Lehren, die aus derselben zu ziehen gewesen wären, gehandelt haben.“ resümiert Hegel in seinen Vorlesungen zur Philosophie der Geschichte über das Verhältnis der gegenwärtigen Praxis zur eigenen Vergangenheit. Das gilt nicht nur für jenen Teil der Gesellschaft, der sein Glück nun wieder in der Hingabe an die deutsche Volksgemeinschaft zu suchen scheint, sondern lässt sich auch an den Reaktionen der bürgerlichen Öffentlichkeit beobachten, die einmal mehr nicht verstehen kann, warum um alles in der Welt nun schon wieder der Faschismus um die Ecke kommt. Die AFD scheint plötzlich vom Himmel gefallen zu sein und bedroht nun unsere demokratische Gesellschaft, in der doch bisher im Groben und Ganzen immer alles gut lief. Monchi, der Sänger einer Punk-Band, erinnert die deutsche Bevölkerung daran, dass wir schließlich nicht in Bangladesch leben, während Friedrich Merz darüber sinniert, wie er die Menschen emotional besser mitnehmen könnte, wenn er ihren Lebensstandard dem von Bangladesch annähert. Insgeheim haben sich längst alle politischen Akteure darauf geeinigt, dass die Geflüchteten selbst das ursächliche „Problem“ sind und die Lösung scheint nun darin zu bestehen, die rassistischen Forderungen der AFD einfach selbst umzusetzen. Zwischen Olaf Scholz‘ Ankündigung im Jahr 2023, nun endlich im großen Stil abzuschieben, bis zum Wahlslogan der AFD – „Wir werden abschieben, bis die Startbahn glüht.“ -, der ihr zum Wahlsieg verhalf, passt kaum ein Blatt Papier. „Migration steuern, bevor es die Falschen tun.“ brachte die FDP diese Politik in ihrem Europawahlkampf 2024 sehr prägnant auf den Punkt, die kaum deutlicher machen könnte, dass die qualitative Differenz zwischen Faschismus und bürgerlicher Gesellschaft relativ ist – die Faschisierung ist ein Prozess. „Der Schoß ist fruchtbar noch aus dem das kroch.“, heißt es dazu in einem Theaterstück von Bertolt Brecht. Die umfassendste Untersuchung zum sozialpsychologischen Schoß des Faschismus in der bürgerlichen Gesellschaft sind wohl die Studien zum autoritären Charakter, die als Reaktion auf den deutschen Nationalsozialismus in den USA durchgeführt wurden. Kein Weg führt an ihnen vorbei, wenn wir das sozialpsychologische Fundament unserer Gegenwart wirklich begreifen wollen.


Die Studien zum autoritären Charakter


Die Studien zum autoritären Charakter sind in ihrer Systematik ein Meisterwerk dialektischen Denkens, das einen bei der Lektüre verstehen lässt, was es bedeutet, einen Gegenstand analytisch zu erfassen, anstatt bei einer oberflächlichen Betrachtung zu verweilen. Sie heben sich in ihrer systematischen Ausarbeitung auch von den sonstigen Schriften Adornos zur Psychoanalyse ab, in denen er sonst oft recht eklektisch auf die Schriften Freuds Bezug nimmt. Das mag vor allem der Zusammenarbeit mit den drei weiteren Autoren der Studie geschuldet sein, deren Mitwirkung an der Studie in der heutigen Rezeption meist unter den Tisch fällt. Die Studien wurden unter der Leitung von Else Frenkel-Brunswik, Daniel J. Levinson, R. Nevitt Sanford und Theodor W. Adorno in einem mehrstufigen Verfahren, das Fragebögen, empirische Erhebungen, ausführliche Interviews und psychoanalytische Deutungsverfahren miteinander verknüpfte, zwischen 1944 und 1949 in Kalifornien durchgeführt. Entgegen eines sehr weit verbreiteten Vorurteils gegenüber dem Konzept des „autoritären Charakters“ geht es in den Studien ebenso wenig wie bei Reich oder Fromm darum, das Bewusstsein der Individuen zum eigentlichen Motor der Geschichte zu erklären. Von einer solchen Psychologisierung grenzen sich die Autoren in der Einleitung unmissverständlich ab: „Man scheint sich heute wohl bewusst, dass es in erster Linie von der Situation der mächtigen ökonomischen Interessengemeinschaften abhängt, ob antidemokratische Propaganda hierzulande eine beherrschende Rolle spielen wird oder nicht, ob jene, mit Vorbedacht oder nicht, sich dieses Instrumentes bedienen, um ihre Machtstellung aufrechtzuerhalten.“ (Adorno et al.) Auch heute dient die Faschisierung der herrschenden Klasse dazu, ihre Interessen gegen einen Großteil der Bevölkerung durchzusetzen. Daran lässt die mächtige ökonomische Interessensgemeinschaft des Silicon Valley, verkörpert von Wahnsinnigen wie Elon Musk und Peter Thiel, nicht …

author: ACG
title: French High School Students Rise Up
content:
From September 17

th

, high school students and staff staged blockades throughout France. This was to protest deteriorating educational conditions. The tempo of these blockades and demonstrations increased on September 29

th

 and 30

th

.


Lack of teachers, teaching assistants, special needs assistants, and nurses; poorly insulated and unrenovated facilities; and untenable class schedules… All high school students in France are suffering the consequences of insufficient funding for the national education system. This has sparked a nationwide mobilisation that is shaking the media and the government.

The national education budget has increased by 30% since 2017, so why is the situation in high schools deteriorating? For the start of the 2026 school year, approximately 4,000 teaching positions were eliminated in both public and private schools across France. Then there is Parcoursup (1) and its unfair selection system, which relies on “digital filters”. Then, in higher education, the freeze on housing benefits will prevent the most vulnerable from finding accommodation. Not to mention the “Welcome to France” decree imposed by the government before the summer, a blatantly anti-immigration project that aims to increase tuition fees for non-European international students. In short, for all high school students, stress is mounting regarding their future studies, all while enduring gruelling schedules and conditions that make optimal learning impossible.


A mass movement emerged. But on October 1

st

, the government sent in its riot cop attack dogs, and there was brutal repression, particularly in working class neighbourhoods. There were mass arrests of students, more than 5,000 in one week. Beatings, injuries, flashball shots, tear gas, mutilations—the number of injured is high.  This has not, so far, deterred the movement, with huge demonstrations across France on October 6

th

.


From the Union Communiste Libertaire website:


“Parcoursup is blocking lives.” With these words, a high school student summed up on Tuesday the reasons for the blockade of his school, a blockade that was part of the widespread student movement that has been mobilizing for a week to demand resources for education. Understaffed personnel, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms

“We lack everything”

 cry the students exposed daily to the stress of constant selection.


In working class neighbourhoods, students are sent to programs they didn’t choose, programs whose curricula are sometimes very opaque. Year after year, educational policies are reduced to managing a workforce in training and increasingly restrictive regulations. Student mobilisations in these neighbourhoods can take on more violent forms and are less like traditional demonstrations. How can we be surprised when we know the social and racial violence they endure daily? And let’s not be mistaken: when students take revenge on their schools, they are symbolically rebelling against this entire system of oppression and selection. We therefore warn staff against the knee-jerk moral condemnation that would dismiss this movement out of hand.


All these young people, who refuse to let their gaze towards the future be fixed only on catastrophe, make us proud.


This generation is aware of the systematic dismantling of its schools, the budget cuts being made at its expense, and the hostility directed towards it. In recent years, it has mobilsed against police brutality, for climate justice, and so on. This high school student movement is therefore not an isolated phenomenon. Its expansion across France since the initial blockades in the Paris region, and its alignment with the public sector strike on September 29th, is not a coincidence but rather the result of conditions shared throughout the country.


There’s plenty of money: let’s take it all! 450 billion: that’s the public money from the French rearmament plan, a windfall for the arms industry to maintain French imperialism. 655 million: that’s the funding allocated to developing AI in the public sector, without any consultation with employees on the usefulness of this tool, but simply to create opportunities for speculation. 1,400 positions: that’s the planned creation for the police and gendarmerie to continue the repression of our legitimate protests. No one can call this a technical problem; it’s a political choice.

It’s a class struggle

 .


The Macron regime is increasingly concerned about this uprising …

author: Abahlali_3
title: Record Fuel Price Increase: A Crisis for the Poor
content:
6 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

Record Fuel Price Increase: A Crisis for the Poor

The record increase in the fuel price, which will take inland 95 petrol to R30.25 a litre from 7 October, will push poor people even deeper into suffering.

We are already living through a devastating social crisis. Around 13.1 million people are unemployed or have given up looking for work. There are around 5 million unemployed young people between the ages of 15 and 34, and the unemployment rate for this group is 47.4%. Among young people between 15 and 24, unemployment has reached 62.8%. Around 3.8 million young people aged 15 to 24 are not in employment, education or training. Around five million people continue to live in shack settlements, and there are around 3,400 shack settlements across the country.

Millions of people do not have sufficient access to healthy food. The Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity group calculated that in September the average household food basket cost R5,488.06, while a basic nutritionally adequate food basket cost R6,655.29. The average cost of feeding one child was R970.27 a month, while the Child Support Grant is only R580 a month.

A worker earning the national minimum wage can work for the whole month and still not earn enough to buy a nutritionally adequate food basket for a household, even before paying rent, electricity, transport, school costs and other necessities.

Official statistics show that 14% of households have inadequate access to food and 8.2% have severely inadequate access to food. Almost one in four South African children under five are stunted.

The social devastation has plunged millions of people into deep suffering, and robbed millions, especially young people, of any hope for a viable future.

We cannot continue like this. Yet in this crisis a corrupt and morally depraved political elite, now organised across a number of political parties, continues to loot public funds. At the same time a deeply cynical business elite continues to make enormous profits from the labour and consumption of poor and working-class people. Supermarkets make massive profits while people go hungry. Executives earn millions while workers struggle to feed their families. Food has become a commodity from which large companies make profit while millions of people cannot afford enough to eat. This is simply immoral and it must be stopped.

The first thing that needs to be done is to stop cutting public spending to please business. Austerity must be immediately stopped and public money must be used for the public good. Social grants must be increased to protect people from hunger. Wages must be increased to give people enough to live on. Public transport must be safe and affordable. The social value of land must be put before its commercial value and land must be made available for housing, food production and recreation.

There can be no food security in a country where wealth and land are so unequally distributed. Hunger is not caused by a lack of food. It is caused by impoverishment, unemployment and inequality, and by a food system in which land, production and distribution are controlled for profit.

We need a massive project to build food sovereignty. Poor people cannot remain dependent on a food system controlled by a small number of large supermarket chains and food corporations. Urban land reform must make land available for people to grow food close to where they live. Municipalities must support community gardens, small farmers, street traders and local food producers, and establish public and community markets where healthy food can be sold directly and affordably.

It is critical that we break the control of the large supermarkets over the food system and build a food system organised around public need rather than private profit.

Food cannot continue to be treated as a commodity in a country where millions go hungry. Access to healthy food must be treated as a right.

In a social crisis of this extent the corrupt political elite, the state and capital have lost all moral and political credibility and we cannot continue to accept their authority while millions go hungry and millions of young people have no future.

Land must be occupied and put to democratically managed social purposes while we build the democratic power of the poor and the working class to put land, wealth and power in the hands of the people.

Thapelo Mohapi 084 576 5117 Snenhlanhla …

author: Mada Masr
title: Syndicate submits prosecution complaint regarding Matsda2sh journalists’ torture, Interior Ministry denies claims
content:
Prosecutors are still investigating the six Matsda2sh journalists who are being held in remand detention for 15 days, effective from the day they were brought before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, according to Hossam Bahgat, the director of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, whose lawyers are leading the defense counsel representing the journalists. 


Prosecutors largely repeated the same line of questioning the journalists faced in the first round of interrogations, focusing on the platform’s editorial policy and their professional backgrounds, according to lawyers informed of the investigations.


 Journalists from the independent fact-checking platform had previously been held at National Security Agency premises for almost an entire week, following the arrest campaign that targeted six of the outlet’s team members. 


After several of the journalists described being forced to record false “confessions” on camera and being subjected to torture at the hands of the National Security Agency officers, the Journalists Syndicate published a

statement

 on Monday night saying its members had decided “unanimously” to file a complaint with the public prosecutor regarding the charges.

 


Although prosecutors had decided that one of the journalists should be sent for a forensic medical examination to document signs of torture, he is yet to be brought in for medical examination, according to lawyers informed of the investigation who spoke to Mada Masr.


One lawyer told Mada Masr he had learned that a heightened security presence was observed on Tuesday morning around the Egyptian Forensic Medicine Authority at Zeinhom morgue, which he said could indicate that the journalists may be sent for the examination in the coming hours. Another lawyer said that the 24-hour delay in conducting the examination may have caused the visible signs of torture to fade beyond forensic recognition.


The Interior Ministry

denied

on Monday that the Matsda2sh journalists, whom it described as Muslim Brotherhood elements, were tortured or mistreated.

 It said that the torture claims were merely “echoed in the Journalists Syndicate statement and on some pages affiliated with the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood” and described the claims as an attempt by the defendants to “evade the charges attributed to them.”


In its Monday night statement, the syndicate board stressed its commitment to legally defending all practicing journalists, regardless of whether or not they have syndicate membership, citing the syndicate law, which requires that journalists already be practicing the profession as a prerequisite to membership.


The Interior Ministry had differentiated, in its announcement of the journalists’ arrest, between those who have syndicate membership and those who do not. 


The syndicate issued its statement following an emergency board meeting on Monday evening that ran for over four hours and was marked by a tense atmosphere, a syndicate source told Mada Masr. Tensions arose over disputes regarding the syndicate’s responsibility to provide legal defense for the five journalists who are not members and the need for action in response to their accounts of torture.


Several members of the syndicate’s general assembly gathered outside the meeting hall while the discussions were underway, chanting for the council to extend the syndicate’s defense to all detained journalists, whether or not they are members, saying “all six are our colleagues,” “you who are silent, speak up and don’t be afraid,” “freedom for Matsda2sh” and “no to torture.”


The syndicate said in its statement that it had submitted memoranda to prosecutors clarifying the legal basis of their intervention in defense of all the practicing journalists.


The syndicate board also indicated the Matsda2sh journalists’ commitment to regularizing their employment status under Egyptian law as evidence of their good intentions, noting they had taken legal steps to document their employment status in 2023 following an incident in which three of the platform’s team were briefly arrested and their names publicly circulated, while a fourth was taken into custody for two days before he was released following the syndicate’s intervention. None of the platform’s team were charged at the time. 

The post

Syndicate submits prosecution complaint regarding Matsda2sh journalists’ torture, Interior Ministry denies claims

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

.

author: Folashade Roberts
title: Old Nollywood 2.0
content:
Scroll to the comments under the movie

Love in Every Word

 on YouTube, and you will find viewers from Lagos to London, Accra, Houston, and beyond, tagging sisters to “come and watch this.” Even though the movie had no cinema release and no streaming deal, it reached 15 million views within a week of its March 2025 release on the Omoni Oboli TV YouTube channel. It reached roughly 30 million by year’s end. Actress and filmmaker Omoni Oboli and her business partner, Tomi Adeoye, launched Omoni Oboli TV in December 2023. Since then, the channel has gained more than two million subscribers. The success of

Love in Every Word

 and its sequel pushed their YouTube television channel past 182 million total views across 550 videos, and it was named YouTube Nigeria’s Top Creator Channel of 2025.

The story and style of

Love in Every Word

 are typical of Nollywood cinema, but there is something about the success of its format that raises questions. Is it an example of a new paradigm for how we understand the present-day movie industry in Nigeria? Or is it marking a return to the spirit of the original Nollywood? Does this format’s mix of “New Nollywood” and “Old Nollywood” betoken a new concept? Perhaps we could call it “Old Nollywood 2.0.”

Sometimes journalists and scholars like to divide film history into neat periods of succession. But looking at the history of Nollywood cinema, the reality is that there have been overlapping industrial formations. For the past three decades, the Nollywood phenomenon and its global impact have been described, analyzed, and debated, and the storyline goes something like this. Once upon a time, in the late 1980s, in the street markets of Onitsha and Lagos, movie theaters were declining because the cost of production and distribution of celluloid films was prohibitive. Independent producers were shooting television drama on video, working with Nigerian television networks, while the Yoruba traveling theater troupes were experimenting with video. Alongside this development, traders and marketers, who were already distributing imported and pirated Hollywood and Bollywood films, began to make and market their own cheaply produced melodrama on VHS.

Before Nollywood, there was a politically Pan-Africanist movie industry across Africa into which the recently liberated postcolonial nation-states enthusiastically invested. In the 1970s, the Nigerian government expanded its involvement in film and cultural production when it hosted FESTAC ’77 and repositioned the existing Nigerian Film Unit (formerly Colonial Film Unit) into the Nigerian Film Corporation, with a mandate to broaden its responsibilities and foster development of the national film industry. Filmmakers such as Ola Balogun and Adamu Halilu made artistically stunning films, sometimes collaborating with Black artists from across the world.

With the onset of structural adjustment policies imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), alongside the devastation of civil wars and repressive regimes, the state’s investment in a liberated media crumbled. What some consider the “golden age” of artistically brilliant, politically progressive Nigerian cinema was diminished. Into the void stepped entrepreneurial, commercially minded filmmakers who took advantage of the straight-to-video format and what economists call the “informal market” of the street. The new “video-films” (first made on VHS and then on VCD and DVD) were quite popular for a multitude of genres, from crime (

Issakaba

, 2001), domestic melodrama (

Violated

, 1996), and family drama (

Rattlesnake

, 1995), to religion (

Agony of a Mother

, 2002), romance (

Keeping Faith: Is That Love

?, 2002), slapstick comedy (

Osuofia in London

, 2003), social mobility (

Glamour Girls

, 1994), urban aspiration (

Domitilla

, 1996), and occult and supernatural narratives (

Living in Bondage

, 1992, and

Nneka the Pretty Serpent

, 1994). The rapid success of these movies far exceeded expectations.

Nollywood’s enormous local and global popularity attracted new investors and renewed interest in theatrical exhibition. The opening of new multiplexes from 2004 created another route to audiences and encouraged a strand of filmmaking characterized by larger budgets, improved production values, and theatrical premieres. The transformation did not stop at the cinema. The South African company MultiChoice/Africa Magic expanded its investment in Nigerian content, while digital …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Can Afford to Imagine Liberation?
content:
I recently had a conversation with an acquaintance who had applied for activist welfare support after the floods in Accra, Ghana this June destroyed much of what they owned. Their appliances, gadgets and other belongings were gone or damaged, rent was still due, and they had the very reasonable fear that the rains could return and the next flood could be worse. They work full-time with a grassroots organization, which can mean having a job without necessarily having the financial security to suddenly move house, replace their belongings and start again. They never received feedback on that application. Through the kind of backdoor follow-up that has become an unofficial administrative system of its own in social justice movements, they eventually learned that the welfare fund was specifically for activists who needed relocation, medical assistance, provisions and other forms of support as a result of their activism.


I understand why such a fund exists. People face threats, violence and displacement because of the politics of the work, and there should be resources when that happens. But I kept returning to the question of what counts as care in activism and what has to happen before suffering becomes recognizable as an activist emergency. A flooded home is an emergency. Losing almost everything you own is an emergency. Having rent due while trying to find somewhere safe to live is an emergency. You can spend your working life asking why the state has failed people, and still discover that the existing welfare responses want to know whether the state failed you because of your activism.


A friend recently underwent surgery and is carrying a substantial medical bill while continuing her work as the executive director of a Lesbian, Bisexual Queer organization. She cannot easily access her organization’s welfare fund because of her position, which would be a conflict of interest, and the external fund does not cover medical needs unrelated to activism.


Professionalization that overlooks precarity


Over time, we have professionalized the work of liberation, and a relatively small group of people now spends their working lives organising, documenting, researching, advocating, and building movements around questions that affect far more people than those on the payroll. Health, safety, dignity, discrimination, economic security and democratic participation remain enormous public questions, while the labour of pursuing them has become professional work. 


If we have decided that social change requires people to do this work as their jobs, what have we built around the people whose working lives now carry it?                                   


Philanthropy has made much of this professionalization possible. The work may be funded while the people doing it remain precarious. This is especially visible among grassroots activists, organisers, mobilisers and younger groups working around social justice, many of whom move from one short contract, stipend or grant period to the next. They are still living ordinary lives around the work: paying rent, taking public transport, dealing with medical expenses, supporting family and trying to meet the everyday costs of being alive. Stipends are often treated as wages for full-time work while covering very little of what a life actually costs. 


This work is also happening amid growing political hostility toward the very questions activists are organising around. Across the continent, gender and sexuality have become an increasingly contested political terrain, with governments and political actors advancing laws and policies that restrict the lives of women, girls and LGBTQIA people, while broader civic spaces are being narrowed through arrests, restrictions of protest, expression and association. In many places, the consequences of being associated with this work can include surveillance, intimidation, detention or violence. Activists are working amid growing militarism and political repression, while being expected to organise, support communities and keep these questions in the public eye. To do this work, therefore, is to work within the consequences of the politics one is trying to change. 


Professional security would mean earning a salary that sustains a life, having insurance and healthcare when things go wrong, and having some form of welfare that can absorb the ordinary shocks of being alive. Without those things, working in a nonprofit can feel almost synonymous …

author: Diba Kosi Bilinga
title: What African Elections Can Learn from the BOORANA GADAA SYSTEM
content:
A Democracy Older Than the Ballot Box


Every election season, much of East Africa braces itself. Incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets. The pattern repeats: disputed results, ethnic mobilizations, coups, or leaders who refuse to leave.


Kenya is already in a political labor pain as the 10

th

 August 2027 election is drawing nearer. Peacebuilding groups estimate the risk of pre-election violence at between 70 and 82 percent, and officials invoke the memory of the 2007–08 post-election crisis as they warn that hate speech, disinformation and organized political gangs are returning to the country’s rallies, according to

The Standard

.


Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the

Boorana Oromo

 have long practiced

rotational

,

peacefully

 transferred leadership. Known as the

Boorana Gadaa system

, it was inscribed by

UNESCO in 2016

 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life and protects women’s rights.


This article asks what East African leaders, electoral commissions and citizens can learn from a system that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups or third-term referenda. It is not a call to replicate Gadaa wholesale, nor a celebration of it — the system has its own limits, discussed below — but an invitation to study its design against the region’s recurring electoral crises.


Lessons to pick from the boorana Gadaa System


To start us off, Boorana leadership rotates on a fixed eight-year cycle among

five Gogeessa

:

Addii Doyyoo, Boru Galmaa, Liiban Kusee, Arero Geedoo and Bulee Dabassaa

. Each governs for one Gadaa period of eight 8 years, then hands over, returning to the first after

40 years

 — a rotation built into the structure itself.


Compare this to East Africa’s modern pattern.

Human Rights Watch

 calls it the “constitutional coup”: leaders who cannot win re-election simply rewrite the laws in their way. Uganda’s Museveni scrapped term and age limits to claim a seventh term in January 2026; Rwanda’s Kagame did the same in 2015, and Burundi’s 2015 third-term bid by Nkurunziza triggered an attempted coup.


Gadaa’s lesson is structural: when a time limit is built into the system itself, rather than a leader’s promise, departure never has to be settled by force.


The second lesson is that the Boorana Gadaa system treats leadership as something built over decades, not switched on by an election. Members pass through age-grades from childhood, absorbing law, custom and ritual responsibility long before they are eligible to lead.


Most African political systems do the opposite: candidates are selected first, and patronage, money and ethnic arithmetic often outweigh demonstrated competence, producing leaders who improvise governance while learning on the job.


The lesson for African parties and civic institutions: build structured pipelines — local councils, youth wings, civil service — that expose future leaders to responsibility long before a national mandate.


Thirdly, at the Boorana

Balli Walirafudhu

 handover ceremony, authority passes from the outgoing ruling class to the incoming one, treated by the whole community as final and binding, as described in

an account of the Gumi Gaayo

.


Kenya’s 2007–08 crisis shows what happens without that script: a disputed result triggered ethnic violence that killed roughly 1,200 people, per

HRW’s investigation

. Tanzania, long seen as the region’s stable exception, saw its own rupture in October 2025, with dozens of political-disorder incidents in three days.


In Gadaa, succession is scripted years in advance. In much of East Africa, it is resolved only after votes are contested — precisely when it is most dangerous to leave unresolved.


Another crucial lesson is that the Boorana society has two broad blocks,

Sabboo Sadeen

 and

Goonaa Bal’aa

, each with its own sub-clans — but the

five Gogeessa

 that hold political authority cut across these lines, so no single clan can capture the system.


Kenya’s 2007–08 violence was driven largely by ethnic mobilizations, with

CSIS

 noting ethnicity as the main axis political elites mobilize around, turning elections into an ethnic census. Reprisal killings in Eldoret and Naivasha targeted communities tied to rival candidates.


Where political identity is inseparable from …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: ROAPE
title: What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?
content:
John Molyneux’s classic statement of Marxist theory and practice

What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? was first published in 1984. The short book provided an incredibly sophisticated description of Marx’s method, and his relentless and insistent focus on the core agency of the working class.


Only the working class – however it is interpreted, described or labelled in social theory – can deliver a revolutionary anti-capitalist project. There cannot be, Molyneux argued, any substitute – no enlightened project of state development, or ‘socialist’ military leadership who deliver socialism on behalf of working people. Molyneux – in restating Marx’s central tenet – emphasised the role of the working class in their self-emancipation. Marx was the original prophet of the self-emancipation by working people. Without this class, and this project, there is simply no Marxism, no socialism, and no possibility of international revolution.


For an African audience the book speaks to multiple failed projects of socialism delivered by military coups, ‘enlightened’ governments and guerrilla movements. Each of these movements at different times dressed themselves in the language of Marxism, class and anti-imperialism but systematically broke genuine efforts at working class power.


What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? speaks directly to those on the continent trying to find a way to a genuine and emancipatory theory and practice of liberation.


Molyneux’ brilliant short book has now been reissued by the UK based publisher Bookmarks, and the Ugandan publisher Editor House Facility (EHF) who focus on readers across the African continent.


The new issue of the book comes with a major new introduction by the Ghanian socialist Gyekye Tanoh. Tanoh writes about the development and transformation of the working class on the continent since Molyneux wrote the book, and the continued capacity of this class to bring about socialist and revolutionary transformation across Africa.  


Join us for the launch of the African edition of

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 on 22 October at 18.30 (BST) with Gyekye Tanoh, Tafadzwa Choto

, 

Martin Empson and Mark Thomas. Reserve your place 

here

.


For readers based in Africa, John Molyneux’s 

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 can be purchased through Editor House Facility


here

. 


Endorsements of the book:


‘John Molyneux cuts through a century of distortion to recover Marxism’s authentic, revolutionary essence. This classic work distinguishes between living theory and dead orthodoxy, showing that Marxism is not a relic of the past but a vital method for understanding and transforming the world. It is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand capitalism and how to change it. For young activists and students alike, it is a must-read as it offers a powerful weapon for today’s struggles.’ 


Tafadzwa Choto

, International Socialist Organisation, Zimbabwe


‘In this book, John Molyneux undertakes a principled exercise by applying Marxism as a “method of analysis” to Marxism itself. He thereby provides not just a description of what Marxism is, but a method for detecting what isn’t. His application of this exercise—in the form of an autopsy of the interests and classes represented by three self-proclaimed Marxist tendencies—provides a valuable model for defining Marxist politics and organizations in our own contexts while enabling us to avoid the “hybrid ideologies of the petty bourgeoisie.” This is crucial, for us in the Global South, where reality differs greatly from that of Europe, thereby demanding a Marxism of contextualized design, not rigid imitation. The method offered is therefore a vital tool in enabling Marxist projects capable of fulfilling its role in “guiding revolutions to victory.” Such is true whether in the Global South or in global contexts marked by increasing economic complications and the co-option of Marxism by bourgeois ideologies fighting for survival amid the clear failure of neoliberal models … One need not agree with all of Molyneux’s conclusions to find his method a timely and indispensable resource.’


Muzan Alneel

,Marxist researcher and writer from Sudan


The post

What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?

 appeared first on

ROAPE

.

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Moataz Hagag
title: State security prosecution releases journalist Rasha Azab on LE10,000 bail
content:
Journalist Rasha Azab was released on LE10,000 bail on Monday evening by the Supreme State Security Prosecution following questioning in relation to a tweet she published in recent weeks regarding the conduct of the Interior Ministry and its impact on the public mood. 


She was questioned on charges of “promoting the perpetration of terrorist acts” and using a website to promote ideas calling for doing so in Supreme State Security Prosecution Case 8025/2026, her defense lawyer, Ragia Omran, told Mada Masr. 


Azab was questioned on her reasons for publishing a tweet, in which she wrote, on September 23, “how long does it take to go from ‘the Interior Ministry are thugs’ to ‘the people want the fall of the regime.’” Azab responded that her tweet was commentary on the case of Dina Ezzat, a woman who called for her husband’s release on social media in September, after he was arrested from their Nasr City home by authorities in their local area. Ezzat herself was briefly

taken

 into custody after she spoke out against her husband’s arrest before she was later released on bail. 


According to the case’s record, 12 people filed complaints at police stations across several governorates against Azab the day after she posted her tweet, Omran said.


The prosecution did not question her about the Matsda2sh case. Azab herself, however, pointed to what she had read on social media regarding

the Matsda2sh journalists’ complaints of torture at National Security Agency headquarters

, when prosecutors asked her for examples of “thuggery” on the part of the Interior Minsitry. She also cited her own subjection to assault during a 2024 protest outside the United Nations Women office, after which she was briefly

arrested

 before being released on bail, as well as threats, pursuit and the theft of her car; incidents she said her local police station had refused to allow her to file a report on.


During the investigation, Azab said that she did not know the Matsda2sh journalists previously and that she knew of them and of their arrest through the statements published by the Journalists Syndicate, and that she had heard that they were tortured in custody via published statements. 


Azab received a

summons

 to the prosecution on Saturday, without explanation of the charges or the incidents under investigation, and was presented on Monday afternoon for questioning. 


She

posted

 to her X account earlier on Monday that she views herself as “once again accused,” after two years of harassment which included her hounding, the theft of her car in 2024 and the “destruction of her life.” 


She added that the summons comes during a time of an ongoing push for “independent journalism and a nation without despotism,” and called for the support of her colleagues present today at the Journalists Syndicate.


The summons came in the wake of an ongoing demonstration at the syndicate, in which Azab had participated, along with dozens of other journalists, in solidarity with the six from independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh who were arrested last week. Upon receiving the summons, her lawyers inquired about the case against her and found that it predated the campaign targeting the Matsda2sh team.

State security prosecution releases journalist Rasha Azab on LE10,000 bail

author: Dennis Ward
title: Mandy Gull-Masty’s balancing act as Indigenous Services minister
content:
Over the past year and a half, Mandy Gull-Masty says a lot of people have asked, “Why is it that you chose to become the Indian agent?”


In May 2025, Gull-Masty, the first ever woman to be elected as the grand chief of the Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee), became the first ever Indigenous person to head up Indigenous Services Canada (ISC).


The minister says she wants to support the vision of First Nations and “give them the tools they need so that they can take the space of determining how they want services delivered and ultimately doing the work of delivering those services, themselves.”


Gull-Masty admits the job comes with “a lot of balancing, a lot of stress, a lot of moments of quiet thought and deep reflection” and that she is “trying to maintain who she is.”


Gull-Masty has a number of high profile issues on her plate, including the reintroduction of the

First Nations Clean Water Act.


Another controversial piece of legislation is Bill S-2.


The government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of stalling on ending

the second-generation cut-off.


Consultation on Bill S-2 wrapped up in July.


While many in leadership have called for Parliament to pass the legislation, Gull-Masty says she’s trying to reflection everyone’s voice.


“It is very clear that while yes, while there are some Nations that want to pursue a one-parent rule, the consultations also demonstrated that there are Nations out there that feel very strongly that they need to be the ones that determine the criteria for what it means to be a citizen of their Nation,” says Gull-Masty on the season premiere of Face to Face.


“I have the unique challenge as the minister to ensure that while I’m trying to create the pathway for those Nations that want to have a one parent rule, I’m also looking to create a pathway for those who don’t,” says Gull-Masty.


Reforming the First Nations child welfare system is also a huge challenge on the minister’s plate.


Indigenous Services Canada Minister Mandy Gull Masty at a news conference on Parliament Hill to announce that money from the federal government to First Nation communities in Ontario for their child welfare systems will start to flow on May 29. Photo: Alison Seymour/APTN.


Next February will mark the 20th anniversary of the original complaint filed with the Canadian Human Rights Commission by the First Nations Child and Family Caring Society and the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) alleging discrimination in the on reserve child welfare system.


A decade ago, the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal (CHRT) ruled First Nations children were being discriminated against.


The AFN and federal government previously agreed to a $47.8 billion dollar deal but that was rejected by a majority of chiefs at an assembly in 2024.


Chiefs in Ontario negotiated a separate, $8-billion deal with Ottawa, which was approved by the CHRT in March.


Since that time, there has been a lot of legal wrangling before the CHRT, some of it over the loss of another commissioner.


Gull-Masty says people need to understand that Canada is looking for clarification on rulings and not “looking to push back” on rulings.


The minister believes the previous approach of trying to find one path forward for all First Nations, such as the First Nations-led and designed

Loving Justice Plan

, may not be the way to go.


“I’m also trying to be respectful of those communities that want to have the opportunity to seek what was put forward in other plans that are presented by the Caring Society,” says Gull-Masty.


“There’s good work there, there’s a lot of research that has been done there. We have referenced it. But ultimately, I really think that the regionalized approach and creating space for Nations themselves to determine what it is they want to do to support their youngest, most vulnerable members is one that is having traction and is one where there is a lot of conversations moving forward and is one where I’m seeing decisions that are leading to support of regionalized agreements,” says Gull-Masty.


Another issue that has been at the forefront in recent months that Gull-Masty believes needs a more nuanced approach, is criminalizing residential school denialism.


Many First Nations leaders expressed their disappointment when the

Canadian Senate

 voted down an amendment in June that would have rendered residential school denialism a punishable crime.

title: Historic Trees Demolished, Land Defenders Arrested and New Treesit at US-Mexico Border
content:
Lochiel, AZ – In the early hours of October 5, Border Patrol agents raided the anti-border camp called “Tierra Libre” on the U.S.-Mexico Border near Lochiel, Arizona. An estimated 200 Border Patrol Agents invaded camp — entering the tracts of private property along the border that had long-shielded land defenders from the authority of the federal agents — and cut down the ancient Grandmother tree that campers had attempted to protect. Less than 24 hours later, land defenders established a new treesit in the immediate path of construction, this time on the Mexican side of the border. 


Although Border Patrol agents were parked along the easement throughout the night, a masked land defender snuck past them and scrambled up into the 50-foot-tall Grandmother tree and into the platform already built there. “This brave warrior climbed right up there,” said Pablo, a land defender who was at camp Tuesday morning. “The new treesit is very much blocking construction, as long as someone is in that tree they will not be able to build their wall.”


Past Coverage:

Treesit Blocks US-Mexico Border Wall Construction for Six Weeks in Arizona


According to multiple sources on the ground who spoke with Unicorn Riot, Border Patrol agents entered private property Monday morning, refusing to show evidence of a warrant allowing them to do so, and refusing to explain what authority granted them that right.


Agents shoved and tackled campers, pointed guns at them, stomped on their necks, and pushed several campers into the barbed wire fence that marks the private property line. One land defender who goes by the name Hoops showed wounds on her hands and wrist to members of the media that she said resulted from agents twice her size tackling her into the barbed wire fence. 


“Border Patrol has been coming onto private property since yesterday morning,” said Rachel, a land defender who spoke with Unicorn Riot about the raids. “No warrants are shown, as far as we can tell there’s no legal ground for them to come onto private property. It seems like they’re pushing through the construction process quickly and will deal with the law later.” 


Construction workers protected by Border Patrol agents used a cherrypicker to cut branches off of the 200-year-old cottonwood Grandmother tree, in which a treesit had been sustained for 71 days. Agents then removed a treesitter stationed to protect the tree from border wall construction.


Within minutes, the Grandmother tree was felled and the treesit destroyed. Ten land defenders were arrested, including the treesitter. Ten more were cited and released. 


BREAKING: For Trump’s wall, Border Patrol cut down the sacred Grandmother Tree, a more than 200-year-old Cottonwood on private property + Indigenous territory.

The tree sitter and many others have been arrested, according to activists @ Tierra Libre anti-border wall camp in AZ https://t.co/oYbG1fasNH

— Mike Ludwig / @mludwig.bsky.social (@ludwig_mike)

October 5, 2026


“The Grandmothers live inside us now,” said an anonymous land defender who spoke on behalf of those at camp. “We make this promise: this wall will not be built! We will tear down what has already severed the land and our peoples, piece by piece.” 


Land defenders established the new treesit in the tall cottonwood tree that land defenders had briefly occupied in August, early on in the campaign. Facing pressure from Border Patrol and Mexican State Police, the treesit had been vacated. It remained unoccupied for over six weeks – until today. 


View this post on Instagram


A post shared by Max Granger (@mxgrxngxr)


Shortly after the treesit was reoccupied Tuesday morning, Border Patrol responded in force, confronting land defenders and attempting to push them back off the easement road that runs along the border.


In the midst of that confrontation, at least five protesters were arrested and taken into custody and five more were charged and released. The situation is actively developing. 


“We stand strong and will not be deterred by state violence or intimidation,” said an unnamed spokesperson for Tierra Libre in a press release emailed to media. “We call on all people of ceremony, all people of conscience, to come join us now in La Noria and Lochiel, to protect the land, to protect the sacred.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Report: Trump Admin Is Deporting LGBTQ Asylum Seekers to Hostile Third Countries
content:
Officials have deported LGBTQ people to Sierra Leone, where they could face life in prison for same-sex activity.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Trump administration has reportedly deported dozens of LGBTQ immigrants who sought or were granted asylum for their sexuality and gender to third countries where they face danger of persecution and criminalization, a new report says.

In an investigation published this week, Reuters identified 40 cases where these LGBTQ individuals were sent to countries that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been designated by the State Department as dangerous for LGBTQ people.

All of these people were granted legal protection in the U.S. for fleeing persecution for their LGBTQ status in their countries of origin, per Reuters. However, more than half of them were ineligible for asylum because of a restrictive Biden-era transit ban on asylum seekers.

Individuals tracked in the report have been deported to countries including Sierra Leone, Cameroon and Eswatini, three countries where same-sex acts are criminalized. In Sierra Leone, same sex acts carry a punishment of up to life in prison. Other countries that have signed deportation agreements with the U.S. have seen abuses against LGBTQ people like conversion therapy and “corrective rape,” the report notes.

The Trump administration has signed third country deportation agreements with at least 35 countries, and has deported over 25,000 people this way, sending them to places that they have no affiliation with. Many governments in Africa and central and South America have signed agreements to receive such deportees, often in exchange for direct funding or other financial incentives.

Reuters noted the story of one man, identified as Abdou Latifou, who fled his home country of Togo after a mob assaulted him and threatened to kill him after he kissed a man. A U.S. immigration judge decided last year that it was too unsafe for him to return home; he recalled thinking, “From this day on, I’m entering a world where I’m free to live as myself.”

But amid its mass deportation campaign, and while knowing that Latifou was gay, the Trump administration deported him to Sierra Leone, where he was held for two weeks under police surveillance before being put on a flight to Togo. Fleeing danger yet again, he went to the Ivory Coast, where he lives in fear of being recognized.

“When an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for them,” Department of Homeland Security spokesperson ​Chandler Rebel told Reuters.

The report is the latest documenting the Trump administration’s deportations of people to places where they may be endangered. Other reports this week found that the Trump administration deported a former political prisoner back to the place he was imprisoned and tortured last week. Jeffrey Jarquín, who led pro-democracy protests against the Nicaraguan government, was reportedly taken directly from the deportation flight to the capital of Managua to a notorious Nicaraguan prison.

The Trump administration is facing a lawsuit from Iranian asylum seekers who say that U.S. officials secretly shared sensitive information, including LGBTQ status, about them with the Iranian government — as it’s tried to deport them into a country where they may face persecution.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians in the U.S., and has deported hundreds of immigrants back to Haiti, which has experienced a surge of violence and hunger.
