title: The cost of US imperialism that we are fighting against
content:
with added reports from Jessica Obciana and Kline Vergara

“Homes are destroyed, livelihoods are lost, nations are lost by interests that are made far beyond our own borders. Even now, initiatives like Pax Silica, supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors are being reordered around the needs of the US war machine, and countries like us [the Philippines] are being asked to serve as suppliers and now become their targets, rather than being allowed to decide our own development,” said Dr. Giovanni Tapang, convener of the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Network.

Various anti-imperialist groups gathered for the webinar Updates from the Resistance: The Current Situation in Iran, Palestine, Venezuela, and Cuba, co-organized by BAYAN, the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Campaign Network, to express people’s solidarity in lambasting US imperialism following its sanctions, blockades, military aggression, and other forms of intervention and coercion against the people.

“This is the war machine that we are fighting against. And as we listen to those who are on the front lines, we learn of their resistance, deepen our understanding, and together strengthen solidarity to defeat this war machine,” Tapang added.

“We have seen the case of Venezuela: how this warfare has been attacking the Global South, attacking the country, and in many, many aspects, not only the political one, military, economic, and cultural, and in social consciousness. Venezuela is under siege now,” said Richard Lobo, Venezuela’s Chargé d’Affaires.

Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at around 303 billion barrels as of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Lobo noted that US intervention in Venezuela extends beyond economic sanctions to political, military, economic, and cultural intervention.

In January 2026, the US launched Operation Absolute Resolve as a large-scale military operation in Venezuela framed around drug trafficking and national security that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores and their transfer to the United States. Such an operation also targeted Venezuelan military infrastructure across Caracas and other locations.

Months after Maduro’s capture, the US laid out an agreement to gain access and control over an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, mineral wealth, and other resources.

Meanwhile, Lobo emphasized that the situation has only amplified the resistance among Venezuelans in defending their sovereignty and their right to determine the country’s political and economic direction.

“Even though we have been under attack […] the people there in Venezuela have been resisting and have been struggling. And one thing that I can say right now is that even with the kidnapping of our president, they believe the government is still in power,” Lobo stated.

More than 5,000 civilians have been killed in the US-Israel aggression against Iran, including 168 girls who were killed when a school was struck in March this year.

“Iran is experiencing aggression by the United States and Israel since the 1979 revolution against a very corrupt government, the Shah’s government. The United States has been trying to overthrow the revolutionary government in Iran, engaging in economic warfare for 46 years,” said Dr. Foad Izadi, associate professor at the University of Tehran.

The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose government had maintained close relations with the US. The revolution fundamentally changed Iran’s relationship with the US, posing decades of diplomatic confrontation, economic sanctions, and political pressure.

“(The US) has also asked Iran to reduce its support for the Palestinian cause. As you know, Iran has been a strong supporter of Palestine. Not only with words, not only with speeches, but with military aid. Iran is the only country that is helping Palestinians with military aid,” said Dr. Izadi, noting that other governments should also learn from them by providing help to those countries fighting against aggression and genocide.

“Iran has learned that if you allow Israelis, genocidal people, the apartheid regime to get away with their crimes in Palestine, they they would want to take over the Middle East and go beyond,” he added.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Fuel hikes squeeze jeepney drivers, commuters dry
content:
Jeepney with signage: "No to Oil Price Hike" (Photo by Roselle Ochobillo/Bulatlat)

By Wendyl Geronimo and Roselle Ochobillo

For commuters, the recent P1 increase in jeepney fares may seem small. But for workers who rely on public transportation every day, the additional peso can add to an already tightening budget.

For jeepney drivers, meanwhile, the bigger burden is not the fare increase itself but the fuel prices behind it.

After several rounds of oil price increases, diesel prices have continued to eat into drivers’ daily earnings, leaving some struggling to provide food, pay rent and keep their children in school.

The pressure was among the reasons transport groups, including the Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahang Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON), held a nationwide strike on Sept. 29 and 30, calling for lower petroleum prices and relief from fuel taxes.

For 52-year-old jeepney driver Teody Bermejo, National Capital Region and Alabang Pasay President said that the additional peso in fare does little to address what drivers actually spend to keep their vehicles running.

Bermejo, who has been driving for around 30 years, said he now spends much of his working day trying to recover the cost of diesel.

He drives from around 4:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m., or as long as 16 hours a day. When diesel was around P50 to P55 ($0.80 to $0.88) per liter, he said he could take home around P1,000 ($15.98), sometimes reaching P1,500 ($23.97).

Now, he said, his take-home income has fallen to around P500 to P600 ($7.99 to $9.59), despite the long hours on the road.

“That is really not acceptable to us because diesel prices have increased by around P52 to P55 ($0.83 to 0.88), while they only added P1 to the fare. There is a huge difference. It really won’t be enough for us.”

For Bermejo, the impact of rising fuel prices has reached his household. He has four children in school, but his income can no longer cover their needs at the same time.

One of his children who was in college had to temporarily stop studying and find work to help the family.

“My child in college had to stop studying for now. In a way, they also had to find a job to help me because my income now is not enough to support all of them in school at the same time.”

He said the family is now trying to continue the education of his other children while making ends meet with his reduced income.

The same struggle is felt by 50-year-old Janet “Arja” Tumbaga Pocsidio, a member of Piston Women who helps operate a Cubao-Divisoria route.

Pocsidio is a mother of five and helps provide for her children and grandchildren. When diesel prices reached around P140 to P145 ($2.24 to $2.32) per liter, she said their earnings from driving became too small to sustain the family.

On some days, her husband would earn only P70 to P80 ($1.12 to $1.28).

The family eventually stopped operating their jeepney for periods because the cost of fuel outweighed what they could earn from passengers.

Pocsidio then worked as a barker, earning around P250 to P400 ($3.99 to $6.39) a day, which she used for food and her children’s school expenses.

The rising cost of basic necessities also changed what the family could afford to eat.

She said they often relied on dried fish and eggs, while even small increases in food prices became noticeable in their daily budget.

Housing became another burden. Pocsidio said their family was paying P6,000 ($95.88) in monthly rent, aside from electricity and water.

Eventually, they were forced to leave their rented home because they could no longer keep up with the payments.

“We were evicted, and we ended up sleeping in our jeep. Yes, we were evicted because we couldn’t afford to pay,” Pocsidio told Bulatlat.

The family later stayed at the Piston San Juan office for about four months, where they paid for electricity.

For her, depending on the organization for shelter was difficult.

“I feel ashamed. I’m extremely ashamed. I’m quite self-conscious, but I have no other choice. I just told myself that I would leave it in the Lord’s hands.”

While drivers struggle with operating costs, commuters are also adjusting their budgets.

Bench Cuabo, a government worker, said that the P1 ($0.02) fare increase may appear minimal but still affects his daily transportation expenses.

He said his usual P15 ($0.24) fare has increased to P17 (0.27), and when drivers cannot provide change, he sometimes ends up paying P20 ($0.32).

author: groundxero
title: ‘We can’t report anything against AP govt’: National media silent on Tirumala Tirupati controversy after ED and CBI probes debunk false claims of ‘beef tallow’ use
content:
In a press release on 17 September 2026, eight months after the Supreme Court-appointed CBI Special Investigation Team (SIT) explicitly ruled out the presence of animal fats in the ghee used for manufacturing the Tirumala Tirupati temple’s prasadam, the Enforcement Directorate has arrested a promoter of a private food company allegedly involved in contamination after lab forensic analysis revealed the presence of seven adulterants. Notably, none of them are animal fats, specifically ‘beef tallow’, the allegation of whose presence triggered outrage and investigation in the first place, and cemented a political upset in the state by amplifying communal tensions.


 


by

 Mouli Sharma


 


On 19 September 2024, Andhra Pradesh’s Tirumala Tirupati temple had taken over national and regional news by storm for an unsavoury reason: an allegation of the presence of animal fats in the temple’s

prasadam

 (consumable offerings to Hindu deities given as blessed alms to devotees), specifically the accusation that ‘beef tallow’ was used in the rendering of adulterated ghee used to make the temple’s laddus. Unverified accounts of ‘lab reports confirming the allegations’, which were amplified by TDP’s CM Chandrababu Naidu himself, eventually led to an FIR about the same being registered on 25 September 2024, followed by a PIL being filed in the Supreme Court by one Dr. Subramanian Swamy.


Over a year later, the allegations were debunked by a Special Investigative Team constituted by the CBI to investigate the case, whose forensic examination categorically ruled out the use of animal fats, though the presence of synthetic adulterants was confirmed.


On 17 September 2026, almost exactly two years later, the enforcement directorate reproduced the same findings. Seven adulterants were listed in an ED press release announcing the arrest of a food promoter allegedly involved in multi-crore transactions behind the procurement of the adulterated ghee—Refined Palm Oil, Palm Kernel Oil, Palmolein, MG-90, Monoglycerides, Myvacet Soft 400 and Acetic Acid Ester—none of which are animal fats of any kind, let alone fats of particularly polarising animals, like cows.


 


On 17 September 2026, almost exactly two years later, the enforcement directorate reproduced the same findings. Seven adulterants were listed in an ED press release announcing the arrest of a food promoter allegedly involved in multi-crore transactions behind the procurement of the adulterated ghee—Refined Palm Oil, Palm Kernel Oil, Palmolein, MG-90, Monoglycerides, Myvacet Soft 400 and Acetic Acid Ester—none of which are animal fats of any kind, let alone fats of particularly polarising animals, like cows.


In the light of both revelations, the dozens of mainstream media outlets across the country who expounded the now debunked claims without any evidence of their legitimacy back when the controversy had first surfaced, fanning communal sentiments within the country’s dominant caste-Hindu population, triggering a rise in hate speech, and cementing the popularity of the then newly elected NDA government in the state, have remained conspicuously silent.


“Unfortunately, we cannot use any news content against the AP government. I cannot say more than that,” he said.


Major newspaper outlets with the largest circulation rates in India; channels with the highest viewership statistics, and websites at the top of Search Engine Optimisation and provenance score rankings—The Times Group, The Express Group, Firstpost, The Hindu, Dainik Bhaskar, NDTV, and many more—all solicit their newsdesk items from this agency. This is possibly why the only visible headlines currently in the public domain that acknowledge this debunking, are the opposition party’s own social media posts, and an article by The News Minute, an independent alternate online news portal focusing on the South.

title: The Algorithm of the Ballot: How Data Decides Democracy Before We Vote
content:
Elections used to be loud. Street-corner rallies, hoarse loudspeakers, campaigners going door to door, entire neighbourhoods gathered around a television for the evening debate. That version of democracy is dying, and most of us haven’t quite noticed the funeral. The real contest now happens somewhere quieter — inside a smartphone screen, in the space between a thumb and a feed. Political persuasion doesn’t shout at crowds anymore. It whispers to individuals, one at a time, and the whisper has been tested, refined, and timed with a precision no rally could ever match.

This isn’t speculation about some AI-run future. It’s already part of how political communication works in India and elsewhere with widespread mobile internet access.

Campaigns describe their own methods as “smart” and “surgical,” and for once the marketing language is accurate. Nobody is addressing an anonymous mass anymore. Every voter is a profile being built in real time — every scroll, every pause, every like or skip can become another data point feeding a model of who you are and what might move you. Linger two seconds longer on a video about unemployment, and your feed may begin showing you more content like it, each one worded slightly differently, until what started as manufactured content starts to feel like your own settled opinion.

What makes this so effective is precisely that it doesn’t feel like anything is being done to you. A curated feed never announces itself as curated. It just feels instinctual — as if the device has learned to think alongside you rather than manipulate you. Two people can work in the same office, live in the same city, share the same friend group, and still inhabit completely different informational worlds. One sees hope where the other sees decline. One sees progress where the other sees collapse. The algorithm isn’t necessarily lying to either of them. It’s simply reflecting their inclinations at them, amplified, until the reflection becomes impossible to distinguish from the self that’s supposedly thinking.

Try this yourself, and it gets uncomfortable fast: spend one full day deliberately engaging with the opposite side of your politics. Like the arguments you find weak. Click into the topics you usually scroll past. Within hours, your feed may begin to recalibrate. The old version — the one that felt so personal, so obviously true — can start to look different, as if it never existed. That should bother you more than it probably does. If a belief can be reshaped in an afternoon just by changing what you click, how solid was it to begin with? Political conviction, it turns out, isn’t always bedrock. Often it’s just a data point that hasn’t been nudged yet.

A Global Infrastructure of Influence

None of this is a local phenomenon. In the United States, campaigns use predictive modelling, experimentation, and targeted advertising to identify voters and test which messages are more persuasive. In China, the digital infrastructure is subject to extensive state regulation, including rules governing algorithmic recommendations and the presentation of information. In the European Union, regulators have moved beyond drafting rules: new regulations governing the transparency and targeting of political advertising became fully applicable in October 2025, imposing significant restrictions on the use of personal data for political targeting.

Different governments, different justifications, same underlying playbook. None of it necessarily depends on coercion, because coercion is visible, and visible things get resisted. The real method can be subtler: build the environment so precisely that a person mistakes the nudge for their own free judgment. Nobody feels manipulated when they’re convinced the idea was theirs all along.

There’s a specific kind of unease in standing inside a polling booth and asking yourself a plain question: was this decision actually made here, in this moment of privacy — or weeks ago, in a server room, by a system that had already modelled the outcome? When results appear close to pre-poll forecasts, “good analytics” is one explanation. Successful engineering is another. At a certain level of precision, the two can start to look identical.

This matters more, not less, in a country as vast and unequal as India. Behavioural targeting doesn’t treat every citizen the same way. Voters with less digital literacy, fewer alternative sources of information, or less social capital to question what their …

author: ALR Editors
title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

title: Sleeper-Cell Report July 2026 – Global Coalition reports 0 confirmed ISIS attacks
content:
An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside


 


Key Points


– Six sleeper-cell attacks recorded by RIC, but the Global Coalition claims 0 attacks were officially claimed by ISIS


– One military personnel was killed, and a further five injured


– A minimum of seven alleged ISIS members were arrested


– A total of 36 civilians were injured, two killed


– An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in Deir ez-Zor


–

Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS mercenaries repatriated from Roj camp


 


In-Depth


In July of 2026, RIC

recorded six sleeper-cell attacks which some publications have attributed to ISIS, according to


North Press Agency

 one of these attacks was claimed by ISIS whereas the


Global Coalition


reported that July was the first month since the territorial defeat of ISIS in 2019, where they claimed 0 attacks. Also this month at least 7 members of ISIS cells were arrested.


On July 7, Bombings struck central Damascus near the Ministry of Tourism and the Four Seasons Hotel, during the visit of Macron the president of France to Syria. Ministry of Interior has attributed the attack to ISIS, the bombing resulted in the killing of one civilian and injury of 36.


On July 8, three attacks happened during the same day and the are believed to have been carried out by ISIS members.

Unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle used machine guns to target an oil truck in Abrahyah town in eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, killing the driver.


Similarly, unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle, attacked a checkpoint of the Internal Security Forces near al-Baserah city bridge.


According to North Press Agency, also on July 8 ISIS

claimed responsibility for the killing of Rashad Khalaf al-Ghurair in the northern countryside of Deir ez-Zor.


On July 15,

unknown gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire on a member of the 72nd Division on the road linking al-Arimah and Manbij in eastern Aleppo countryside, injuring the him.


On July 18,

two unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire directly on member of the Defence Ministry


near al-Awsajli junction in eastern Manbij city.


On July 9,

Syria’s Interior Ministry announced its security forces had dismantled several ISIS cells in southern Syria, arresting a senior leader and several members accused of involvement in assassinations and financing terror.


On July 28,

Syrian Internal Security Forces and the General Intelligence Service in Aleppo announced the arrest of individuals allegedly affiliated with the ISIS, during a security operation in Aleppo and its surrounding countryside.


An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, in an incident that sparked widespread concern among residents.


During July, Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS were repatriated from


Roj Camp, which houses families of ISIS members, and returned to Tunisia. Additionally, Tunisian citizen Bilal Chawachi was sentenced to 55 years in prison after being convicted on terrorism-related charges, specifically traveling to Syria and fighting alongside the extremist organization.


Germany sentenced an Iraqi man to life imprisonment and his former wife to nine years and six months in prison after convicting them of enslaving and torturing two Yazidi girls while they were members of ISIS in Syria and Iraq between 2015 and 2017.


Three U.S. citizens pleaded guilty to terror charges, prosecutors said the defendants communicated through encrypted messaging applications between July and November 2025 and planned to travel to Turkey before crossing into Syria to join ISIS. 


* Due to the low rate of confirmed ISIS attacks RIC has decided to stop publishing monthly sleeper-cell reports and instead share a bi-annual summary of ISIS activity throughout Syria.

author: Unknown
title: Karasu: Democratization is for everyone
content:
KCK Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu discussed developments in Kurdistan, Turkey, and the Middle East during a special program on

Medya Haber

.


Referring to the ongoing “Peace and Democratic Society” process, Karasu noted that the movement had taken the necessary steps, but that the Turkish state was still resisting. He said that a century-old problem such as the Kurdish issue could not be resolved through old laws, an outdated legal framework, or an old political approach.


Reminding that the existing laws had failed to resolve the issue, leading to decades of conflict, Karasu stressed that new laws guaranteeing freedom must be enacted in order to resolve the problem.


This is the first part of the interview.


Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan sent a message to the Peace and Democratic Integration conference held in London. A notable assessment in this message was that if the republic does not become democratic, democratic integration will not be realized either. How should this be understood?


Now, we speak of democratic integration and unification. The unification of two things: the unification of the Kurdish people with the state and with the Turkish people on a democratic basis. And what is this democratic basis? It will be based on the recognition of the fundamental, democratic rights of the Kurdish people. On one hand, it is integration, and on the other, it is democratic. Without democracy, there could be no integration. In this regard, local democracy is an absolute prerequisite. All obstacles facing the Kurds – regarding their language, culture, and identity – must be removed. Democratic integration is, in fact, the democratization of the republic. Contrary to what some claim – that democratic integration can be achieved without recognizing any of the Kurds’ rights, demands, or legal claims – such a thing does not exist. We do not seek this solely for the Kurds. Rêber Apo does not seek it solely for the Kurds either. We cannot demand democracy only for ourselves. To demand democratization is to demand it for everyone. Rêber Apo has made this clear. It is for the Alevis, for women, for workers, and for the environment. It’s not as if integration is just an agreement between the Kurds and the state. All communities will benefit from this. Democratic integration is necessary for all communities. It is necessary for Alevis as well. The Alevis’ freedom of belief and their democratic rights must be recognized. That is what democratic integration is. There is no such thing as a centralized, all-controlling integration – no such integration exists. Integration does not mean accepting the policies that the Turkish state has implemented up until now. That is not what Rêber Apo means by democratic integration. It is an integration for all oppressed ethnic and religious communities. All of them will be part of this democratization.


Democratization is not tied to certain individuals or a particular group. That is not how it should be understood. The democracy and democratization we understand apply to all communities. It is the democratization of the Republic; it is a democratic Turkey. This must be understood exactly this way. Any other interpretations are pure nonsense. There’s no need for demagoguery. This is a nonviolent solution. Because a nonviolent solution is necessary for Turkey, and it is necessary for us as well. It is not a solution involving the establishment of a separate nation-state. We have abandoned that idea. But democratic integration does not mean turning oneself in to the state; it certainly does not mean giving up the Kurds’ fundamental democratic rights. No one should misunderstand this. Nor does integration mean that someone will go somewhere, become a civil servant, or serve as a state official – democracy isn’t like that, and neither is integration. Integration is a contract with society. It is a compromise reached with society. It is the recognition of society’s fundamental rights. At its core, it is the recognition of local democracy. This is true for Turkey, as well as for Rojava and all other parts of Kurdistan.


Democratic integration is not about someone going somewhere, speaking on behalf of others, becoming a civil servant, or assuming government authority – that is not democratic integration. Do the rights of society not recognize democratic foundations? Is there local democracy? That is integration. Integration must be properly understood everywhere – in …

author: Vashti Fox
title: Three years of Palestine solidarity
content:
In mid-October 2023, after the first major march against Israel’s attacks on Gaza, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK, Ben Jamal, said to his staff: “We are probably going to need to be responding to this through marches until potentially Christmas”. He was wrong. The protests did not abate. As Israel’s offensive in Gaza continued, the number of actions across the world multiplied rapidly, eventually blossoming into one of the largest and most sustained antiwar movements in generations. From the world’s largest cities to the smallest hamlets, millions of voices rose in the same chant, with the same cadence: “Free, free Palestine!” 

The numbers tell part of the story. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an international monitor, estimated that, in the three weeks after 7 October, some 3,700 demonstrations calling for a ceasefire and showing solidarity with Palestine took place in almost 100 countries and territories. In the first months of the genocide, most were in the Middle East and North Africa and were especially frequent in Yemen, Iran, Turkey and Morocco. In several of these countries, major government or religious institutions backed the demonstrations. 

In the West, however, governments were overwhelmingly hostile. In France, for instance, pro-Israel demonstrations were legal and encouraged. But the Macron government banned all Palestine solidarity demonstrations on 12 October, Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin determining that they were “likely to generate public disorder”. Nevertheless, on 22 October, 15,000 people took to the streets chanting “Gaza, Paris is with you!”

Two years after 7 October, ACLED provided data to SBS Australia showing 50,122 Gaza-related protests, the overwhelming majority in support of Palestinians—more than 40,000 Palestine solidarity events took place between 7 October 2023 and 5 September 2025. In contrast, just 3,120 pro-Israel demonstrations took place, more than two-thirds of them (2,159) held in Israel. 

What was striking about these actions was not simply their geographic breadth but their regularity. While the movement against the Iraq war in 2003 organised the largest single set of coordinated antiwar demonstrations in history, attracting an estimated 12 to 14 million people on 14 and 15 February, it did not sustain such mass mobilisations. The Palestine solidarity movement, by contrast, mobilised consistently over three years. London, for example, hosted the largest demonstrations in the UK, with 100,000 on 21 October, 70,000 on 28 October, 30,000 on 4 November, and 300,000 on 11 November 2003. Then, in 2024, 400,000 attended a demonstration on 9 March, followed by 200,000 again in March, April and October. 

Israel is a major participant in US-dominated imperial capitalist networks, and governments across the world (of all political colours) have been reluctant to break economically, politically or even symbolically from the Israeli-US coalition. Mass mobilisations, regardless of how mass and how determined they are, are unlikely on their own to force a government to break these relationships, especially in this new era of intensifying imperial competition. The stakes are simply too high. 

Nevertheless, the Palestine demonstrations were important for several reasons. They aimed not just to express moral outrage at Israel’s brutality but also to push their own governments for a change of policy. The demonstrations first demanded (with many local specificities) a ceasefire, and then, the longer the genocide continued, that their own governments break militarily, economically and diplomatically from Israel itself. 

Furthermore, the size and consistency of the demonstrations forced the issue of Gaza into the public debate. Governments responded differently to these protest movements, but most Western countries (with the notable exception of the USA) eventually backed the call for a ceasefire. (Of course, it was too late to stop the murder of tens of thousands of Gazans.). Some European governments, such as Spain and Ireland, moved more significantly in the direction of breaking ties with Israel, while others enacted more symbolic changes such as the recognition of Palestine and increased measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. None of these stances was anywhere near enough, but they likely would not have happened without the protest movement.

While protest movements’ impact on governments matters, the …

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #300 w Emma Hagberg on ‘Comrades, Not Friends’ & The Revolutionary Front : October 8, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. Emma is the author of Comrades, Not Friends: The Revolutionary Front, Antifascism, and Class Struggle (PM Press/Working Class History, 2026), translated by Gabriel Kuhn and with a preface by Tomas Rothaus (both of whom have been previous guests of the show).

According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. Two years later, the organization folded.

See also : Presentation on the book about Revolutionära Fronten (Revolutionary Front) (April 13, 2025).

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Judy Mundey
title: Judy Mundey: ‘Public housing needed as housing crisis deepens’
content:
This is a slightly abridged version of a speech by Judy Mundey, housing campaigner and women's rights activist, to a meeting focused on NSW Labor’s development plan in the Bays West precinct, organised by Better Futures Coalition on September 29.

The Sydney Morning Herald, in May, referred to twin babies born to a mother who lived and gave birth to them in a tent on the banks of the Murrumbidgee River at Wagga Wagga in NSW. One died; the other had to be hospitalised.

A local councillor said the tragedy was a predictable result of systemic failures to address homelessness. He put the problem down to a lack of public housing.

The SMH editorial referred to the surge in people living in cars, tents and caravan parks, describing it as having echoes of the Depression era.

In Sydney, people are sleeping in the St James railway station tunnel, parks and other forms of less than salubrious accommodation.

Then there is the scourge of domestic violence and the desperate need for safe housing for the victim-survivors. For many women it is a choice between living with domestic violence or homelessness. The refuge system is unable to cope and thousands are on the waiting list for public housing.

Renting in the private property market also presents problems.

A recent estimate said that, nationwide, more than 1.25 million low-income households are in financial stress. Even where people can find rental accommodation, it is often less than stable.

A new report from Adelaide University said children who grow up in rental housing move every 2.3 years, on average, and that by the age of 14 a child in private rental had moved an average of six times, with some as often as 10 times.

Such frequent moves can incur or inflict other disadvantages, such as changing schools and the loss of friendship, sporting and social relationships.

We are not only in the midst of a housing crisis, we are experiencing a systemic failure to address it.

There is no shortage of promises meant to rectify the problem. Recently, NSW Labor announced some 9,400 homes would be built in the Woolahra/Edgecliff area, with towers of 32 and 34 stories. Almost all such proposals involve the private sector and that has not always gone well.

People will recall the examples of developer-built projects with serious defects, such as Opal Towers in 2018 and Mascot Towers in 2019, with some homes remaining uninhabitable.

Peoples’ lives have been ruined. They save and borrow, only to find they cannot not live in their new home but there is no financial recovery. At that time, developers were able to employ private certifiers.

The explosion of defect-riddled apartment project failures with their multi-million dollar repair bills prompted the NSW government to appoint NSW’s first Building Commissioner in 2019.

But then came the collapse of Dyldam disaster in 2020, one of NSW’s biggest apartment builders, with debts of half a billion dollars. The NSW building regulator identified serious defects in a 230 apartment development in Baulkham Hills, including defects so serious as to be labelled a threat to human life. That development is still undergoing repair work.

There are almost daily reports about the impact of these dodgy developers.

The latest dodgy developer in the spotlight is Bathla. It has collapsed, owing debts of $3.3 billion. Many buyers have been left in the lurch, losing large sums paid as deposits.

Bathla’s work was not only riddled with defects, it also engaged in unsafe work practices. It was fined $135,000 in 2018 over a serious injury on a project at Doonside and was slapped with more than 300 notices by Safe Work NSW relating to safety issues.

Thousands of partially-built properties have been left unfinished.

These collapses has inevitably had a devastating effect on those further down the supply chain — suppliers, sub contractors and employees are owed, as are those who paid deposits.

Bathla’s collapse is also a disaster for the national housing supply, as there are 14,000 apartments stalled.

The NSW target for new housing is already running well behind target.

The Chris Minns Labor government pledged to build 378,000 homes by mid 2029. This requires 22,000 homes to be delivered each year until mid 2029. There appears to be a massive disparity between the government’s promises and its actual delivery.

Notwithstanding these dodgy developer disasters, Labor seems wedded to private development.

But there is an alternative — public housing …

author: Editors
title: The world since 7 October
content:
Gaza is a generational touchstone and the key dividing line of politics in the West. It has laid bare the lies of the society we live in. It has exposed the genocidal bloodlust of the political right. And it has tested official “progressive” liberal politics, which has so often shown itself to be utterly hollow or cowardly. 

Anyone can now use Google Maps’ satellite view to see for themselves the apocalypse wrought by Israel and its allies over the past three years. Gaza City, once home to around 700,000 people, is a mostly bombed-out hellscape of ruins. The same is true of Beit Hanoun, Jabalia and other major centres. 

Rafah was a city thousands of years old, first recorded in an inscription from 1303 BCE. It has now been wiped off the face of the earth. Google still displays location markers for what once existed: “Kamal Adwan School”, “Playground”, “Musab bin Amir Western Mosque”, now a pile of rubble—“temporarily closed”, according to Google.

About 80 percent of structures in the Gaza Strip have been damaged; two-thirds of those are destroyed, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees. Israel has used the so-called ceasefire since last December to systematically demolish remaining structures in the 60 percent of the Strip occupied by its forces, while killing another 1,200 Palestinians and herding around 2 million into unliveable tent cities in an ever-shrinking concentration camp.

When millions around the world poured into the streets to take a stand against this barbarism, they were viciously attacked and slandered by the institutions of our “democracy”, which have cried about “social cohesion” while turning a blind eye to the genocide and the growth of fascism they are helping to stoke.

The ruling class and the political establishment want to go after not just the Palestine movement, but the left more generally, which has naturally been at the centre of that movement. Hence the persistent effort to define antisemitism as a problem of the left rather than the far right, to ban the word “genocide”, and to criminalise opposition to the state carrying it out. 

This is not because loyalty to Israel itself is so important to the establishment, but because this loyalty test is a proxy for loyalty to Australian capitalism; a test of subservience to Australian billionaires, bosses and bureaucrats. 

Will you keep your mouth shut? Will you force that student to remove their keffiyeh? Will you cancel that author? Will you censor that article? Your answer will determine your place in Australian society. With troublemakers pilloried and purged, the apparatus can be hardened, ready to oversee the next war, the next genocide, the next round of cutbacks and layoffs, the next racist campaign against immigrants and refugees, as capitalism lurches towards its next crisis.

Despite the establishment’s intimidation and slander, and partly because of it, a seismic shift in attitudes has occurred. A July Pew Research poll found that 79 percent of Australians have a negative view of Israel, and just 4 percent have a strongly positive view. Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets. The movement globally has been big, defiant, and defining for so many people who have thrown themselves into it. 

Yet it has not produced a widespread radicalisation or a sizable new left committed to confronting and overthrowing the capitalist system more broadly. There are many reasons for this, from the relative weakness of far-left organisations going into this period, to the weakness of the workers’ movement and spinelessness of trade union leaders.

The depth of feeling and moral commitment to the cause of Palestinian liberation is palpable, but the general political level remains low. Instead of generalising from the atrocity in Gaza to develop a critique of capitalism and imperialism, there is an obsession with the pro-Israel lobby, and there are illusions in reactionary opponents of the US and Israel such as the Iranian regime. Instead of open debate about the best strategies and tactics of resistance, recriminations focus on who is qualified to lead campaigns against the Australian government—not based on ideas or organisational skills, but on individuals’ identities. 

While our side sustained the largest anti-war movement in Australian history, the far right, rather than the left, has emerged as the most organised political force and is making all the running to push society in its desired direction: more …

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #299 w Leena van Deventer on GamerGate & the grievance economy : October 1, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Leena van Deventer [Bluesky]. Leena is a game developer, writer and researcher. Among her current interests is the concept of:

Hetconning (n.) — the deliberate retroactive straight-washing of history. Hetconned, the project, maps how the contemporary far-right market different post-truth fantasies to recruit and radicalise people into fighting for the Christo-nationalist project.

author: Justice Not Jails
title: Stop the closure of Aboriginal community-controlled YiSSA housing
content:
Residents and the wider community are organising to stop the Northern Territory Country Liberal Party (CLP) government’s decision to close the Yilli Short Stay Accommodation (YiSSA) in Garramilla/Darwin.

YiSSA is an Aboriginal community-controlled facility that provides low-cost short-stay accommodation. It is used by people undergoing renal dialysis, families escaping domestic violence, homeless residents and people and families visiting Garramilla to access essential services.

When the CLP government’s announced YiSSA’s closure in July, 230 residents were reportedly living there, including 85 children. A further 300 people were on the waiting list.

YiSSA is owned by a private company, Ausco, while the land is owned by the NT government. The CLP government offered $3 million to buy YiSSA, but Ausco rejected the offer as too low. The federal government then announced it would contribute $3.5 million to assist the NT government in keeping YiSSA open.

The CLP government refused to purchase YiSSA. Instead, it has decided to evict residents and relocate them to Batchelor, more than 100 kilometres from Garramilla.

YiSSA’s proposed relocation to Batchelor will disconnect residents from public transport, services, employment opportunities and support networks, as well as schools for children who have been living at YiSSA. It will restrict people’s ability to access essential healthcare, as they will be outside the Danila Dilba catchment area, and there is no public transport between Batchelor and Garramilla.

The NT already has the highest rate of homelessness, sitting at nearly 12 times the national average.

The CLP government’s decision to evict YiSSA residents will make this worse. It will also put hundreds of vulnerable people needing to access renal treatment and schooling in a highly precarious position.

YiSSA residents are urging the CLP government to stop the eviction. The government’s decision has also sparked deep concerns from Aboriginal service providers and NT legal organisations.

Amid the controversy over the CLP government’s eviction of YiSSA residents, and in the final days leading up to the eviction, the NT government is hosting the Australian Homelessness Conference in Garramilla.

Justice Not Jails has organised a demonstration on October 7, outside the conference, calling on attendees to pass a motion urging the CLP and the federal governments to reverse the decision.

[Sign the petition to stop the closure of YiSSA housing here. Attend the community demonstration at 8am, October 7, outside the Darwin Convention Centre.]

author: Nick Everett
title: How the media sold the Gaza genocide
content:
When 700,000 Rohingya were forced to flee Myanmar for Bangladesh amid widespread killings, sexual violence and village burnings in late 2017, an

Age

editorial pleaded for Australian government action: 

“There is a genocide happening today in Myanmar. Our government should urgently, repeatedly and loudly call for international intervention, and lead in imposing sanctions. We should send bountiful aid to the victims, and halt economic and diplomatic relations with Myanmar unless and until the savagery is stopped. All of us, as Australians, should shun travel to Myanmar for tourism or business. And our government should, as it did with the Syrian refugee crisis a few years ago, rapidly engineer an intake of Rohingya refugees.”

The

Age

 didn’t wait for an International Court of Justice ruling before issuing its dire warning. It repeatedly used the term “genocide” to describe the Myanmar state’s atrocities despite no case of genocide having been brought before the ICJ at the time (it wasn’t until late 2019 that Gambia brought such a case and the ICJ still hasn’t ruled on it).

After three years of Israeli genocide in Gaza, no similar editorial can be found in the

Age

, nor in any of the mainstream media in Australia. That is despite Israel having killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including over 21,280 children who,

according to

 a UN Commission of inquiry, have been targeted as “part of a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza”. 

Indeed, “genocide” is a term that journalists—at the behest of their editors—routinely shun, despite the ICJ’s preliminary ruling back in January 2024 that there is a plausible case Israel is committing genocide. And when the term is used, we are reminded that Israel denies such claims, despite the UN Human Rights Council, the International Association of Genocide Scholars and numerous international human rights organisations having all concluded that Israel is indeed committing genocide in Gaza.

It is not just that the media fail to acknowledge this simple fact. For the past three years, they have been accessories to Israel’s crimes: dehumanising Palestinians, sanitising Israel’s atrocities, and silencing its critics. 

In his groundbreaking book

How to Sell a Genocide

, author Adam Johnson sets out to “prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the genocide in Gaza was enabled, facilitated, and cheered by establishment US media providing cover for months of a nihilistic campaign of starvation, bombing, arbitrary detention, shooting and sexual violence”.  

Johnson’s approach is methodical and meticulous. His research draws on more than 12,000 articles and 5,000 TV clips from nine major outlets during the first year of the genocide, including the

New York Times,

 the

Washington Post,

CNN


and


MSNBC


(now MSNOW

)

. He focuses on the liberal media because “there was a Democratic president in office when the genocide began in earnest, and support from Democrats in Congress and in the think-tank and media world was dispositive [decisive] in continuing said genocide during the given time of my study”.

Johnson argues that the “centre-left” (i.e., liberal) media engaged in “an elaborate framework of excuse-making, deflection, faux-savvy realpolitik, orientalist tropes, and glaring double standards … to justify the White House’s lockstep support for producing carnage everyone could easily witness across their social media timeline on a daily basis”.

“The primary role of [US liberal] media”, he argues, “was to rationalise, negotiate, obscure and ultimately, deny the most inconvenient of truths: a genocide carried out, defended and authorised by elite liberals and liberal institutions”.

Johnson demonstrates how the media were willing accomplices to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to portray 7 October as Israel’s “9/11 moment”, and to equate Hamas violence with that of ISIS, despite the two Islamist groups being implacable enemies. They did so by repeating and perpetuating a series of lies that emanated from Israeli media spokespeople: that Hamas beheaded 40 babies on 7 October 2023, that they targeted children and that they systematically used rape as a weapon of war.

Johnson cites evidence that the first claim was repeated, “without evidence of skepticism”, by more than a dozen journalists from outlets such as CNN, the

New York Post

, CBS, Reuters, Sky News, MSNBC and NBC in the days following 7 October. The claim first …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Pacific Islands tell Australia not to cop out on cutting emissions
content:
Vanuatu’s climate minister Ralph Regenvanu has been sounding the alarm over climate change. As the four-day pre-COP31 meetings get underway in Fiji, he continues to argue countries need to take “urgent action” to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Regenvanu points to the United Nations Environment Program report, which, in September, found that the world is set to cross the Paris Agreement threshold in the next few years, with a best-case scenario peak temperature of 1.8°C (others suggest 2°C). The report said the impact of climate change will be increasingly dangerous, but that it is still possible to bring temperatures down to the agreed global goals.

Regenvanu also pointed to the International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) advisory opinion that countries have a responsibility to achieve the goal of limiting climate warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, but that those responsibilities extend beyond domestic emissions.

He said if emissions are not rapidly reduced within the next four years, any overshoot of 1.5°C, “even a fraction of a degree”, is not an abstract problem for Pacific nations; it will mean reefs, freshwater and land are destroyed.

Regenvanu said Australia’s argument that it is only responsible for cutting the greenhouse gases it emits within its borders is untenable. He said the ICJ’s advisory opinion specified the 1994 United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was not the only climate change framework countries must abide by.

The UNFCCC was agreed to when there was less understanding about the devastating impact of climate change. It aimed to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations “at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic (human-induced) interference with the climate system”. It said that level needed to be “achieved within a time-frame sufficient to allow ecosystems to adapt naturally to climate change, to ensure that food production is not threatened, and to enable economic development to proceed in a sustainable manner”.

Importantly, it put the onus on developed countries to lead the way.

The goal of the Paris Agreement, adopted by 195 parties in Paris in 2015, is “to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels”.

Australia is jointly hosting COP31 with Türkiye in November, and this week is hosting a pre-COP meeting in Fiji.

The Coalition, predictably, says it is a waste of money. One Nation wants Australia to adopt Donald Trump’s policy and immediately withdraw from COP.

Chris Bowen, energy minister and chief negotiator for COP31, has moved to allay fossil fuel corporations’ concerns, telling The Australian in June that he will not be using his role to push for a phase-out of coal or gas exports.

More telling about Labor’s position on COP, however, are its actions; it has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since it formed government in 2022 on a mandate to stop dangerous climate change. The Coalition then, and now, was talking up expanding fossil fuels and uranium mining and exports.

Labor is using its “middle power” status at the pre-COP meeting in Fiji to push Pacific Island states to accept what it puts on the table.

Bowen and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese say they are listening to Pacific Island nations’ concerns about climate change being the real security threat. But Australia is using a loophole in the Paris Agreement that allows countries not to count downstream, or exported, emissions from fossil fuels it mines for export.

This allows major fossil fuel exporters, such as Australia, to pretend to be on track with their climate goals. Australia is content to exploit this loophole to allow publicly subsidised corporations to expand their exports of coal and gas. Australia is one of the world’s largest exporters of liquefied natural gas.

Australia’s 2035 climate targets may look reasonable on paper, but they are fake; they downplay the country’s actual contribution.

This is why Regenvanu is right to point to the ICJ’s — unfortunately non-binding — advisory opinion. It said that all states have obligations to “act” to stop significant hardship to the climate or environment. In other words, preventing climate harm is the duty of all countries, but particularly those of the Global North.

Pacific Islands nations have, for decades, been saying they must not be made a sacrifice zone.

But just like Australia’s aid program has for years been tied to its sub-imperial objectives in the region, so too is its …

author: Emily Lassam
title: French high school students on the march
content:
“I like this kinda thing because it’s revolutionary”, a 16-year-old high school student told me as we stood out the front of her school in Nice at 7am on the last Wednesday in September. As we talked, students started arriving from across the city to join the blockade of the school, the Lycée Parc Imperial, the largest in the area.

Hundreds of students trickled in, and suddenly it was hard to tell where the sea of high schoolers started and ended. Some carried things to help build the barricades to stop anyone from entering the school.

I asked the 16-year-old if she knew all the students or whether they were from other schools. She pointed out a group of high schoolers who must have travelled from another school and said: “I don’t know them, but we are all comrades”.

This wasn’t the first blockade she had been part of at this school, but she said it was different to previous blockades. This time, it isn’t just one school but more than 1,000 being blockaded.

Videos and photos of French students holding Palestinian and Algerian flags, calling for revolution, chanting against the far-right National Rally and fighting against intense repression are sweeping social media.

This comes at a moment when a growing wave of student protests and revolts is sweeping across the world. Last year, there were the Gen Z revolts that were led by students and swept across Nepal, Indonesia, Madagascar and a whole series of countries in the Global South.

In July, hundreds of thousands of students in India joined huge protests and forced the education minister to resign. At the end of August, tens of thousands of students in Germany struck from school to protest the introduction of forced military conscription. Across Chile in early October, thousands of students and teachers took to the streets to protest possible education cuts. And in Australia, high schoolers have been at the forefront of the fight against Pauline Hanson, organising two successful school walkouts in opposition to her.  

French students are protesting the terrible conditions in their schools, for both students and teachers. Schools are forced to deal with inadequate funding, large class sizes, decrepit facilities and low staff pay and morale. To make matters worse, further cuts are planned in the upcoming national budget. And it’s not just schools facing cuts.

President Emmanuel Macron has announced the budget will include £54 billion in cuts and a fourth wage freeze for the public sector. On 29 September, thousands of public sector workers went on strike in anticipation of these cuts, with many strikers visiting high schools to show their solidarity with students. Teachers are also planning to strike on 6 October.

Students at Parc Imperial said their school was far from the worst, but even here the conditions are terrible. Class sizes often exceed 35 students, and the classrooms meant to accommodate them are too small and have limited, if any, heating and cooling. Temperatures can reach 40 degrees inside in summer and are freezing in winter. During the day, they said, students often do nothing for long periods because there aren’t relief teachers to cover absent teachers, often because the conditions are so bad. Students are also angry about the competitive Parcoursup system that pits them against each other to get into university.

While students and teachers struggle to manage in these conditions, the head of Parc Imperial lives on campus in luxury with his own gym and “wine cave”. Bad as this is, the main enemy, the high schoolers said, is the government. Macron puts billions into the military and police but refuses to adequately fund schools.

The cops’ crackdown on the high schoolers has been severe. The 16-year-old Imperial Parc student showed me the gauze, disinfectant and cream she had brought in her bag in case any students were injured. She hadn’t expected to use it, but ended up caring for a number of people whom the cops had tear-gassed and injured. She said she had been “naive to think the police would do nothing because we are minors. I am 16, most people are 17, 15, 14 we are very very young”. Across the country, police have injured hundreds and arrested thousands of high schoolers.

One of the first schools to start the blockade movement was Paul Éluard in Saint Denis (north of Paris). Saint Denis is a poor and migrant area that has been particularly neglected by the Macron government. Students report that the food there is inedible, rats and …

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Lizzie O’Shea: ‘Surveillance technology is a threat to democracy’
content:
Lizzie O’Shea, a writer, lawyer and founder of Digital Rights Watch, told the New South Wales Council for Civil Liberties’ (NSWCCL) annual fundraising dinner and journalism awards on October 1 that rapidly developing surveillance technology is throwing up many challenges.

Digital technology and democracy are in a “significant amount of tension”, O’Shea said. She added that defending civil liberties is not about “clever people working to impose civil liberties on everybody else”, but that campaigners “have to convince a critical mass that they have to defend their own rights”.

Referencing the origins of professional policing in London in the late 18th century, she described it as “a period of immense technological disruption”, as the Industrial Revolution was reshaping society.

The new police force, O’Shea said, was used to “monitor, enforce and impose the new conditions of social order”. Specifically, it ensured merchants’ profits and prevented dockworkers from supplementing their wages by pilfering stock. The idea was to get the state and industry to collaborate, with a “form of surveillance of everyday people”.

“Policing was talked about as a new science in the detection and prevention of crime,” she said. The spectacle of force “offered an economical and effective way of maintaining order”.

O’Shea said it helps explain the state’s decisions in the digital age. “Like their historical counterparts, modern police understand the power of surveillance in enforcing a form of discipline.

“‘Safety’ is about preserving social order, rather than reducing harm. By allowing law enforcement and intelligence agencies to tell us what is safe, we allow them to use technology in increasingly oppressive ways.

“Rapid technological advances have been accompanied by disruptive transformations in social relations, and an acceleration of policing has often been a response.”

O’Shea described advances in technology in the 21st century as being “a fundamental threat” to democracy. She said more than 100 “security” bills have been passed over the past two decades, connected to surveillance, national intelligence agencies and law enforcement, and 875 new offences have been created.

Many have sought to repurpose existing systems of corporate surveillance for state surveillance, while surveillance technology companies receive lucrative government contracts.

O’Shea also said Labor has “effectively abandoned” regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and facial recognition technology.

“Less than 10% of Australians think it’s reasonable for a retailer to ask for your biometric information to access their services, but on an almost daily basis they will experience this.

“Everyone is telling us that AI is fundamentally important — politicians, the financial markets, a media that takes industry sources as truth — but a study by the University of Melbourne found that Australians are among the least optimistic in the world about artificial intelligence.

“More people are concerned about the negative outcomes than the benefits … 87% would be more inclined to trust and use AI products if international standards were in place to protect them.”

O’Shea pointed to the campaign to remove Palantir from Coles stores and the defeat of a data centre proposal in Lane Cove as examples of where most people’s attitudes lie.

“The hand of power is seeking to crush us, but we have the capacity to land a counterpunch,” she said. “This is the time for organisers, agitators, lawyers, ratbags and policy nerds to work together to build an alternative future where civil liberties are protected and our democracy can flourish.”

NSWCCL president Timothy Roberts told the gathering that the NSWCCL aimed to be an “ever-watchful guardian” of civil liberties, noting the huge challenges. He referenced last year’s March for Humanity, across the Sydney Harbour Bridge, when 300,000 people marched to protest Israel’s genocide in Gaza and demand that Labor act.

“It felt like the flame of liberty could not burn brighter or stronger — we must continue to celebrate that occasion as an example of the collective exercise of our human rights,” Roberts said.

The NSWCCL’s journalism awards went to Guardian journalists Ariel Bogle and Nino Bucci for uncovering the use of “less-lethal” weapons by police. Star Observer journalist Jacques Nieuwoudt won the young journalist award for his coverage of police raids of LGBTIQ spaces on Oxford Street.

title: Balık tutmak için denize açılmıştı: Maden işçisi İlker Mızrap kayboldu
content:
Bartın — Bartın'ın Amasra ilçesinde balık tutmak için 4,5 metre uzunluğundaki teknesiyle denize açılan maden işçisi İlker Mızrap'tan (35) haber alınamıyor. Sahil Güvenlik Komutanlığı ekipleri, Mızrap için denizde arama çalışması başlattı.

Büyük Liman'dan dün saat 16.00 sıralarında teknesiyle denize açılan İlker Mızrap, geri dönmedi. Dün saat 19.00 sıralarında eşine ‘Balık tuttum, geliyorum’ mesajı atan Mızrap'a ulaşılamadı.

Ailesinin 112 Acil Çağrı Merkezi'ne yaptığı ihbar üzerine Batı Karadeniz Sahil Güvenlik Grup Komutanlığı ekipleri ve balıkçılar tarafından denizde arama çalışması başlatıldı.

Arama çalışmaları denizde 3-4 mil açıkta devam ederken, Mızrap’ın ailesinin endişeli bekleyişi sürüyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Soraya Kishtwari
title: Home Secretary Defends Palestine Action Ban by Invoking ‘Skinheads’
content:
Shabana Mahmood has defended the government’s ban on Palestine Action by saying its supporters should face the same law as “skinheads” who back a neo-Nazi organisation.


Speaking on

the Rest Is Politics podcast,

 the home secretary was asked about the thousands of people arrested for publicly supporting Palestine Action. 


Mahmood, who was previously a vocal supporter of the Palestinian cause, said that while she was “very uncomfortable” seeing people she knew “falling foul” of the law, it had to be applied consistently.


“When you get a group of skinheads standing outside a mosque, holding up a placard saying ‘I support National Action’, I’m going to want the Section 13 support offence to be applied,” she said.


“And I’m going to want the police to go and arrest those people… And I’m going to want them to degrade the capacity of a white supremacist terror organisation to recruit more members.”


National Action is a neo-Nazi organisation which was proscribed under the Terrorism Act in 2016.


Palestine Action was proscribed by former home secretary Yvette Cooper in July 2025, making it a criminal offence to belong to or express support for the group.


“You have to do these jobs in a consistent way that stands the test of time,” Mahmood said. “I’m not going to reopen every decision every previous home secretary has made. Was it lawful? Yes it was. Does it meet the legal test? Yes it does.”


She added that a decision to repeal the ban would involve having “to literally relitigate everything”.


Asked what triggered the government’s decision to outlaw the group, she said: “It’s proscribed because it’s met the test for proscription within the Terrorism Act,” and that “the facts of their behaviour and the escalatory effect of their behaviour” were contributing factors.


Critics of the ban, however, argue that the central question is not whether Section 13 should be applied consistently, but whether Palestine Action should have been placed under terrorism legislation in the first place – and whether expressing support for the group should constitute a terrorism offence.


A spokesperson for campaign group Defend Our Juries accused Mahmood of “missing the point entirely”, saying she had provided “no evidence that Palestine Action should have been proscribed in the first place”.


The

Morning Star quoted the spokesperson

 as saying: “The fact that elderly and disabled people are being arrested as terrorists for holding signs should be no less shocking.” 


Defend Our Juries has organised multiple protests against the ban on Palestine Action, resulting in mass arrests, most recently at the

Labour Party conference in Liverpool

.


Mahmood’s comments strike a different tone to that of foreign secretary Ed Miliband who told delegates in Liverpool that Britons were

“right” to be outraged by the plight of Palestinians

.


In June, the court of appeal upheld the government’s decision to proscribe Palestine Action, overturning an earlier high court ruling that found the ban unlawful. This was followed by a

supreme court ruling in July

 allowing Palestine Action founder Huda Ammori to appeal the ban. The hearing is expected this autumn.

title: Ein Flüchtlingsbekämpfungs-Deal nach dem anderen: Deutschland und die EU und ihre »Migrationspartnerschaften«

author: Erica Malatesta
title: New Stormy Petrel Now Out!
content:
This is the 8th edition of our theoretical magazine in which we discuss issues in more depth. Articles include:


Dossier on AI, Work in the Future Society, Age Verification, the General Strike, Mujeres Libres, and a letter from a reader on veganism.


Editorial


Now and tomorrow


Now: Hope in Every Heart or Business as Usual?


Andy Burnham’s accession to power doesn’t mark any radical change in the direction of the Labour Party. He backs the Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s immigration reforms, increasing the wait for indefinite leave to remain from five years to between 10 and 20 years. He supports expanding the use of detention centres. He wrote recently in

The Times

 that “Increasing our national security, in every sense, will be my first priority,” and that arms manufacture would be central in “regenerating and reindustrialising the country.” He threatened that he would “not be squeamish about cutting welfare” to invest more in the arms industry.


He intends to proceed with the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats and with the building of Trident nuclear submarines. He urged EU countries to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles. He signed a military AI deal with Ukraine, accessing Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs database. This huge AI database holds data collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the war zone in Ukraine. They capture footage of millions of objects and the data is then fed back to the Avengers Lab to train new AI models. This will be used to protect military bases from “protesters and hostile actors trying to gain intelligence.” The Burnham administration also will work with Ukraine to explore the development of next-generation low-power AI chips to power drones and robotics.


Burnham appointed Kanishka Narayan as the first AI minister, signalling Labour support for AI, whilst coming out with rhetoric about independence from US Big Tech.


He continues to back Israel and its genocidal policies. Whilst we have experienced the hottest summer on record, Burnham talks about new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea, exhibiting a complete unconcern about the connection between fossil fuel and climate change. He talks about a “business-friendly socialism”, as if such an obscene coupling was either possible or desirable.


The Future Society


“A map of the world that does not include Utopia, is not even worth glancing at, for it leaves out the one country at which Humanity is always landing… Progress is the realisation of utopias.”


Oscar Wilde


The theme of this issue is ‘The Future Society’. This came about because of our experience of people asking questions about what an anarchist communist society will be like, such as ‘How will it be possible?’, ‘What about crime?’, ‘What about jobs that no one wants to do?’ When many Marxists, and others, envisage a future society it usually involves automation and advanced technology, including AI. While we reject ‘anarcho-primitivism’ (see Issue 7 of Stormy Petrel), we take a critical approach to technology, especially AI. We need to ensure that it will actually enhance our lives as well as be compatible with environmental and resource concerns.


In order to address some of the questions about an anarchist communist society, in each topic we first address the reasons why the status quo is a disaster, both for the working class and the planet. We then also look at the struggles going on today. The attacks on workers’ organisation, surveillance, the insidious insertion of AI into all areas of life, the environmental effects of resource plundering, war, and the drive for growth at any cost, not only have tragic consequences today, but will make it harder for us to create the future we want. We will only be able to collectively create an anarchist communist future if we overthrow capitalism and begin to establish a vision and the foundations for this society.


We have to envision a different future. There has been an ideological onslaught over the past few decades with the capitalist slogan of ‘There Is No Alternative’ advanced over and over again. Any idea of an alternative future is mocked and laughed at. The 19
