author: ACG
title: When history accelerates: Maricarmen’s eviction
content:
We publish below the statement from the Spanish group Liza on the Maricarmen mobilisation and the need for revolutionary organisation.


Context: On Saturday, September 26, thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction of 87-year-old disabled  Maricarmen Abascal from her home. Her door was broken down by local riot police, and she was evicted on a stretcher despite the resistance of a cordon of protesters. Maricarmen, who had lived in her apartment for 70 years, instantly became a symbol of the housing crisis plaguing Spain, particularly in major cities. Whose fault is it? Rampant gentrification, in which real estate developers systematically buy up buildings in city centres, taking the opportunity to “revise” rents. Maricarmen’s rent, which was around 500 euros per month, was increased by 275% to 2,750 euros! Anger swept across Spain, withtens of thousands mobilised and fifty demonstrations,, particularly in Madrid, where the demonstrations, claimed as involving as high as 500,000, culminated in an impromptu encampment at Puerta del Sol, reminiscent of the 2011 protests that sparked the Indignados movement. This time, a few nights of occupation were enough for the real estate company that had evicted Maricarmen to reverse its decision, release her from the hospital, and reinstate her in her apartment, cancelling the rent increase it had planned to impose. While applauding this outcome, the Puerta del Sol “campers” are maintaining the pressure, as numerous other evictions are taking place daily across Spain. They are demanding that the “socialist” government enact a new, more protective law to curb rising purchase and rental prices.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez promised once more to introduce a new bill to regulate rent levels.  However, this was blocked by the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox and the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat). Sánchez has now called a snap election.


On the political climate and the need for revolutionary organisation


“Revolutions have their own rhythm, punctuated by accelerations and decelerations. They also have their own geometry, in which the straight line breaks at the bifurcations and sharp turns of history.” Daniel Bensaid,

Politics as a Strategic Art


There is a fundamental difference between chronological time and political time. The former unfolds in a seemingly uniform manner: days follow days, and development is linear. The latter, however, under the dialectical logic of a contradictory reality, is very different: There are historical periods in which months or even years seem to contain very few substantial transformations, while there are moments in which, in a matter of days, political reality can be radically transformed.


This means that political time cannot be understood simply as the succession of events on the calendar. It is, above all, the pace at which the relationships between social forces, institutions, organisations, and the possibilities for political action change. There are specific events that, based on the accumulation of internal contradictions, appear as turning points, making possible, in qualitative terms, what until recently was unthinkable.


A society can remain seemingly stable for years and yet be accumulating contradictions. These contradictions don’t necessarily manifest themselves immediately. They can remain separate, partially invisible, or even appear unconnected. An economic crisis, a labour dispute, a housing crisis, a particular police action, a popular mobilisation, or an institutional crisis may seem, individually, like isolated phenomena. However, they can establish connections between them: each event modifies the conditions under which the next ones occur, and each new conflict can amplify, accelerate, or transform the previous ones. It is at this point that the acceleration of political time appears, the concrete expression of latent contradictions.


It is not that an isolated event creates a revolutionary situation out of thin air. Rather, it happens that a prior accumulation of contradictions finds certain events capable of condensing them and making them politically visible. The event then acts as a catalyst for processes that were already developing in society.


“Men make their own history, but they do not make it as they please; they do not make it under self-chosen circumstances, but under circumstances directly encountered, given and …

author: Sebastian Lotzer
title: City Of Blood [Part l]
content:
Mein Gespräch, meine Lieder


Mein Hass und mein Glück


Mein Tag, meine Nacht, mein Vor, mein Zurück


Meine Sonne und Schatten, Zweifel, die ich hab


An dir und in mir bis zum letzten Tag


Deine Straßen, wo ich fliehe, stolper und fall


Deine Wärme, die ich brauch, die ich spüre überall


Klaus Hoffmann – Berlin


„Das Gedächtnis der Menschheit für erduldete Leiden ist erstaunlich kurz. Ihre Vorstellungskraft für kommende Leiden ist fast noch geringer.“


Bertolt Brecht


2004 verkaufte der Berliner Senat in einer SPD-PDS Regierung 65.000 Wohnungen der städtischen Wohnungsgesellschaft GSW zum Schnäppchenpreis von 400 Mio Euro an private Spekulanten, der Wohnungsbestand ging 2011 schließlich an die Deutsche Wohnen über, die mittlerweile in einer Fusion mit Vonovia zum größten börsenorientierte Wohnungsunternehmen in Deutschland wurde. 2019 werden 6000 Wohnungen, also rund 10 Prozent der 2004 verkauften Wohnungen, für 920 Mio Euro vom ‘rot-rot-grünen’ Senat unter Federführung der PdL Stadtentwicklungssenatorin zurückgekauft. 2021 werden dann für knapp 2,5 Milliarden Euro an die 15.000 weitere Wohnungen mit Schwerpunkt Kreuzberg von Deutsche Wohnen/Vonovia zurückgekauft. Seitdem dürfen sich die Mieter in den Hochhäusern rund um das Kottbusser Tor über steigende Mieten und explodierende Nebenkosten freuen, die alles weit in den Schatten stellen, was die Profitmaximierungsexperten der Deutsche Wohnen zu verantworten hatten.


Sämtliche im Zuge der Kahlschlagsanierung Ende der 70er entstandenen ‘Neubausiedlungen’ rund um das Kottbusser Tor weisen einen extremen Sanierungsstau auf, ständig fallen wichtige Infrastruktur wie Fahrstühle aus, behinderte Mieter, die auf Rollstühle angewiesen sind, sitzen teilweise monatelang in ihren Wohnungen fest. Wie sich die städtische Wohnungsbaugesellschaft HOWOGE, die jetzt auch in Kreuzberg besitzt, eine “Mieterfreudliche Sanierung” vorstellt, exekutierte sie jüngst in Reinickendorf, wo 170 Mieter mit einer Vorlauffrist von nur 6 Monaten darüber informiert wurden, dass ihre Wohnanlage komplett saniert werde und sie Umsetzwohnungen verteilt über das gesamte Stadtgebiet erhalten sollen, was gegen jede Rechtsprechung auf eine ‘Wohnortnahe Umsetzung’ verstößt.


Während börsenorientierte Unternehmen wie die ‘Deutsche Wohnen’ aufgrund von medialen Meltdowns gezwungen waren, besonders skandalöse Zustände in ihren Wohnungsanlagen abzustellen, glänzt die HOWOGE seit Jahren mit der weitgehenden Verweigerung der direkten Kommunikation mit ihren Mietern und dem Aussitzen von Problemen. Bezeichnenderweise wechselte der operative Leiter des Vorstandes der HOWOGE im Frühjahr dieses Jahres zu genau dem technischen Dienstleister, der in den letzten Jahren zahlreiche Aufträge der diversen ausgegliederten HOWOGE-Tochtergesellschaften erhalten hatte. Eigentlich können die betroffenen Berliner Mieter im Nachhinein wahrscheinlich froh darüber sein, dass sich der “Sieg” des ‚Volksentscheids Deutsche Wohnen und Co enteignen’ bisher im typischen Berliner Wohnungssumpf verloren hat. Denn nun kommt ja der “Vergesellschaftungshammer” der PdL.


Verkauf dich nicht


Berlin


Jung bist du nicht


Du alterst so schnell


Buckelst zu sehr


Trägst an den Geldern der Freier so schwer


Die werden gehn


Dich sterben sehn


Berlin


Geliebte Berlin


Klaus Hoffmann


“Ein Drittel Heizöl, zwei Drittel Benzin” sangen Slime einst, in Berlin bauen die Punks jetzt Molotows mit Urin und rufen dann dazu auf, nicht zu einer laufenden Räumung zu kommen, weil das den Standort der ‘angemeldeten Mahnwache’ gefährden würde. Der ‘Wohnungskampf’ in der geschichtsträchtigen Hausbesetzer-Hochburg Berlin ist auf den Hund gekommen, während der TikTok Wahlerfolg PdL auf dem harten Boden der staatstragenden Realität aufgeschlagen ist. Erste Bauern werden geopfert, die Nahost Frage wird erneut in Neukölln entschieden und zur der Demo von DGB und anderen Verbänden gegen den Generalangriff von BlackRock Merz auf die Überreste der “sozialen Marktwirtschaft” kommen gerade mal ein paar tausend Leute, darunter die wichtigsten Repräsentanten der aus dem geschichtlichen Mausoleum auferstandenen K-Gruppen. Es scheint, als habe Disney das Playbook für seine neueste dystopische Serie direkt an den künftigen ‘rot-rot-grünen’ Senat weiterverkauft. Während draußen alles in Kleinstaaten zerfällt, die Mauern hochgezogen werden und der Klimawandel und Pandemien ihr Werk verrichten, macht Berlin weiter auf weltoffen. In Wirklichkeit aber lebt lediglich …

author: Joe Sandler Clarke & Joshua Carroll
title: Spain’s PM Calls Snap Election After Rightwingers Block Housing Reforms
content:
Spain’s socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez has called a high-stakes snap general election for 29 November, after rightwing parties blocked a package of housing reforms. 


Demonstrators in Madrid and other cities returned to the streets in their tens of thousands over the weekend after a package of measures approved by the minority coalition government failed to win enough votes in parliament on Friday. 


In a televised address announcing the election on Monday,

Sanchez said

: “We must mobilise and secure a much broader progressive majority in parliament, one that allows us to overcome the elites… and continue transforming Spain.”


The

planned reforms

 included a ban on evictions for vulnerable people until the end of 2030, a ban on property funds buying homes until the end of 2028. They also included a rule forcing landlords to provide compensation to tenants, under certain conditions, when the landlord does not renew their contract. 

 


Sanchez’s government drew up the reforms in response to protests sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her flat in central Madrid. 


Maricarmen Abascal was forced out of her home of 70 years after Urbagestión, the company that owns her building, increased her rent from €500 (£428) per month to to €2,650, before offering to lower it  to €1,650. 


Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was allowed to return and pay €533 in rent after the protests began. But her story galvanised a mass movement drawing on anger over soaring rents. 


Sanchez’s decision to call an election is a gamble; his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party is trailing in the polls behind the rightwing People’s party (PP), which leads a powerful opposition coalition in parliament. 


If the polls prove to be correct, the election could allow the far-right Vox party, a PP ally, to enter government as a coalition partner. A far-right party has not held power in the central government in Spain since the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975. 


But Sanchez is considered a shrewd political operator who has beaten the odds before. Despite never winning an outright majority, he has been able to hold together a series of unlikely coalitions to remain in power for eight years.  


“You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs,” Sanchez said in his

address

, “or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility.”

title: On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the…
content:
On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further. “At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.” Days earlier, many across Spain had watched in shock as news channels showed Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman with a disability, being evicted from the home where she had lived for seven decades. The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other.

Maricarmen, 87, waits at home for police to arrive before being evicted from the home where she lived in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press via AP)

Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.” Abascal’s lawyers reportedly reached a deal for her to return home on Monday evening. “If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone,” her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told reporters, saying it could “help to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general”. At the encampment earlier on Monday, many described the days of nationwide protests and the encampment as a turning point in a movement that had long simmered as rents rose by 80% within a decade, while the cost of homes climbed by 63%. “We need stability,” said David Iglesias, 25, as he described how the ever-soaring prices had forced people to put their lives on hold to try to keep a roof over their heads. “People who want to have children should be able to do so, even if they are renting. People who dream of becoming musicians or barbers should have the chance to do so and not have to worry that they need to work, work, work to pay for housing,” he said. “It’s an endless loop that is undermining the mental health of young people.” As he spoke, a large banner flapped nearby, reading: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, cryptobros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.” […] It was a nod to the informal camp slogan, launched by housing campaigners and oft-repeated by protesters in recent days: “Either the rentier economy falls, or the government does.”

[Video]: “Hundreds of protesters across Spain took part in pot banging demonstrations to demand political action over soaring rents, evictions and the shortage of affordable housing. The protests come ahead of a parliamentary vote on Friday on measures to strengthen tenant protections.”

author: Cormac Mills Ritchard
title: Demolishing the idea of public housing
content:
The United Nations’ special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, usually deals with slum demolitions in third-world countries. Last month, he took aim at the Victorian Labor government, claiming its demolition of Melbourne’s 44 public housing towers and the “forced evictions and mass displacement of approximately 10,000 residents” could be a violation of their

human rights

. This follows a Victorian parliamentary inquiry in December, which called for an

immediate pause

 to the demolitions, and a class action against the demolitions filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal (IMCL), which has been granted special leave to

appeal

 to the High Court on 7 October.

Despite growing challenges, Premier Ben Carroll is ploughing ahead with the demolition of Melbourne’s public housing towers. Of course, Labor doesn’t characterise what it’s doing as “eviction” and “demolition”, but “renewal” and “redevelopment”, which it claims will increase the number of residents on the estates from 10,000 to 30,000, and replace towers that have “reached the end of their useful life”. There is no truth to this.

If Labor’s multi-billion-dollar project is aimed at addressing the waiting list for social housing, it’s missing a couple of zeros. Only 11,000 of the new residents will be in social housing, an increase of just 1,000. As of June this year, there were 58,021 people on the Victorian Housing Register’s

growing waiting list

, of which 33,253 have been assessed as “priority”—mostly those who are currently homeless or experiencing family violence. The redevelopments will mean that just 1,000 more people will have places in social housing ... by 2051.

The redevelopment won’t help others affected by the housing crisis, either. The other 19,000 residents of the new mixed-tenure developments will live in a combination of build-to-rent, a model that the

 Age

 has found to be between 20 and 70 percent

more expensive

 than the market rate, and “affordable housing”, which is not that affordable and does not provide long-term security, as exposed by a recent

Four Corners


investigation

. 

The North Richmond public housing precinct is a telling example. In September, the state government briefed the City of Yarra on its plans for the tower at 139 Highett Street. The

Age

 reported last month that the tower, which currently has 220 public housing units, will be replaced with a development that has

only 150 social housing units

 and 650 build-to-rent units.

Simon is a former resident who grew up in the North Richmond precinct after his parents emigrated from Vietnam. After the latest announcement about the precinct, he attended a community meeting of public housing tenants who demand the towers be refurbished rather than demolished. He told

Red Flag

 that his parents, a labourer and kindergarten worker, were both poorly paid. Living in the public housing tower allowed them to escape the anarchy of the private rental market. “We knew what the rent was next week and didn’t have to worry about eviction or not being able to afford food. I could attend school and university without many issues. That security meant you could plan your life”, he said.

“Social housing” is an umbrella term that covers both public housing, run by the government, and community housing, run by not-for-profits. When Labor talks about social housing, it usually means community housing—so its claim to be replacing 10,000 public housing places with 11,000 social ones actually represents a huge cut in public housing.

Public housing rent is capped at 25 percent of a household’s income or the market rate, whichever is lower, while community housing providers can charge up to 30 percent. However, community housing organisations (CHOs) are entitled to 100 percent of any tenant’s Commonwealth Rent Assistance and can charge extra fees on top. In its

submission to the inquiry

, IMCL notes that some of its clients pay up to 50 percent of their income to a CHO through “rent, utilities, lift fees, concierge and management fees”. Community housing residents also have fewer rights than public housing residents; West Heidelberg Community Legal found that “long-term community housing tenants were 3 to 5 times more likely to face eviction than public housing tenants”.

Worse still, unlike the government, CHOs don’t have to allocate places based on need, which means that the more the social housing waiting list is serviced by community rather than public housing …

03 Οκτώβρη 2026 πλ. Πανεπιστημίου Βόλος

Όλα αυτά είναι μια σύμπτωση γεγονότων απλά σε έναν κοινό χρόνο;


Όχι. Το δολοφονικό καθεστώς της ΑΓΕΤ – Lafarge, τα αλλεπάλληλα και σχεδιασμένα κρατικά εγκλήματα, οι δολοφονίες όσων εξαιρούνται από τις ροές της κερδοφορίας του κεφαλαίου και οι “θερμοί” πόλεμοι των ιμπεριαλιστών είναι πτυχές ενός γενικευμένου κοινωνικού πολέμου. Οι μορφές αυτού του πολέμου είναι η κανονικότητα όλων μας, που με διαφορετικό τρόπο μπαίνουμε στο στόχαστρο ενός συστήματος που δολοφονεί με πατέντα, με σχέδιο και με στόχο.


Σε αυτόν τον γενικευμένο πόλεμο το ζητούμενο είναι η αναζήτηση μορφών πολέμου των “κάτω” εναντίων των “πάνω”. Μορφών αγώνα και πάλης, που με διάρκεια, στόχο και μαχητικότητα θα επιχειρήσουν να επιβάλλουν το δίκιο των καταπιεσμένων.


Αξιοποιώντας την πλούσια εμπειρία των τελευταίων χρόνων, και με συνείδηση πως εισερχόμαστε σε έναν κύκλο περεταίρω κλιμάκωσης αυτού του κοινωνικού πολέμου, ο Συντονισμός Συλλογικοτήτων Βόλου επιχειρεί μέσα και από το Φεστιβάλ που διοργανώνει να δημιουργήσει το πεδίο συζήτησης, ενοποίησης και χάραξης ενός αγωνιστικού σχεδιασμού που να φιλοδοξεί να υψωθεί ως αντίπαλο δέος στον γενικευμένο κοινωνικό πόλεμο του κεφαλαίου.

title: Belo Horizonte, Brasil: barricada por cero desalojos y contra la ley de gentrificación
content:
Texto disponible en portugués y español. Fotos al final.


ES


El jueves 1 de octubre, la Avenida Antônio Carlos fue parcialmente bloqueada con neumáticos en llamas y una pancarta instalada en el Viaducto Senegal en protesta por las amenazas de desalojo de ocupantes de viviendas en el centro de Belo Horizonte y la Ley 574, que afectará al centro de la ciudad ampliado y a barrios como Concórdia y Lagoinha.


Los manifestantes bloquearon 3 carriles, causando retrasos en el tráfico y mucho ruido para denunciar un proyecto de ciudad donde la vivienda no es un derecho para todos, sino una mercancía que unos pocos venden y de la que se lucran.


El derecho a la vivienda y la función social de la propiedad, ambos garantizados por la Constitución, son atacados por la especulación inmobiliaria y una lógica urbana accesible solo a los ricos.


Como consecuencia, las ocupaciones de Maria do Arraial, en la Rua da Bahia, y Kasa Invisível, en la Av. Bias Fortes, así como las ocupaciones de São Paulo y Casa Rosa en la Rua Santa Catarina, corren riesgo de desalojo.


Para colmo, el alcalde Álvaro Damião (União Brasil) y la alcaldía de Belo Horizonte presentaron el Proyecto de Ley 574, que establece la denominada Operación Urbana Simplificada (OUS) para la Regeneración de Barrios del Centro. Bajo el pretexto de promover la “regeneración” y la “revitalización económica” del centro y la periferia, se trata claramente de un amplio paquete de beneficios para que las grandes empresas inmobiliarias especulen, construyan edificios en edificios de gran altura, aumenten los alquileres y desplacen a los residentes y la vida comunitaria de la zona.


¡UN DESALOJO MÁS Y LA CIUDAD SE PARALIZARÁ!


 


PT/BR


BELO HORIZONTE: BARRICADA POR DESPEJO ZERO E CONTRA A PL DA GENTRIFICAÇÃO


Dia 1 de outubro, quinta-feira, a Av. Antônio Carlos amanheceu parcialmente bloqueada com pneus queimando e faixa instalada no Viaduto Senegal

contra as ameaças de despejo de ocupações de moradia no centro de BH e a PL 574

, que vai afetar o centro expandido da cidade e bairros como Concórdia e Lagoinha.


Manifestantes bloquearam 3 faixas, causando lentidão e muito barulho para

 denunciar um projeto de cidade onde a moradia não é um direito de todos, mas uma mercadoria para poucos venderem e lucrarem.


O direito à moradia e a função social da propriedade, ambos garantidos na Constituição, são atacados pela especulação imobiliária e uma lógica de cidade acessível apenas para os ricos.


Como consequência disso,

 estão em risco de despejo

 as ocupações Maria do Arraial, na Rua da Bahia e a Kasa Invisível, na Av. Bias Fortes, ocupação São Paulo e a ocupação Casa Rosa na Rua Santa Catarina.


Para piorar, o prefeito Álvaro Damião (União Brasil) e a Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte apresentaram o

PL 574

 que institui a chamada

Operação Urbana Simplificada (OUS) dos Bairros do Centro

. Com a desculpa de promover a “regeneração” e a “dinamização econômica” da área central e pericentral. Porém, é obviamente

um grande pacote de benefícios para as grandes empresas do mercado imobiliário especularem

, verticalizarem os bairros, aumentando aluguéis e expulsando moradores e a vida comunitária da vizinhança.


A manifestação de trancamento da avenida realizada hoje por populares é também um chamado para que outras comunidades, grupos e movimentos se unam em torno da resistência contra os despejos, contra a gentrificação e por uma cidade onde caibamos a todes!


OCUPE TUDO!


MAIS UM DESPEJO E A CIDADE VAI PARAR!

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit’s low-barrier shelter to open in January
content:
Uquutaq Society’s new $40-million low-barrier shelter is slated to open in Iqaluit in January.


The new building is located downtown at 158 Nipisa St., near The Snack Restaurant.


Uquutaq Society’s emerging new three-storey facility includes 44 low-barrier shelter beds on the second floor and 13 single-room transitional housing units on the top floor. The main floor will be a warming centre during the day. (Photo by Daron Letts)


“This is a low-barrier site, meaning you don’t need to be sober or unimpaired [to enter],” said society CEO Laurel McCorriston in an interview in September.


Named by elders as Ullivik, which means “the place you wait for the tide,” the three-storey, 44-bed facility will offer

 16 beds for women, 24 beds for men and two rooms for

couples, which can also serve as private space for individuals in need of quiet or privacy.


The building includes an additional 13 single-occupancy transitional housing units on the top floor.


Currently, the only other low-barrier facility in the city is the society’s 17-cot overnight shelter at 534 Niaqunngusiariaq Road, which accommodates five women and 12 men nightly.


Last year, that shelter provided more than 6,000 overnight stays and served more than 800 meals of caribou, char and maataq.


“Ullivik provides a huge increase in services for people,” McCorriston said.


The first floor features a commercial kitchen, dining room, showers and a laundry —

part of a year-round warming centre that is accessible daily. It includes a self-contained room with sofas, armchairs and a television.


A first-floor balcony will serve as a smoking section, preventing guests from smoking in the streets, McCorriston said.


Ainiak Korgak was among the elders at Iqaluit’s Elders’ Qammaq last year who brainstormed names for society staff to choose from.


Frobisher Bay’s tides, among the biggest in the world, ebb and flow on a 12-hour cycle, making Ullivik an apt name for the new shelter, he said, in an interview Thursday.


Ainiak Korgak, among those at Iqaluit’s Elders’ Qammaq who brainstormed names for Uquutaq Society’s new $40-million low-barrier shelter. (Photo by Daron Letts)


Ullivik symbolizes “renewal,” Korgak said.


“The tide comes in and takes away your shortcomings,” he said. “That’s one way of looking at it.”


The new facility

developed “pretty fast,” McCorriston said.


The society applied for funding in February 2023.

Forgivable and repayable loans through the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corp. covered a little more than half the cost. Indigenous Services Canada chipped in $13 million and the Qikiqtani Inuit Association contributed $1 million.


Reaching Home, a homelessness program managed by Housing, Infrastructure and Communities Canada, pitched in $500,000.


NDL Construction Ltd. is leading the build, originally scheduled for completion in December.


Uquutaq’s next initiative is the $27-million Butler Supportive Housing Project, located next to Capital Suites at 804 Aiviq Street, which will provide 32 additional single-occupancy supportive housing units. The long-term housing option includes support staff on site.


Piles were installed this summer and structural steel was added this month.


That federally funded project is expected to be completed by 2028.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: French High School Students Lead Mass Protests over School Funding, Inequality; Thousands Arrested
content:
Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today amid massive student-led protests over school funding and inequality. The demonstrations began in September at a single school in the economically deprived suburbs of Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated school buildings beset by rats, falling debris and more. But the scope of the protests has widened amid a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people, largely underage students, since the movement began. Violent police tactics have led to serious injuries. One protester lost an eye after being hit by a rubber bullet, while another lost a hand when he picked up a police stun grenade.


We hear from an anonymous protester who describes the violence meted out on students, who “aren’t even adults yet,” and from Claire Vigneau, general secretary of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, the French student union, who reports from a protest in Rennes, Brittany, “where we are trying to escape from the policemen that are chasing us with tear gas and with water cannon[s].”


“The amount of spending that France has done on education has stagnated, if not declined,” explains French American journalist Cole Stangler. “The critiques that high school students are making are actually very similar to what teachers’ unions have been saying for quite some time.”


“Everyone is deeply, deeply angry. We are completely fed up [with] the living conditions, the school conditions, the work conditions that we have,” says Alys Rowlands, a university student in Lille and also a member of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante. “The true violence is the violence of the state that we are being faced with all day, every day, all year. That’s the true violence: having no money, having difficulty finishing the month, having less and less help from the state, having to choose between eating and putting your heating on during the winter.”

author: Unknown
title: Iran executes two more people over anti-government protests
content:
Iran’s judiciary announced that two people accused of involvement in the killing of four police officers during anti-government protests earlier this year had been executed.


According to Mizan, the judiciary’s official news outlet, Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Reisi were executed by hanging on Monday morning after the Supreme Court upheld their death sentences. Authorities did not disclose when the two men were arrested or when their trials took place.


Iran’s judiciary accused the two men of involvement in the killing of four police officers in the central city of Isfahan. The court also sentenced them to death on charges of membership of an armed group and threatening national security.


The protests began in Tehran in December over economic grievances and quickly spread to many parts of the country, developing into demonstrations directly opposing the government. The protests intensified particularly on 8 and 9 January, with serious clashes and loss of life reported across the country.


Iranian authorities claimed that more than 3,000 people were killed in the unrest, including hundreds of security personnel. The Tehran government has described the violence as “acts of terrorism” directed by the United States and Israel.


Human rights organisations outside Iran, however, have reported much higher death tolls and said security forces deliberately opened fire on protesters.


Executions on the rise


The number of executions in Iran has reportedly risen, particularly in recent years. According to Amnesty International, Iran carries out more executions than any country in the world except China.


Figures released by Norway-based Iran Human Rights and Paris-based Ensemble contre la peine de mort (ECPM) showed that Iranian authorities executed at least 1,639 people in 2025. The figure was reported to be the highest annual number of executions recorded in the country since 1989.


Iran’s judiciary also announced on Saturday that another person had been executed after being sentenced to death for using a weapon against police officers during the same protests.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Exhibit on Palestinian heritage, struggle opens in UP
content:
An art exhibit opened at the University of the Philippines (UP) this week celebrating Palestinian Heritage Day on Wednesday, also Al-Aqsa Flood’s third anniversary. A selection of photographs, crafts, and devotional objects are on display at UP’s-College of Fine Arts (CFA) Art Gallery representing Palestinian way of life and struggle against Zionist occupation and genocide.


Palestinian Ambassador to the Philippines Mounir Anastas and UP President Angelo Jimenez opened the month-long exhibit entitled “Palestine: Living Heritage, Enduring Steadfastness,” offering visitors a direct connection to the nation’s enduring cultural traditions.


Photographs of historic sites across the West Bank are juxtaposed alongside images of Gaza’s heritage sites before and after their destruction by Israeli occupation forces.


Ambassador Anastas acted as the exhibit’s first guide, explaining traditional Palestinian arts, ranging from embroidery, painting, and devotional items. He expressed appreciation to the university and its Office of International Linkages as well as the CFA for their commitment to cultural preservation, education, and international solidarity.


Palestinian Ambassador to the Philippines Mounir Anastas and UP President Angelo Jimenez opened the month-long exhibit. (Palestinian Embassy photo)


CFA meanwhile said the exhibit presents as testimonies a culture’s enduring beauty and vitality amid the systematic annihilation of Palestinian identity, collective memory, history, and land.


The country’s foremost fine arts school said the exhibition is a presentation of “Palestinian visual culture to testify to the catastrophic loss of a people’s physical and cultural memory alongside the genocide happening across the Gaza Strip today.”


By putting the spotlight on both tangible and intangible cultural heritage in this time of crisis, the exhibit extends the message of solidarity and aspiration for social justice, the University said.


​

Protest rally for Palestine in Manila


Meanwhile, various organizations announced a protest march to the United States Embassy in Manila to commemorate the third anniversary of the Al-Aqsa Flood on Wednesday.


The Philippine chapter of the International League of Peoples’ Struggles, Bagong Alyansang Makabayan, and the Philippine-Palestine Friendship Association said US imperialism and its agents are “genocide-complicit states.”


“The Palestinian resistance is a beacon to our resistance. It inspires all peoples struggling for national and social liberation, and therefore, we must support their resistance as if it were our own,” the groups said.


Up to 80,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces, including children and journalists, since October 2023.


United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres urged a permanent ceasefire in Palestine, demanding the that humanitarian assistance and full respect for international law are scaled up in the occupied Palestinian territories. #

 (Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Chris Walker
title: At Ohio Campaign Rally, Trump Threatens to Withhold Aid If Democrats Get Elected
content:
“I’m not going to help” if an Ohio Democratic candidate for governor wins, Trump said.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In a campaign speech in Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday, President Donald Trump suggested he would withhold federal funds from the state if voters elect Democratic politicians in this year’s midterm races.

Trump appeared to conflate two different political races, discussing U.S. Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) Senate reelection campaign and Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s campaign for governor in the same statement. (Husted is running against former U.S. Senator and Democrat Sherrod Brown, while Acton is facing off against Republican candidate for governor and Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy.)

“Jon Husted…calls me all the time. He always wants money,” Trump said during his speech. “If Amy Acton got in, I don’t know anything about her.”

“I’m not going to help her, probably, she hates me, I guess,” Trump added.

Trump’s speech also featured vulgar attacks against Democrats in general. At one point, he encouraged those in attendance to “just get out and vote” for Republicans.

“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big, and we’re going to shove it up their ass,” Trump said.

The president made a number of bizarre claims during his Saturday night speech. He claimed that he has one of the highest IQs “anywhere in the world,” telling the audience it was around 1,775. Such an IQ would indeed be the highest, as no IQ test has ever measured above 300. He also said that polls are “fake,” complaining that they didn’t take into account his plans to campaign in the final weeks of the race — a statement that is technically true but misleading, as polls question respondents about their current attitudes. And he reiterated an unlikely (and legally dubious) promise to deliver $5,000 checks to every American adult if Republicans win the midterms.

Trump has already withheld disaster aid from states for seemingly political reasons. In a series of Truth Social posts in late June, Trump announced hundreds of millions of dollars in disaster aid funds going to states that backed him in 2024, while ignoring some requests from states that backed his opponent, Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

An analysis from the Urban Institute around that time showed that, since Trump reentered the White House, over 84 percent of requests from states that voted for him won approval, as opposed to only 41 percent of requests from states that didn’t back him. Approvals, when they did occur, happened twice as fast for red states as for blue ones.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

author: dev
title: La mobilisation lycéenne à travers les yeux d'une professeur du 93
content:
J'voudrais écrire avec mes tripes, mon corps, ses joies et ses dégoûts, loin de toute moraline (Nietzsche) parce que les tribunes de circonstance, les communiqués, syndicaux ou autres, les déclarations d'intention, les mots creux, les rodomontades resteront lettre morte et ne sont que vétilles en considération de ce qui se joue en ce moment dans les lycées de toute la France, et au-delà (universités, monde du travail, perspective du 17 octobre…).


DÉGOÛTS !


L'intersyndicale nationale, au soir du 2 octobre, après plus de 5000 interpellations en 5 jours (pire qu'au plus fort du mouvement des Gilets Jaunes) et des centaines de cas de violences policières avérées, n'est pas même foutue d'appeler à la grève et à manifester le mardi 6 octobre (date posée par le mouvement lycéen pour une grande journée d'actions). Elle préfère en effet le « dialogue social », soit la complicité avec les pouvoirs en place, à la solidarité et aux véritables changements… L'intersyndicale qui précise encore dans ses communiqués qu'il faut que le gouvernement

entende

 les revendications lycéennes, déclaration totalement hors sol, comme si, de là où nous en sommes, le lion affamé allait entendre la plainte de l'antilope… Bref, l'intersyndicale, avec ses éternels atermoiements, c'est le maintien du système tel qu'il est, or certain.es ne le comprennent toujours pas, ce qui est bien désespérant, alors même qu'elle s'est évertuée à faire perdre tous les mouvements sociaux conséquents des dix dernières années (au moins), à commencer par la mobilisation contre la contre-réforme des retraites.


La liste des exactions de la police est tellement longue qu'un recensement exhaustif ne peut en être dressé : tentative de noyade à Belfort par un flic en civil, tentative d'écraser des élèves, par un flic à moto au Blanc-Mesnil, tentative d'homicide à Troyes : une voiture de police fonce à vive allure sur une foule de jeunes, calmes, réunis dans une rue, tout en les gazant depuis les vitres ouvertes du véhicule, étranglement d'une lycéenne de 14 ans à Alençon, éborgnement d'un lycéen de 16 ans, à Argenteuil du fait d'un tir à bout portant de LBD. À Tours, Maël, 16 ans a aussi été éborgné, Mâchoire brisée du fait d'un tir tendu de grenade en plein visage d'Eden, 15 ans, dans le Val d'Oise

 [

1

]

.


Etc.


Une copine me raconte : présence de flics avec des chiens à Carnot (collège-lycée à Paris 17è), mouvement de foule à l'intérieur du collège, son fils de 11 ans blessé au genou dans la panique. Bah au moins, il détestera la police, et pour longtemps !


Dans mon lycée du 93, au terme de deux jours de blocus, on dénombre 5 élèves placés en garde-à-vue dont l'un, mineur, sera peut-être déféré au tribunal ; des blessures : une jeune fille, à l'œil, ayant reçu un projectile suite à l'envoi de gaz lacrymogène par les forces de l'ordre, d'autres présentant des contusions dues à des coups de matraques ; des mises en joue d'élèves par des flics armés de LBD et moult tirs de gaz lacrymo ; des insultes, évidemment ; des intimidations : un flic en mode prêcheur qui déclare à un élève : « tu sais, ce que tu fais là, à la mosquée, même si tu le confesses, on t'le pardonnera pas »… Et aussi une voiture bélier fonçant à vive allure dans le tas, pas de blessés mais une catastrophe aurait pu avoir lieu.


À noter que les élèves embarqués l'ont été alors qu'ils n'étaient plus devant le lycée mais sur le chemin les reconduisant chez eux, par des keufs en embuscade aux environs du lycée, bel exemple de crapulerie et veulerie.


On les pensait bien soumis, pour toujours


Dociles à souhait


Esclaves, sans fin


Dominé.es sans répit


Qui ça ?


Les sauvageon.nes des banlieues, les relégué.es des quartiers populaires… mais ils n'en peuvent plus et relèvent la tête !


Dans mon lycée du 93, depuis des années, on « joue » aux chaises musicales, il n'y a bien souvent pas assez de chaises pour les classes à 35, il faut donc aller en chercher dans d'autres salles qui, de fait, connaîtront à leur tour le même sort, le problème n'est donc pas réglé et se poursuit sempiternellement. Les chaises, en outre, de piètre qualité, sont pour beaucoup endommagées, s'entassent dans les salles et ne sont pas jetées


Depuis l'an passé, Pécresse a fait installer des systèmes bloquant les fenêtres qui s'ouvrent donc à peine maintenant, empêchant toute réelle ventilation ; système anti-suicide paraît-il, mais les élèves peuvent allégrement se jeter dans le vide depuis les passerelles menant …

author: groundxero
title: ‘The Struggle Continues’ for Today’s Generation of French Students
content:
The French student movement has a long history of political activism based on organized protests and occupations not only for the improvement of their learning experience and school conditions but also against capitalism, consumerism, imperialism, and police repression.


 


By

C.J. Polychroniou


Common Dreams


 


France

 is presently in the throes of nationwide student

protests

 that have turned increasingly violent as the police crack down on students, using tear gas and heavy-handed tactics as students blockade entrances to their schools and even set fire to several schools across France.


 


The students, aged between 15 and 18, are protesting over poor school conditions (overcrowded classrooms, crumbling

infrastructure

, heavy workloads, teacher shortages) and demand increased funding for schools. Thousands have been

detained

, mostly minors, and dozens injured, including some 50 law enforcement officers.


 


The high school protests begun in Aubervilliers, a low-income Paris suburb, but quickly spread nationwide, as usually happens with students protests in France. University students have now joined high school schools across France, thus creating an even more volatile situation for the French government. Incidentally, the student protests are unfolding alongside massive public-sector protests over pay and working conditions.


 


French students have also shown that they are always on the side of the workers’ fight for better working conditions and in their struggle for an alternative socioeconomic and political order.


 


France is indeed in crisis mode, economically, politically, and socially. Weak growth and deteriorating public finances have been the norm for several years now, while

austerity

 is being advanced by the political establishment as the only available solution to the country’s economic problems and financial misery. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu presented an austerity-driven government

budget

 on October 1 that proposes 43 billion euros in new fiscal measures to reduce the deficit.


 


However, the

budget

 bill is surely expected to face a rough ride as France has a deeply divided parliament that has repeatedly rejected austerity-driven budget proposals, forcing in fact several prime ministers since 2022 to step down. Lecornu’s government may very well be the next one to collapse as it is highly unlikely that either Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party or Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party (which France’s

Interior Ministry

 has actually classified as far left) will make compromises, especially in light of the fact that France’s next presidential election is scheduled for April 18 and May 2, 2027, and looks like the

run-off election

 will be between Le Pen and Mélenchon.


 


In addition, France’s

bond market

 is under growing pressure as its 10-year yield has reached the highest level since 2002. With the cost of borrowing money hitting a peak, France, which has faced sluggish growth for years, is likely to see even slower growth in 2027 than in 2026. This situation seems to be serving the far-right RN party particularly well, which has already scored a “

historic victory

” by securing enough seats in the recently held Senate election to establish its own caucus for the first time.


 


In the meantime, the student protests are being used both by Le Pen and government officials to

target

 Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s party for allegedly deploying agitators and using rhetoric to stoke students’ anger.


 


There is little doubt that the concerns of French students are legitimate. Their grievances with the poor state of schools have been building since this summer’s

heatwaves

, which exposed “the poor state of schools, with poor insulation and no air conditioning,” according to

Vincent Latour

,

 a professor of British Studies at the University of Toulouse-II-Le Mirail. Moreover, the president of Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), 19-year old

Ryad Rani

, said that student grievances had elicited no response from the government and that the movement will continue with the protests until its demands are satisfied.

activism

title: Mobilisation lycéenne : infos pour la semaine du 5 octobre
content:
Appel de la coordination lycéenne.

RDV

 de mobilisation. Répression, arrêtés préfectoraux...


Lundi 5 mobilisation dans les lycées. Mardi 6 octobre manif 14h République et assemblée lycéenne 17h


Samedi 3 octobre on était 300 lycéens de toute la région parisienne réunis en assemblée de coordination.


La colère a commencé parce que c'est la casse sociale dans les lycées de banlieue. Le tri des pauvres et des riches à lécoale, c'est mort on refuse. On revendique la fin de Parcoursup. On revendique des moyens, des professeurs et des

AESH

. On veut des classes qui ne sont pas à 35, du respect pour tous les élèves, des bourses qui arrivent à temps, des lycées où il n'y a pas de rats, ni de plafonds qui s'écroulent, ni de l'amiante, ni des salles à 40° en été.


On revendique un avenir pour les lycéens de banlieue. On sait que la méritocratie c'est un leurre. Y'a pas de raison que nous, on ait une éducation et un avenir de seconde-zone comparé aux lycées privés ou des beaux quartiers. Et derrière, on sait qu'on n'a pas d'avenir dans ce système où ce sont les riches qui décident. On veut savoir où va l'argent et on veut qu'il aille là où y'a besoin

 

! Le gouvernement il met des milliards dans l'armée, dans les patrons, dans la police. C'est ça la violence. Alors nous, on ne se laissera pas diviser par les discours contre les casseurs, on est tous ensemble.


Le gouvernement, l'extrême-droite et les grands médias, ils ont tout tenté pour nous faire taire. Toute la violence de la police on l'a vu. les fermetures de lycées, on les a vu. Ceux qui disent qu'on est insctrumentalisés ou qu'on est bêtes, on les a vu. Ok, noté. Ok, ils ne veulent pas qu'on se mobilise. Ok la répression a pour but de faire peur, que notre colère s'éteigne et de nous diviser. Les 5000 lycéens arrêtés doivent tous être relâchés sans aucune poursuite.


On va continuer de se mobiliser. Et on ne s'arrêtera pas au lycée non plus. On n'est pas seuls. Les gens du monde du travail se joignent à la mobilisation. Et notre colère, elle peut parler à tous les jeunes, même en dehors de la France.


Alors nous, on va construire la grève lycéenne

 

! On appelle tout le monde à nous rejoindre et à se mettre en grève : les profs, les parents, les étudiants, les pompiers, les autres travailleurs. ils nous la mettent à l'envers

 

? On leur remet 68 et on ira plus loin. Les syndicats appellent à la grève mardi, il faut que tout le monde nous rejoigne

 

! Et si ça sort les gilets jaunes avant même le 17 octobre tant mieux

 

!


On veut prendre notre lutte en main : c'est les lycéens mobilisés qui doivent décider de leur mouvement, et c'est à personne d'autre de décider à notre place. Donc sur chaque blocage, devant chaque lycée, il faut prendre la parole, so'ganiser nous-même et décider ensemble.


Dès lundi, partout on se mobilise. Et mardi, on doit tous aller en manifestation à République à 14H. On y sera en tête de cortège de la coordination lycéenne Paris x Banlieues. On appelle tous les lycées à venir, à se préparer leur banderole. Et derrière, rendez-vous pour tous les lycées mobilisés en assemblée de la coordination lycéenne Paris x Banlieues à 17h. Parce qu'après mardi bien sûr qu'on va continuer

 

!


Un communiqué de parents d'élèves d'Aubervilliers


Parents d'élèves : une présence solidaire auprès des lycéen·nes mobilisé·es


Depuis une dizaine de jours, des milliers de lycéennes et lycéens, dans toute la France mais en particulier dans le 93 et à Aubervilliers, manifestent leur colère.


Cette colère est aussi la nôtre : contre le manque de moyens, la dégradation du bâti scolaire, l'exposition aux canicules, les absences d'enseignant·es non remplacées, le manque d'infirmières, d'assistantes sociales, de psychologues et de médecins scolaires, les emplois du temps surchargés, l'inertie de l'Éducation nationale face aux agressions sexuelles, sexistes et racistes, la sélection arbitraire et inégale de Parcoursup…


La colère des lycéen·nes d'Aubervilliers s'exprime la plupart du temps de manière pacifique, joyeuse et déterminée. Elle n'est bruyante que pour ceux qui ne veulent pas l'écouter.


Rien ne justifie la répression policière, les gaz lacrymogènes qui pénètrent jusque dans les écoles primaires alentour, ou les violentes interpellations dont nous avons été témoins. Ce ne sont pas des «

 

casseurs

 

», ce sont nos enfants

 

; ce ne sont pas des «

 

violences urbaines

 

», mais un mouvement social portant des revendications …

author: Amy Goodman
title: Police Violence Causes Serious Injuries as French High School Students Protest
content:
Students protest teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and dilapidated school buildings beset by rats and debris.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today amid massive student-led protests over school funding and inequality. The demonstrations began in September at a single school in the economically deprived suburbs of Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated school buildings beset by rats, falling debris and more. But the scope of the protests has widened amid a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people, largely underage students, since the movement began. Violent police tactics have led to serious injuries. One protester lost an eye after being hit by a rubber bullet, while another lost a hand when he picked up a police stun grenade.

We hear from an anonymous protester who describes the violence meted out on students, who “aren’t even adults yet,” and from Claire Vigneau, general secretary of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, the French student union, who reports from a protest in Rennes, Brittany, “where we are trying to escape from the policemen that are chasing us with tear gas and with water cannon[s].”

“The amount of spending that France has done on education has stagnated, if not declined,” explains French American journalist Cole Stangler. “The critiques that high school students are making are actually very similar to what teachers’ unions have been saying for quite some time.”

“Everyone is deeply, deeply angry. We are completely fed up [with] the living conditions, the school conditions, the work conditions that we have,” says Alys Rowlands, a university student in Lille and also a member of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante. “The true violence is the violence of the state that we are being faced with all day, every day, all year. That’s the true violence: having no money, having difficulty finishing the month, having less and less help from the state, having to choose between eating and putting your heating on during the winter.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today as massive student-led protests spread over France over school funding and inequality. The demonstration began in September at a single school outside Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school buildings. But the scope of the protests has widened amidst a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people since the movement began, about 85% of them high schoolers.

These are the voices of two students protesting in Paris earlier today.

HUGO VETZEL: [translated] For us, it’s, first of all, in support of the high school students who started blockades a few days ago. I think we all have a role to play in this movement, and the more we are, the more we will be heard. And I think this is not a fight of a few handful of people, but a more global fight for the youth. …

We feel despised, because when the answer is violence, that means, in a way, democracy is no longer working. But we feel especially that there is such a gap between the elites and us, and we feel we are creating unease, because we are disrupting so much that they are using force to shut us up.

MONA FALLACARA: [translated] I am quite happy because, for once, we see a real movement of the youth everywhere, and we hear about it. But then, what I deplore is that the media is showing more of the violence done by the students before their demands, which are vital. And yes, there is a bit of violence, but it’s not everywhere. …

France’s budget will come to a vote soon, so we hope there will be a higher budget for education. And for the presidential election next year, as well, we hope for a bit of change after 10 years of President Macron heading the country.

AMY GOODMAN: France’s official independent national human rights body has expressed deep concern over what it called the state’s disproportionate use of force in response to the protests. On Monday, Democracy Now! reached a French student who described the violent police crackdown. For her safety, she asked not to be identified.

PROTESTER: During the protests, people, students receive tear gas, receive — like, get hit …

title: Lottare nell’Antropocene: tossicità, grandi opere e conflitti territoriali
content:
Se la crisi ecologica è una crepa nel sistema, quali strumenti di pratica e d’analisi possiamo usare per forzare la breccia? Quali categorie ci permettono una lettura del presente che colga nella catastrofe reali possibilità di conflitto?


Da Radio Blackout


In questo

primo episodio di Cicorie

, cominciamo ad affrontare il problema della periodizzazione e dei termini che usiamo per designare il nostro tempo inaugurando una delle rubriche che ci accompagnerà nelle varie puntate: “

Indovina chi viene a Cene?

”.  Capitalocene, Plantagiocene,Tecnocene, Cthulucene, Proletariocene: tantissimi sono stati i neologismi che hanno caratterizzato il dibattito accademico dell’ecologia politica. Nonostante questa iper-produzione di termini specifici non ci convinca, vogliamo comunque partire da alcune riflessioni che questi stimolano per approfondire il punto di vista sulla realtà. Per iniziare ci inoltriamo nel dibattito più classico: quello tra Antropocene e Capitalocene. Un dibattito che caliamo nel contemporaneo e che facciamo interagire con ciò che è successo e succede al di fuori delle aule universitarie.


Ne parliamo nella prima parte dell’episodio insieme a

Emanuele Leonardi

, Professore di sociologia all’Università di Bologna e compagno storico dei collettivi di Ecologia politica.  


Segue un approfondimento sul volume “

Tossicità. Voci, saperi e conflitti in una zona di sacrificio

” (Orthotes, 2026), lavoro di ricerca di comunità incentrato su vita e lotta nei territori limitrofi al polo chimico di

Spinetta Marengo

 in Alessandria, segnati dall’avvelenamento da PFAS.


A chiaccherare con noi di conricerca e inquinanti eterni

Eleonora Bechis

, ricercatrice, compagna e curatrice del testo insieme a Vittorio Martone, Rosalba Altopiedi e Andrea Filippo Ravenda. 


Nell’ultima sezione del programma, ci rivolgiamo direttamente ai territori e alle forme di mobilitazione che continuano ad animarli, conquistando spazio e assumendo dimensioni sempre più conflittuali.

Ripercorriamo la marcia in Bassa Val di Susa “

Fermiamo insieme l’Avigliana-Orbassano

” del 3 ottobre attraverso i contributi e le voci di chi vi ha preso parte per poi spostarci a Reggio Emilia, dove la mobilitazione cittadina di

Bosco Ospizio

 si trova a un punto di svolta. A fare il punto della situazione in collegamento con noi da Reggio Alessio, dell’

Assemblea Permanente per la difesa del Bosco

.


Concludiamo con una breve panoramica sull’attualità – tra ritorno all’atomo in Italia, crisi energetica e caro carburanti – mettendo in

focus

 le recenti

mobilitazioni degli agricoltori

 del Centro e Sud Italia, che tra nuovi blocchi stradali e vecchie rivendicazioni tornano a prendere la parola e a scendere in strada.


Qui sotto l’audio integrale dell’episodio!

author: Soraya Kishtwari
title: French Teen Loses Hand After Police Use Grenade Amid Student Protests
content:
A teenager lost his hand in France after a police grenade exploded during widespread student protests on Monday, amid mounting reports of violence by officers. 


The 15-year-old boy was injured outside Auguste-Béhal high school in the northern town of Lens, in Pas-de-Calais, where riot police had been deployed after protesters reportedly threw objects at officers.


It is not yet clear what type of grenade it was or exactly how it caused the injury. A police union source told AFP the boy

appeared to have picked it up

, but a

girl reportedly standing nearby

 told regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord this was false. 


“I was there, I saw it. He didn’t pick it up,” she said. 


Witnesses told

Le Monde

 that riot police had pushed protesters back before throwing the grenade. 


On 28 September, a police officer shot a tear gas grenade and struck a 14-year-old boy named Eden in the face at close range,

Le Monde reported

. 


“Eden has a double jaw fracture, several of his lower teeth have been pulled out, and all his upper teeth are broken,” his lawyer, Elsa Marcel, told a press conference. His mother added that he can only consume liquids: “His jaw is sealed shut with just enough space for a straw.” 


In another incident, a 16-year-old lost sight in one eye after reportedly being hit with a rubber bullet. An investigation is underway to clarify what happened.


In total, six judicial investigations into alleged police violence have been opened since a wave of student protests erupted at the start of the academic year over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions. Students have described leaking classrooms, deteriorating buildings and going months without teachers.


Education minister Édouard Geffray said 190 students had been injured since the protests began, while the Interior Ministry reported 650 injuries among police officers, including a female officer who was chased and kicked. Seventy-eight school staff members have also been injured. The figures do not distinguish between serious and minor injuries. 


Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said student grievances were

“legitimate” and promised action

 on teacher shortages, school repairs and overloaded timetables, with some pupils starting as early as 8am and finishing as late as 6pm.

Unions

 say the government needs to reverse cuts to education rather than offer limited measures.


As many as

200,000 people

 were expected to join a national day of action on Tuesday, with 1,800 schools due to be blockaded as teachers, trade unionists and parents join demonstrations.


Parent groups, led by the Fédération des Conseils de Parents d’Élèves, the largest federation of public school parent associations, have also

called on parents to join the protests

.


The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents high schools, said Tuesday that the number of people mobilising had reached a “

new record

”.


Amnesty International

said

: “Protests have been met with unnecessary and disproportionate force by police, including the unlawful use of tear gas grenades and rubber bullets. The Ministry of Interior announced that there have been more than 5,000 arrests of protesters and stated that 85% of those arrested have been children.”

author: dev
title: Ritchy Thibault, premier prisonnier du mouvement lycéen
content:
Interpellé en pleine rue jeudi dernier, l'écrivain et voyageur Ritchy Thibault a été emprisonné. Il lui est reproché un discours prononcé à Saint-Denis lors d'une assemblée générale de lycéens. Une audience se tiendra ce lundi à 13h au tribunal de Bobigny qui statuera sur sa libération dans l'attente d'un procès ou son maintien en détention, ce qui serait un très mauvais signal envoyé aux lycéens plus que jamais mobilisés.


Il y a des fabricants de destins qui l'aimeraient clandestin.


Certains commencent dans des amphithéâtres, d'autres dans les caravanes ou sur des rond-points de campagne. Celui de Ritchy Thibault semble, lui, avoir trouvé un drôle de raccourci : viré de l'hémicycle en tant qu' attaché parlementaire, on le retrouve forcément dès le premier jour de la mobilisation aux abords d'un lycée de banlieue et de nouveau devant les tribunaux pour sa prise de parole.


Le voilà érigé en quasi responsable de la contestation, incarnation autocentrée pour le Parquet - proclamée d'une jeunesse qui ne supporterait plus rien — ni l'ordre, ni l'autorité, ni les institutions, et encore moins ceux qui prétendent les représenter. À chaque mobilisation son cortège, à chaque polémique sa réponse proportionnée, à chaque interpellation sa détermination sauf qu'à chaque fois ou presque il y a un mort, qui un voyageur traîné sur 100 m par la Municipale qui un maire véreux cloitrant une aire de « gens-du-voyage ».


Voir en Ritchy Thibault une sorte de porte-parole naturel des populations opprimées semble se dessiner assez fiablement au fil des mois et parfois des semaines, au fil des émeutes, et manifestant en première ligne pour la fin des coups et des étranglements sur la voie publique jusqu'au fond des mitards.


Chatgpt dirait : c'est là que le personnage devient intéressant. Il se retrouve quasiment à chaque procédure a établir un rapport de force - comme un rapport de farce - une variante de la fameuse Défense de rupture. On le voit à chaque fois argumenter - dans ce régime de parole qui est le sien à des joutes assez réussies et brillantes de tentatives d'auto-désarrestations (désarrestation = lorsqu'un groupe de personnes tentent de libérer physiquement un•e camarade au prise avec la Maréechaussée.) Dans cette nouvelle économie de la contestation, l'arrestation devient parfois une ligne de CV, la convocation une médaille et le passage devant la justice un épisode supplémentaire dans le récit héroïque du rappel historique - à chaque fois situé des personnes, persécuté (génocide des voyageurs, parquages, apartheid de l'Etat français envers des populations).


L'atout de Ritchy Thibault, ce n'est pas qu'il parle trop. C'est qu'il a fait de la confrontation avec le pouvoir une méthode, un médium — et que le pouvoir judiciaire, lui, a les moyens de transformer chacune de ces confrontations en procédure, le transforme en tribune.


La vraie question devient : justice qui protège l'ordre public ou justice qui finit, volontairement ou non, par devenir un instrument de mise au pas d'une parole et se prendre les pieds dans le tapis d'une bienséance confinant à l'absurde du droit commun en sytème politique. Ritchy Thibault nous montre avec délices, les affres de toute assignation - et autres rapports de dominations - qu'ils soient éducatifs, issus du monde les ronds de serviettes et des pantoufles, voire des patins pour cirer les Parquets. Blague à part, la bascule judiciaire, voire carcérale peut vite arriver, une incarcération, des amendes, des menaces de mort à la pelle montrent que le fil est ténu mais il tient la ligne. A nous tous de le sortir de là.


#FreeRitchy

author: bert
title: Rote Hilfe freut sich über erneuten Mitgliederzuwachs
content:
Rote Hilfe freut sich über erneuten Mitgliederzuwachs


Nachdem die Kündigung aller ihrer Konten der Roten Hilfe

e. V.

 zum Jahreswechsel 2025/26 bereits eine große Welle der Solidarität eingebracht hatte, kann sich die linke Schutz- und Solidaritätsorganisation nun über einen erneuten Schwung an Neueintritten freuen. Hintergrund ist eine Kampagne gegen die Spitzenkandidatin der Partei Die Linke in Berlin, Elif Eralp, die nach eigenen Angaben bis 2025 Mitglied des Vereins war. Große Teile der bürgerlichen Presse nutzten dies dazu, eine Kampagne gegen Eralp zu lancieren und unterstellten ihr und ihrer Partei die Nähe zu einem „Terrorhilfe-Verein“ oder „Extremisten-Nest“. 

Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe ordnet die Kampagne ein: „Den hohen Wellen, die Elif Eralps frühere Mitgliedschaft plötzlich schlägt, sehen wir gelassen entgegen. Es scheint doch ein recht hilfloser Versuch zu sein, eine linke Bürgermeisterin in Berlin zu verhindern, die der Bevölkerung unter anderem die Vergesellschaftung großer Wohnungskonzerne versprochen hat. Wenn nun ihre ehemalige Mitgliedschaft in der Roten Hilfe einer der größten Skandale um ihre Person sein soll, haben ihre politischen Gegner*innen wohl nicht viel Material für die Diffamierungskampagne gefunden«. 

Das tagelange Medienecho brachte der Roten Hilfe einen weiteren Anstieg der Mitgliederzahl auf über 21.000. Auch der Fraktionsvorsitzende der Partei Die Linke im Bundestag, Sören Pellmann, verkündete demonstrativ seinen Beitritt. 

„Wir freuen uns, dass sich erneut so viele Menschen solidarisch mit der Roten Hilfe zeigen. Wir erinnern uns an prominente Mitglieder wie Clara Zetkin oder Kurt Tucholsky in der Roten Hilfe Deutschland zur Weimarer Zeit,« so Brückner weiter. »Wir unterstützen Menschen etwa bei Gerichtsverfahren und setzen uns gegen den Abbau von Grundrechten ein. Dass diese offen und transparent geleistete Arbeit immer wieder zum Anlass für Diffamierungen und politische Angriffe genommen wird, zeigt umso deutlicher, wie wichtig eine starke linke Schutz- und Solidaritätsorganisation ist. Deshalb unterstützt uns, tretet bei, schafft Rote Hilfe!«

title: Assemblée ouverte de la caisse de solidarité Kaliméro
content:
Kaliméro est une caisse et une assemblée solidaire des prisonnier·e·s de la guerre sociale. La prochaine aura lieu le jeudi 8 octobre à 18h et se tiendra au 19, rue burnouf à Paris (19

e

).


La prison est un des rouages de ce système basé sur l'exploitation et la domination que nous voulons raser au sol, c'est pourquoi nous envoyons des mandats à celles et ceux accusé·e·s d'actes de révolte dont nous sommes solidaires.


Une caisse de solidarité a besoin de continuité. Nous n'avons ni sponsor, ni mécène, aussi avons-nous convenu d'un rendez-vous par mois pour collecter des sous pour alimenter la caisse. Ces rencontres sont également l'occasion d'échanger sur nos pratiques face à la répression, d'assurer le suivi des différentes histoires et de discuter des situations qui se présentent. Elle est également un moment de discussion autour des possibles moyens d'esquive, de résistance et d'auto-organisation offensive contre la machine judiciaire et carcérale.


Dans un souci de régularité, ces rencards ont été fixés le 2

e

 jeudi de chaque mois.


Pour envoyer de l'argent, pour demander des informations, ou pour être tenu·e·s au courant des prochains rendez-vous de la caisse et être inscrit·e·s sur la mailing-list de Kaliméro, écrivez à kalimeroparis(at)riseup.net

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Progressives and Republicans Introduce Competing Bills to Rein In Flock Cameras
content:
The Ban Flock Act aims to slow the rise of Flock-style cameras amid rising fears about AI mass surveillance.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Republicans and Democrats in Congress have introduced competing legislation to rein in the government’s use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs) following widespread abuses by police and intense public backlash to the powerful surveillance technology.

ALPRs allow police to track vehicles and their drivers across expansive areas by using a variety of easily searchable data points from images captured by the cameras. The Ban Flock Act, backed by some Democrats and progressives, would halt federal funding to slow the rise of AI-powered surveillance nationwide. A competing GOP bill creates legal guardrails for police when using ALPR data but would not “ban” license plate surveillance by the federal government.

Introduced on October 2 by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), the Ban Flock Act would prevent federal funds from being used to purchase ALPRs, including but not limited to Flock cameras. In order to incentivize a “moratorium” on the use of ALPRs by local police, only state and local governments with laws or policies in place to prohibit the use of ALPRs could continue receiving financial assistance from several federal entities, including from the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security, Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Health and Human Services.

The bill would also ban the use of both ALPRs and the data gathered by them at the federal level while creating a legal avenue for lawsuits against the federal government over privacy violations.

However, the legislation would not place an outright ban on the use of Flock and similar cameras attached to license plate analytics software, nor would it ban the use of AI-powered surveillance systems by local governments and private actors. The Ban Flock Act would also allow Congress to pass legislation allowing police to use ALPRs for a specific purpose with privacy restrictions, including deleting data after 48 hours. ALPRs used to collect tolls are exempt from the bill.

Speaking at an event in Bakersfield, California, on October 5, Sanders linked Flock cameras to the controversial rapid advances in AI. While the AI systems that enhance ALPR surveillance are not the most controversial frontier models still in development, AI-powered search engines made by Flock Safety and its competitors to analyze data collected by ALPRs make the systems much more powerful.

When asked by Sanders if they had heard of AI data centers and Flock cameras, the crowd booed.

“We are looking at the possibility [of] the evisceration of privacy rights in America,” Sanders said.

Flock Safety is the leading manufacturer of ALPRs along with competitors such as Axon and Motorola Solutions, which some cities are turning to as the Flock brand becomes increasingly controversial. With an estimated 120,000 ALPRs installed nationwide, Flock’s cameras alone record and analyze about 20 billion images of vehicles each month. The anti-surveillance group DeFlock has mapped more than 143,000 ALPR cameras across the lower 48 states.

ALPRs are not new, but the technology has advanced rapidly in recent years and is often integrated with AI, allowing police to effortlessly search for vehicles and people without needing to enter a license plate number. ALPRs capture images of each passing vehicle, recording location, date, and time, as well as the vehicle’s make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, and then turn these into searchable data points.

For example, when police in Lenexa, Kansas, put a local activist under ALPR surveillance in 2025 after he wrote an op-ed criticizing city officials and was investigated in connection to a petty vandalism case, they were able to easily track his grocery shopping habits and even identify his shoes, according to internal records.

In a statement, Ocasio-Cortez said the widespread integration of AI-powered cameras into everyday life is “unconscionable.”

“Across the country, Big Tech companies like Flock Safety have built a mass surveillance system to harvest Americans’ private and personal data without their consent,” Ocasio-Cortez said on October 2. “AI-powered cameras are …

author: groundxero
title: Barricades, Internet Shutdown, Mass Detentions: Delhi Police Violent Crack Down on Protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and SIR
content:
Thousands of protesters gathered around Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 2 October, defying the denial of police permission and a sweeping security clampdown imposed to prevent the protests from taking place. Barricades sealed the designated protest site from all four directions, mobile internet was suspended across central Delhi, several Metro stations were shut, and riot-control forces were deployed in large numbers. What followed was a day of mass detentions, many involving the use of force against women, students, journalists and other protesters. The violent crackdown came amid a renewed call for mobilisation for a ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’ and ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with organisers calling the 2 October action only the beginning of a wider protest movement.


 


New Delhi, 2 October 2026


by

Mouli Sharma


 


“Thousand is a lowballed estimate,” said a lawyer’s group called

Lawyers for Detainees

, one of several such collectives formed after the historic protests that shook the national capital a mere three months ago after uproar against repeated failures and irregularities in the conduct of public examinations under the tenure of former Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Now, recent history is attempting to recreate itself as a similar uproar against the government’s Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and the recent revelations of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s alleged role in the same has led to widespread national outrage.


 


“85 people have been detained in this station alone,” said Adv. Surya Prakash, who was present at the Badarpur police station. “We have reports that at least 20 buses filled with detainees left the protest site during the day. Many detainees were released informally at random locations far away from the centre of the city, while still more were taken to stations like this one. The actual number of detentions is much higher than whatever numbers will be produced here at the stations,” he said.


 


The figure, though, may include repeat detentions, the most prominent case being of AISA president Neha Bora herself, who was detained at least three times from the same location outside the Royal Plaza Hotel, near the East entrance of the protest site near the Kerala Bhawan canteen, first alongside psephologist and activist Yogendra Yadav, a second time with several student protesters of other parties, and a third time again with fellow AISA leader Anjali of the Delhi University. Former Delhi CM Atishi, independent journalist Harsh Yadav, and at least 700 more students were detained through the day.


 


“700 is the count we have so far from police stations taken across the city,” said Adv. Vertika Mani, also a part of the lawyers’ collective. “But that obviously cannot account for the many detainees who were released at unofficial locations.”


 


The CJP’s ultimatum to the government of witnessing a ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ should Gyanesh Kumar fail to resign within 48 hours (given on 25 September, the deadline for which had long since passed) kicked off with a bang on Friday, as an identical call for the police-defying protest in Shivaji Park, Mumbai was given by countless student, labour, farmer and other political organisations at the eponymous Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, led by prominent activists including Neha Bora, Yogendra Yadav, Nandita Narain, and Prashant Bhushan. Hundreds of civilians took to the streets on the morning of 2 October, on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti, only to be met with armed state forces deployed in massive numbers and a once-designated protest site cut off from their access through curfews (Section 163 of the BNS was declared in the region, without any justification beyond prevention of a ‘crowd forming’) and police barricades blockading entrances to the site from all four directions, dispersing protesters across a wide 2km radius.
