title: Lessons in Hare Hunting: Inside Britain’s School Beagle Packs
content:
The private schools schooling children in a masterclass of wildlife criminality.


Recently we revealed the

full footage of the Stowe School Beagles

 during what school headteacher, Dr Anthony Wallersteiner, describes as a

“huge variety of activities”

 available to pupils, including

“field games…beagling”

.


Kennedy giving direction to the pupils


The school’s Games Coach, Phillip Kennedy, was in the fields surrounding Crockwell Farm, alongside school pupils, ‘coaching’ them as the Stowe School Beagles hunted a hare.


The school lesson ended with a dead hare and a criminal conviction for its Games Coach.


The now-deleted reference to Kennedy’s role at the Stowe School.


Kennedy pleaded guilty to hunting a wild mammal with dogs after drone footage captured his pack chasing the hare, first through the farmyard and then across open fields before catching and killing her against a fence.

Police said

 that Kennedy knew allowing his dogs to chase and kill the hare was cruel and illegal.


Just as importantly, the footage shone a spotlight on something that has gone on behind the closed doors of some of Britain’s most prestigious private schools: children being introduced to illegal hunting, more than twenty years after hunting wild mammals with dogs was banned.


There are serious safeguarding questions which Stowe School, in particular, appear determined to ignore. What risk assessments are made before children are taken out with packs of hunting dogs? What are staff instructed to do when those hounds begin pursuing a live animal? What safeguarding procedures kick in when pupils witness that animal being caught and killed?


Nothing in the footage suggests this was some unexpected aberration. They all know the routine, the kids congratulate each other, congratulate the dogs. Nobody looks shocked. The huntsman joins in with the handshaking. They’ve clearly done this before haven’t they!


Games Coach Philip Kennedy congratulating pupils as the hounds rip the remains of the hare apart close by.


Stowe is not alone.


There are other school beagle packs still taking children out into the countryside, maintaining the hounds and traditions of hare hunting.


Eton College has one of the oldest and most famous school beagle packs in the country.


Its history stretches back to the nineteenth century

. Long before the Hunting Act, generations of Eton boys learned their “hound lore” by pursuing hares with the school pack. Boys became Masters and Whips, and learned to handle hounds.


The Hunting Act came into force in 2005, but school lessons in hare-hunting continue.


In 2013, eight years after the ban, the Hunt Saboteurs Association

revealed plans

 for a Young Hare-Hunters’ Day at Eton. This was no historical re-enactment of hunting, children were actually being offered coaching in the skills and traditions of hare hunting.


Pupils were to receive training in hare hunting from experienced huntsmen, including Steven Duckmanton, the huntsman of the Dummer Beagles.


Steven Duckmanton, hare-hunting huntsman of the Dummer Beagles. Image: West Midlands Hunt Saboteurs.


In 2024,

West Midlands Hunt Saboteurs

 put a drone above those same Dummer Beagles. The footage they captured showed a hare breaking from the field and the pack pursuing her line across field after field, whilst hunt staff watched.


In October 2015,

footage was filmed

 at an Eton College Beagles meet in North Yorkshire, which showed a live hare fleeing across a field with the pack in pursuit. The footage was handed to North Yorkshire Police in January 2016 and Eton announced an urgent investigation.


Eleven years after hunting with dogs had supposedly been consigned to history, one of Britain’s most prestigious schools was having to investigate its own beagle pack over footage of a hare being hunted.


This year, Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg revealed his eldest son had brought 41 Eton beagles home with him during the school holidays.


His son, Peter Theodore Aphege Rees-Mogg, left Eton this summer. He wasn’t a mere follower of the hunt – he had been a Master of the Eton College Hunt during his final year.


Peter Theodore Aphege Rees-Mogg at home out with the Mendip Farmers Hunt. Image: Mendip Hunt Sabs.


Peter’s mother Helena, herself a regular fox hunter and meet host for the

recently-charged

 Mendip Farmers Hunt, went even further in an article published in September 2026.


Writing about why she believes Eton should remain an all-boys school …

author: Unknown
title: Soma’s deadly ‘fate’: 355 miners killed in 13 years
content:
Another mining accident occurred last Thursday in Soma, Manisa, a district known for the Soma Kömür Işletmeleri A.Ş. disaster in which 301 mine workers lost their lives 12 years ago. Workers had warned the company management about shortcomings in occupational health and safety, yet the accident occurred despite those warnings. This is why such preventable accidents are described as work-related killings. Companies seek to keep their profit margins as high as possible by failing to carry out regular maintenance or fully implement occupational health and safety measures, while facing no meaningful sanctions for these failures. Under such conditions, workers’ health and lives effectively become another cost to be cut.


In a feature article,

Yeni Ya

ş

am

 underlined that figures covering mining accidents in Turkey since 2013 show that 70 percent of workers killed lost their lives as a result of mine collapses and crushing, poisoning or suffocation. Manisa ranked first in mining-related worker deaths, followed by Zonguldak. The largest number of deaths occurred in lignite and hard-coal mines, followed by marble, chromium and copper mines. The mining sector has expanded steadily since 2010 and is expected to grow further in the coming years, with the state preparing legal frameworks such as the so-called “Super Permit Law” to facilitate that expansion. Alongside the loss of workers’ lives, the sector has also caused ecological destruction. Workers have been killed in mines for years, while those who survive often struggle to receive their wages. Alongside the widely known struggle of Doruk Maden workers, it is estimated that more than 40 miners’ strikes have taken place since 2013.


Land grabs and ecological destruction by the mining and energy sectors


The 1.061 billion tonnes of mining waste produced annually in Turkey is physical evidence of an irreversible rupture in nature’s metabolism. This process of ecological destruction is intertwined with severe labour exploitation, while documented work-related deaths also reveal the human cost of the industry. The collapse of the heap-leach site at the Çöpler Gold Mine in İliç, Erzincan, on 13 February 2024, which killed nine workers, did not only claim the lives of those workers. Millions of cubic metres of cyanide-contaminated waste spread across the area, polluting approximately 300 decares of land. The toxic waste is believed to have reached the Euphrates River through the Çöpler Stream and from there spread into the wider river basin. This is only one example of such destruction. Hydraulic fracturing carried out for mining and oil exploration, exploratory drilling involving core sampling, and mining operations conducted without the consent or approval of local communities all contribute to deforestation. Such activities also dispossess villagers of their land, indirectly displacing rural populations and forcing them to migrate to major cities, where rapid urbanisation often pushes them into precarious employment.


The ecological destruction caused by mining operations is not confined to distant places, nor is it damage that can simply repair itself over time. Mining sectors in Turkey, Congo and similar countries operate in conditions where neither wage security nor occupational health and safety are guaranteed. The damage is not limited to cyanide and other toxic substances contaminating soil and air; it also affects mine workers’ bodies. Slow Death (Yavaş Ölüm), a documentary directed by İlkay Nişancı and presented by Aslı Odman, examines the deaths caused by thermal power plants in Elbistan over a period of 40 years, including the deadly effects of ash falling on residential areas. From this perspective, mining and other environmentally destructive activities do not cause ecological devastation only in the “outside world”; that destruction also takes place directly in the bodies of the workers whose labour sustains these industries. What miners spend during years underground extracting coal and other minerals is not only their physical strength and time, but also years of their lives. This, too, is regarded as a dimension of ecological destruction.


Soma: A graveyard for workers and a landscape of mines


The

Report on the Struggle Against Extractivism,

 prepared by the Polen Ecology Collective and published in recent months, included data for Manisa compiled by the Health and Safety Labour Observatory (ISIG) covering the period from 2013 to 2025. The data …

author: The Canadian Press
title: Don’t mistake attendance at a press conference as support for a pipeline, chief says
content:
The grand chief of Treaty 8 First Nations stood behind Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last week as they announced the

Pacific Link pipeline

 was the first project deemed to be in the “national interest” under the Building Canada Act.


But Trevor Mercredi said his presence shouldn’t be taken as a vote of confidence.


“I want to be clear that our presence should not be interpreted as support for the project,” Mercredi told The Canadian Press.


“Leadership was there to ensure our nations are not left behind. There are significant concerns that must be addressed, and it does not mean the pipeline is a done deal.”


The national interest designation under the Building Canada Act, puts the pipeline proposal in line for streamlined oversight and approvals.


The government said it will work over the coming year to complete consultations on the project itself, and to secure environmental safeguards, financing and Indigenous partnerships. It wants construction to begin in September 2027.


Some 130 Indigenous communities were given just two months for consultations on whether the pipeline should be granted a national interest designation, and that was still more than the government had planned.


A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says potentially impacted Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.


First Nations leaders have warned the federal government risks violating their rights with “national interest” designations through the Major Projects Office and the controversial Building Canada Act.


Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada’s obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, nor their rights under the Constitution.


The UN declaration, which Canada adopted, states Indigenous groups must provide their free, prior and informed consent before decisions are made that could adversely affect their rights or lands.


Mercredi, who sits on the Indigenous advisory council in the Major Projects Office, said the Carney government appears to be flying the plane “as they’re building it” in a bid to strengthen the Canadian economy in the face of trade pressures with the United States.


“Sometimes when that happens you’re going to hit the ground, and that ground is our First Nations. Because regardless of any legislative changes, regardless of their processes, we still have our rights — they’re still intact,” Mercredi said.


“What they’re doing is weakening their own processes to develop the resources, which does not work in their favour if a (legal) challenge comes from a nation. They can still hold the key. That’s what people have to remember.”


First Nations along the ‘Pacific Link’ pipeline route are not happy with the Prime Minister’s announcement. Photo: Government of Alberta submission to Major Projects Office


It’s the same message he’s brought to the Major Projects Office. He isn’t sure if they’re listening — or if they even want to talk.


The government has been criticized by some Indigenous leaders for limited consultations, without providing much detail, about whether to designate the project under the act.


Mercredi said the Indigenous advisory council wasn’t tapped to offer feedback on if the consultation time frame was long enough or if a 10 per cent ownership stake for Indigenous groups was enough.


He said that, had he been asked, he would have said no to both.


“This is a concern that we have with the MPO. What is our purpose as an advisory council?” Mercredi said.


“We hear that we’re part of the process, but in instances like this it’s obvious that we are not.”


Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has said staff in the Major Projects Office do not understand how to work with First Nations communities and that “junior staffers” aren’t helping to build relationships.


She also said CEO Dawn Farrell has been unavailable to meet with leadership, including at Assembly of First Nations gatherings.


The Canadian Press has reached out to the Major Projects Office for comment but has not yet received a response.


Lawyer Jesse McCormick, co-chair of the Liberal party’s Indigenous Peoples’ Commission and a lawyer with Pape Salter Teillet LLP, questions how the national interest designation and eventual pipeline construction could have looked if …

title: Desinformación climática y extractivismo: organizaciones presentan una investigación en el Congreso
content:
Imagen: Asambleas del Curru Leufu (Río Negro).


El conflicto por el futuro del Golfo San Matías se libra en el territorio, las calles y los tribunales, pero también en el campo de la comunicación. Este martes 6 de octubre, a las 13, la Multisectorial Golfo San Matías, junto a Roots, la Asociación Argentina de Abogados/as Ambientalistas y la Red Ecosocialista, presentará en el Salón Auditorio del subsuelo del Anexo A de la Cámara de Diputados de la Nación (Avenida Rivadavia 1841, CABA), los resultados de una investigación sobre desinformación climática y extractivismo. En la charla, titulada «Desinformación climática, empresas transnacionales y medios de comunicación», presentarán los principales hallazgos de la investigación

 «Narrativas de desinformación en el Golfo San Matías», realizada en el marco de un programa de Roots junto a Climate Action Against Disinformation, que identifica un ecosistema de medios tradicionales y digitales, contenidos coordinados y publicidad paga que presenta el avance de proyectos petroleros y gasíferos en la Patagonia como desarrollo, empleo y progreso, mientras invisibiliza impactos socioambientales, información científica y voces críticas de las comunidades afectadas.

Por ANRed.


Este martes 6 de octubre, a las 13, la

Multisectorial Golfo San Matías

, junto a

Roots

, la

Asociación Argentina de Abogados/as Ambientalistas

 y la

Red Ecosocialista

, realizará en el Congreso de la Nación la charla titulada «

Desinformación climática, empresas transnacionales y medios de comunicación».

 Allí se presentarán los principales hallazgos de la investigación «

Narrativas de desinformación en el Golfo San Matías

«

, desarrollada por integrantes de la organización rionegrina en el marco de un programa internacional impulsado por

Roots

 y

Climate Action Against Disinformation

.


La actividad busca llevar al ámbito parlamentario una discusión que atraviesa de manera directa a las comunidades costeras:

cómo se construye consenso alrededor de proyectos extractivos y qué lugar ocupan los medios, las redes sociales y la publicidad digital en ese proceso

. Según la investigación,

en el caso del Golfo San Matías se detectaron medios digitales de reciente creación que simulan ser portales informativos locales, contenidos automatizados y repetidos y una fuerte inversión en publicidad

 para amplificar determinadas narrativas.


Imagen: Asambleas del Curru Leufu (Río Negro).


El territorio en disputa es una de las regiones de mayor biodiversidad del Atlántico Sur:

el Golfo San Matías y la Península Valdés albergan ballenas, delfines, lobos marinos, aves migratorias y numerosas especies marinas, además de contar con áreas naturales protegidas

. Sobre ese espacio avanzan proyectos hidrocarburíferos vinculados al oleoducto

Vaca Muerta Oil Sur

, un puerto petrolero en

Punta Colorada

 y la futura operatoria de

buques de GNL

.


La investigación reconstruye también el proceso político que permitió ese avance.

En 2022, la Legislatura de Río Negro modificó la Ley 3308, que desde 1999 protegía al Golfo de actividades hidrocarburíferas, para habilitar la construcción del oleoducto Vaca Muerta Oil Sur

. El estudio señala que aquella reforma se realizó

sin consulta previa a comunidades indígenas y en una sesión cuestionada por organizaciones socioambientales

. Desde entonces, distintas comunidades y asambleas sostienen acciones judiciales, movilizaciones, campañas y actividades para disputar el modelo de desarrollo impuesto sobre el territorio.


En ese contexto, la investigación identifica una construcción comunicacional que presenta los proyectos petroleros y gasíferos como sinónimo de progreso. El informe señala que empresas,

organismos estatales y medios convergen en una narrativa que enfatiza empleo, inversión, desarrollo y reactivación económica, mientras los impactos ambientales y las resistencias territoriales quedan relegados

. La investigación también detectó un crecimiento de nuevos portales digitales y publicaciones patrocinadas alrededor de momentos clave de la expansión del proyecto.


Uno de los aspectos más relevantes del trabajo es que amplía la definición de desinformación: «la

desinformación climática

 no funciona solamente a través de noticias falsas o datos incorrectos: opera en diferentes niveles a partir de

narrativas históricamente diseñadas, con financiamiento, construyendo artificialmente consenso, amplificando determinados discursos a través de …

author: Chase Woodruff
title: Case at Supreme Court Could Have Profound Consequences for Other Climate Suits
content:
With help from the Trump administration, Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil have asked the court to quash the lawsuit.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Attorneys representing two Colorado local governments are set for a high-stakes legal showdown over climate change Monday at the U.S. Supreme Court, where they’ll ask justices to allow Boulder’s lawsuit seeking monetary damages from two fossil fuel companies to proceed in state court.

With help from the Trump administration, the two companies, Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil, have asked the court to step in and quash the lawsuit, which was filed in 2018 by Boulder County and the city of Boulder. The plaintiffs are seeking monetary damages under state tort law “for the substantial role (the companies) played and continue to play in causing, contributing to and exacerbating climate change.”

Monday’s Supreme Court hearing in the case, known as Suncor v. Boulder, follows another unprecedented summer of record heat, extreme drought conditions and destructive wildfire activity impacting communities across Colorado. Boulder’s suit is one of more than 30 similar cases filed to date by state and local governments nationwide as human-caused climate change, mostly the result of fossil-fuel combustion, pushes average global temperatures to dangerous new highs.

“This case is really about who’s going to bear the costs of all of these accelerating effects that we’re experiencing on the front lines here in Colorado,” Chris Winter, an environmental attorney and executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center at the University of Colorado School of Law, said in an interview. “Are those costs just going to fall on the shoulders of all of the taxpayers and citizens and our local governments? Or is the oil industry going to be at least partially responsible for their role in contributing to this crisis?”

Exxon and Suncor, a Canadian oil giant that operates Colorado’s only fossil fuel refinery, argue that federal law preempts Boulder’s efforts to hold the companies accountable in state court. The defendants have tried and failed repeatedly to have the case dismissed or removed to federal court, most recently in May 2025, when the Colorado Supreme Court issued a ruling allowing the case to proceed.

Soon after that ruling, however, the companies asked the U.S. Supreme Court, where conservatives hold a 6-3 majority, to step in. Their petition asks the nation’s highest court to rule that federal statute “precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate.”

In February, justices agreed to hear the case, which is set to be among the most closely watched proceedings on the court’s docket for the 2026-27 term, and one of its highest-profile climate change decisions ever. A ruling from the court could have profound consequences for the dozens of other lawsuits seeking climate-related damages from fossil fuel companies, as scientists warn that catastrophic impacts from higher temperatures will continue to accelerate.

In an unusual move, President Donald J. Trump’s administration filed an unsolicited brief in support of Suncor and Exxon’s petition shortly after it was filed, urging the court to overturn the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision, which it called “contrary to the Constitution.” Alongside petitioners and respondents, U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer will be given time during Monday’s oral arguments to represent the Trump administration’s position in support of the companies.

“We’ve seen this administration really bend over backwards to serve the interests of the fossil-fuel industry, and this case is just one of many examples,” Winter said. “A lot of us who watch the court and have studied these issues for a long time are quite troubled by some of the legal arguments this administration has used, to try to undercut the ability of the states to protect (their) citizens, and to insulate the oil industry from liability for its actions.”

In another unusual development, Justice Samuel Alito, one of the Supreme Court’s most conservative members, recused himself from further proceedings in the case last week.

Though the court’s announcement did not explain why, environmental advocates had called for Alito’s recusal because he owns stock in at least two oil …

author: groundxero
title: Purulia’s Bero-Chandi Pahar Faces Renewed Threat from Granite Mining
content:
Community-led ecological restoration and a centuries-old cultural landscape face destruction as quarrying resumes; villagers allege criminalisation of resistance


 


Purulia, West Bengal:

 The Bero-Chandi hillocks in Purulia’s Raghunathpur subdivision are facing renewed threats from granite and stone mining, with local communities and environmental activists warning that continued quarrying could destroy a landscape shaped by decades of ecological regeneration, traditional worship and local cultural history.


 


An appeal issued by those supporting the local resistance has called on civil society organisations, environmental groups, human rights organisations, student movements and cultural activists across West Bengal to intervene against what it describes as the “aggressive granite stone mining” now threatening Bero-Chandi Pahar. The appeal demands an immediate and unconditional halt to all granite and stone mining activities and the withdrawal of criminal cases against villagers and environmental activists.


 


Ecological Restoration and Wildlife Resurgence


 


According to the appeal, the Bero-Chandi hillocks are far more than geological formations. They represent a vibrant, living landscape in which ecology, community life, traditional practices and literary history are closely intertwined. The area had suffered extensive loss of tree cover for decades. Local residents subsequently undertook sustained community-led afforestation, gradually restoring the green cover and reviving the local ecosystem.


 


The restoration reportedly brought back a range of wildlife, including striped hyenas, wild pigs, Indian pythons, jackals and two species of rabbits, alongside numerous resident and migratory birds. The return of avifauna, the appeal states, also contributed to improved soil enrichment, water retention and the local micro-hydrological cycle.


 


This fragile ecosystem and the peaceful lives of the local communities protecting it face imminent destruction due to resumption of aggressive granite stone mining.


 


Living Cultural Heritage and Historical Roots


 


The Bero-Chandi hills are deeply intertwined with the spiritual and cultural identity of the region. The sacred worship of Devi Chandi at this site dates back at least 300 years, anchoring the traditional spiritual practices of the local populace.


 


The landscape holds profound literary value for Bengal. It served as the central backdrop for Bibhutisbhusan Bandyopadhyay’s classic Bengali masterpiece,

“Rankini Devir Kharag”

 written over 80 years ago.


 


The hills harbour ancient natural cave systems that form an integral part of the local terrain and ecosystem.


 


It is this historical and cultural heritage that villagers say is now at risk from renewed quarrying.


 


Villagers’ Resistance

to Mining and Criminalisation of Dissent


 


Low-intensity granite quarrying in the region began around 2014. Facing the threat of ecological devastation, local villagers mounted a peaceful yet resolute resistance, eventually succeeding in stopping operations by 2018.


 


Commercial mining operations, however, resumed in 2024. The resumption was preceded by the targeting of local leadership and environment activists. At least 14 villagers were implicated in fabricated criminal charges, thrust into police custody, and incarcerated for 14 days before securing bail. The use of state force and intimidation to silence environmental defenders and suppress local resistance to mining is a gross violation of democratic norms and community rights.


 


For the communities resisting the mining, the issue is not simply one of land use or quarrying. They argue that the destruction of the hillocks would also mean the loss of a regenerated forest landscape, wildlife habitat and water catchment areas on which surrounding agriculture and community life depend. They warn that continued industrial-scale granite and stone extraction could permanently damage sacred sites, cultural traditions and geological formations associated with the hills.


 


Urgent Appeal to Civil Society


 


The appeal argues that local communities have shown exemplary courage in safeguarding their environment, but they cannot be expected to confront politicians backed powerful commercial mining interests on their own, particularly amid a reign of intimidation and repression.


 


It calls on democratic organisations, environmental and human rights groups, students, cultural …

author: Unknown
title: Kurdish women’s movement delegation visits COPINH in Honduras
content:
A delegation representing the Kurdistan women’s liberation movement visited COPINH in Honduras, in Mesoamerica. COPINH (Civic Council of Popular and Indigenous Organizations of Honduras) is an organization dedicated to struggle and resistance, composed primarily of self-administered indigenous communities.


The Lenca people are one of the indigenous peoples of Central America, primarily distributed in southwestern Honduras, though their territories extend as far as San Salvador. To this day, many communities continue to resist in the mountains of that area, basing their survival on agriculture and livestock farming, carried out without industrial methods and in harmony with nature. On the slopes and among the trees, they grow corn and coffee, with corn being the staple food for these peoples. Following the Spanish occupation, they resisted fighting the colonization with a war led by the legendary Lempira. Despite this, they were subjected to forced conversion to Christianity; however, this failed to erase ancient traditions that still persist today, such as the “compostura” (a ritual of thanksgiving to Mother Earth for her bounty) or the spiritual connection to rivers, the earth, and fire. The spiritual dimension permeates every aspect of life, including political work: every assembly and every important gathering begins with the construction of an altar, on which—in addition to photos of the martyrs—earth, corn, incense, and candles of different colors are placed, carrying the purifying power of fire.


The Lenca communities, drawing their strength from their leader Berta Cáceres, have decided to carry on Lempira’s resistance and fight against those who seek to destroy their lands, their identity, and their very existence. COPINH is an organization founded on March 27, 1993, in response to the call of the Lenca communities, who decided to rise up to defend life, territory, and dignity. Since then, it has served as the organizational space where these same communities come together to fight in defense of their rivers, mountains, culture, and rights as indigenous peoples. They define themselves as follows: “COPINH is a space where we learn, analyze, dream, and act collectively against the injustices afflicting our peoples. We have based our struggle on three pillars: anti-capitalism, anti-patriarchy, and anti-racism. Through them, we confront the powers that seek to dispossess us, divide us, or silence our voices.”


Berta Cáceres was one of the founders of COPINH


The principal founder of COPINH was Berta Cáceres, born in 1971, who possessed the ability, education, and discipline—along with the love and determination necessary—to channel the Lenca people’s anger over the expropriation and destruction of their lands for the sake of capitalist interests, leading them to significant victories against extractivism. Her strength and charisma inspired many communities to organize, fight, and hold their ground in the struggle, even as the companies seeking to destroy their territory carried out a brutal crackdown, killing and forcing countless indigenous community activists into hiding. Berta was a woman and a feminist, recognized as a leader by the Lenca people for her actions and her closeness to them. We can recall here some of her most famous quotes, such as “Wake up, wake up, humanity: there is no time left!” and “Mother Earth—militarized, fenced off, poisoned, where basic rights are systematically violated—demands that we act.”


In fact, COPINH’s struggles have focused on defending the land, opposing deforestation, and opposing dams that were destroying rivers. In particular, it is worth recalling the struggle against the hydroelectric dam on the Gualkarque River, planned by the Honduran elite in collaboration with the Chinese multinational Sinohydro, which would have blocked one of the most vital waterways in Lenca territory. This river is not only a source of water and life, but also the home of sacred spirits that must be free to flow and not be stopped by dams built for extractive purposes. Led by Berta, the communities rose up and ultimately succeeded in preventing the dam’s construction, asserting that they were not defending nature but were part of nature itself, which was defending itself. This struggle led to severe repression; local witnesses report finding the bodies of their comrades thrown into the river and carried downstream by its current. Against this backdrop, on the night of March 2, 2016, four …

author: Curtis Johnson
title: Trump’s Repeal of Roadless Rule Would Declare Open Season on Protected Forests
content:
A public policy expert described the move as “the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

On August 18, Donald Trump’s United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) officially proposed eliminating the national Roadless Rule. If finalized, the repeal would strip protections from 44.7 million acres of wild intact forest.

The rule, passed in 2001, protects in total 58 million acres of forest from road building, logging, fossil fuel extraction, and other development. Forests in Idaho and Colorado, which have their own state roadless laws, would be exempt, at least for now.

The USDA, which oversees the U.S. Forest Service, initially gave the public only 30 days to comment on the plan. They were forced after public pressure to allow 15 additional days, until October 6. Opponents are aiming to mobilize 1 million public comments during this short period, as well as sponsoring public events speaking out against the repeal.

One hundred and eighty environmental, conservation, and citizen’s groups have been joined by tribes, sportsmen, wildland firefighters, and businesses dedicated to tourism, in submitting a joint public comment or otherwise speaking out against this decision. A letter in support of the Roadless Rule and opposing recission has been signed by 164 congressional representatives.

The recission is “the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history,” according to Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. Spivak told Truthout the Roadless Rule shelters “hundreds of threatened and endangered species. It provides incredible recreation opportunities — hunting, fishing, hiking. These were really the last of the forests outside of wilderness that had not been opened up to industrial development.”

The roadless-area forests contain immense old-growth trees, pristine rivers that are filled in the summer and fall with some of the last healthy salmon runs in the country, and trail through some of the U.S.’s grandest scenic beauty. These forests help protect some of the country’s remaining wild species — grizzly bears, wolverines, and endangered lynx. They host key migration corridors for antelope, elk, and mule deer. They protect headwaters of streams providing clean drinking water to 24 million people in the country.

The current protections include 9.3 million acres of the Tongass rainforest in Alaska. The Tongass contains incredible landscapes — rugged ocean coastlines, glacial fjords, snow-capped peaks, wild rivers, and old-growth forest. Concentrated in the Tongass are Earth’s largest remaining intact stands of coastal temperate rainforest, making it a vital carbon sink for curbing climate change. Its trees capture approximately 44 percent of all the carbon stored by U.S. national forests, absorbing 1.5 times more carbon than the U.S. emits annually.

Opening the Tongass and all roadless forests to destruction would be a crime against nature. And further opening the Tongass to development would be yet another crime against Native peoples. The Tongass is the ancestral homeland of the Tlingit and Haida Indigenous peoples. A joint statement from the tribes condemns the decision to rescind the rule, saying it was taken “without any prior consultation with our Tribe or other Southeast Alaska tribes. As a sovereign tribal nation, we do not recognize the validity of federal actions impacting our traditional homelands when undertaken without meaningful government-to-government consultation, as required by law and respect for our inherent sovereignty.”

The statement continues, “The Tongass is more than an ecosystem — it is our home. It is the foundation of our identify, our culture, and our way of life.”

The USDA proposal claims to “reduce regulatory burden and return decisionmaking for the management of inventoried roadless area to the land management planning process at the individual national forest level…. Recission of the national-level prohibitions provides responsible officials with flexibility to better guide management of the National Forest System lands and respond to changing local resource conditions.”

Describing these relatively untouched forests — rich with species, habitat, and natural wonders — as “resources” is a dead giveaway to the proposal’s actual intent.

LNG steht für „Liquefied Natural Gas“ (Flüssigerdgas) und gelangt derzeit hauptsächlich aus den USA, wo es durch Fracking gewonnen wird, über Norddeutschland in deutsche Haushalte. Nun zeichnet sich eine ähnliche Tendenz durch Spannungen zwischen den USA und Europa ab. Die deutsche Bundesregierung muss jetzt entscheiden, ob sie für den dafür notwendigen Ausbau der Infrastruktur im Golfo San Matías in Patagonien eine ungebundene Finanzkredit-Garantie (UFG) erteilen will, wie die deutsche NGO urgewald berichtet. author: Esperanza
title: Entrevista a Martin Curiche, Camila Huaracan y Sofía Dietz: Operación Huracán, a 9 años aún no hay justicia
content:
Para este registro, nos reunimos con Martin Curiche ex-preso político mapuche incriminado en el montaje de la llamada «Operación Huracán 1» en septiembre de 2017, junto a otros siete dirigentes mapuche y no mapuche, mediante una serie de pruebas falsas implantadas y manipuladas por Carabineros y un civil.


«Cuando se dio toda la operación fue por un tema específico, por dos temas en este caso: estaba el juicio

Luchsinger Mackay

 y a la vez, el

Caso Inglesia

. Fue en ese entonces cuando nos reunimos amigos, pu lamngen y familiares de los presos y decidimos que podiamos hacer algo, podíamos romper ese círculo mediático que la prensa no estaba dando, en conjunto con una red de secundarios y la red de apoyo infantil. El dia 100 de huelga de hambre, porque los peñis del caso inglesia para poder anular un tema que era la asociación ilícita, nosotros empemos a hacer movilizaciones y decidimos levantar un punto de reunión permanente a las afueras de la cárcel». Relata Martin.


El dia 23 de septiembre de 2017, luego de producirse un segundo desalojo en el punto de reunión fuera de la cárcel, Martín Curiche es detenido bajo una orden emanada por el Tribunal de Temuco.


Curiche fue acusado de «asociación ilícita,incendio territorista y de estar en un supuesto grupo de WhastApp donde se comunicaban para comenter ciertos detilos». Imputaciones que finalmente fueron desacreditadas al quedar al descubierto la implantación de pruebas falsas por parte de funcionarios y altos mandos de Carabineros con el apoyo de un civil.


Han pasado 9 años desde la Operación Huracán 1 y Martin, cuenta que hasta la actualidad existen recupercusiones. La exposición mediática y el papel de las grandes cadenas nacionales de comunicación influyeron en la opinión pública de manera negativa.


«Cuando ya se descubre que fue un montaje de todo, el tema de buscar trabajo se vio difícil… (9 años después) Pensando que ese tema estaba zanjado hasta la fecha sigue con réplicas. Cuánto tiempo más tiene que pasar para que eso se borre del expediente de uno, del curriculum en este caso, porque es lo primero que se muestra cuando uno postula a un trabajo».


El otorno familiar y de la comunidad también ha quedado marcada, dice Martin «se empieaza a ver más visitas de carabineros en ese tiempo, para mi zona era escaso ese tema pero después que sucedió eso, la visita de carabineros en el territorio fue excesiva en ese período que duró la famosa Operación Huracán».


Camila Huaracan, una de las abogadas de Martin, quienes actualmente están el en juicio «Operación Huracán 2» como querellantes, comenta:


«trabajamos en el mayor fraude procesal sistemático en el cual se pudo acreditar que los altos mandos realizaron obstrucción a la investigación, también falcificación de prueba y esto netamente, fue perpetrado por altas esferas de Carabineros de Chile, a través de la dirección de inteligencia de la Dipolcar y también de Uioe; Unidad de Inteligencia Operativa Especializada».


Las representantes en este juicio donde Curiche, ahora en calidad de víctima, se refieren al grave hecho de cómo altos mandos de carabineros actuaron para encarcelar injustamente a dirigentes mapuche y la lentitud para encontrar justicia. «Vemos con preocupación cómo ha existido, un obstáculo para acceder a la justicia… vemos cómo acá se ha retrasado a tal punto de que ocurrieron casi 7, 8 años para que recién se comenzara la preparación de juicio oral y ahora vamos a los 10 años y tenemos una sentencia condenatoria en pimera instancia, pero aún así tampoco se condenaron a todos los carabineros…»


Ahora a casi 10 años, existe una sentencia condenatoria hacia los entonces, funcionarios de Carabineros y un civil, sin embargo no todos fueron condenados, sino sólo seis de ellos.

«Por ejemplo el General Blu, el capitán Marín o también Teuber, que ellos participaron en estos montajes, no van a ir a la cárcel, van a estar con libertad vigilada y a muchos de ellos igual se les abonó todo el tiempo que estuvieron en medida cautelar… Vemos que la justicia sí funciona de manera distintas cuando los imputados o las víctimas son mapuche o son altos mandos de Carabineros. Lo vemos como el mayor ejemplo de la crisis de esta república y de estos órganos de Carabineros». Camila Huaracan, abogada.


«La rápidez con la que se efectua cuando los imputados son pertenencientes al pueblo mapuche es muy distinta cuando los imputados son pertencientes a altos mandos de carabineros»

author: Arianna Astuni
title: Lillehammer’s “Other” Olympics: The Mad in Norway International Film Festival
content:
T

hey arrive—amidst airline strikes, taxi strikes, train strikes, airport closures, heavy luggage woes, and all the other obstacles that make traveling a challenge—in Lillehammer, Norway.


Photo by Kermit Cole


It doesn’t elude me that the small Norwegian town that hosted the big Olympics welcomes this group. They arrive ready to win, too. Their whole lives are about fighting to win—winning back lives and winning back the truth. This is a celebration, not of a finished goal—their work will be forever—but of notches in belts and the realization that they are not alone in this battle. They come mad, from every country, their own Olympics, to change the practices of antiquated psychiatry and views on mental illness and over-medication of those deemed mentally ill.


As an American, Lillehammer is synonymous with Tonya Harding and Nancy Kerrigan. As a human, madness is synonymous with King Lear, the Mad Hatter, the Joker, and Charles Manson. The consequence of the caricature. The evil of an individual. Contention rules our definition of things we don’t know. And things that scare us are “othered.” We wait hopefully for them to be tempered and extinguished. They are systematically silenced through practice and language.


Foucault says language is not a neutral tool. It is the means through which power shapes how we think and act, and even what we can know. It’s a device for social control, a way of staunching the free flow of meaning. There is no outside of language. So one must fight to take back the control, the “authorship” of the language that defines and binds them.


I close my mouth and beg my mind to prepare me anew, a blank slate. I listen for the language reclaimed, honored to be in Lillehammer, Norway, at this Mad in Norway International Film Festival: Rethinking Mental Health.


The Lillehammer Cinema sits at the intersection of Stortorget and Kirkegata, nestled fortuitously between the Lillehammer Kunstmuseum and the bibliotek. A few steps down the sidewalk stands the famous Birkebeiner sculpture (King Hakon IV as a baby, carried to safety in the arms of a hero on skis and later associated with strengthening Norway), proudly welcoming visitors to the city.


The mild hubbub of anticipation bounces off the walls as I enter to get my badge. Three days of films on the experience of madness from those with lived experience, struggling to find their way in a world that deems them worthy only of being highly medicated and silent. Three days of films by those working alongside them in the trenches, fighting to change how madness is defined and treated.


Photo by Kermit Cole


The winding stairs of the cinema lead to a Willy Wonka lobby. The brightness of hard candy, soft candies, loose candies, bagged candies, and popcorn (with bacon!) mimics the diversity of the people milling about. With first-day inhibitions and nervous newness, we enter for the opening ceremony.


We sit in the red comfortable chairs of the massive cinema, leaving space between us, quietly focused and reverent. The opening ceremony asks us to reconsider what we think we know. The Mad in Norway leaders remind us that “voices that don’t shy away from difficult truths are how a system changes.”


This is not anger or clinical discussion. The speakers remind us that the best medicine for humanity is another human being.


We are comfortable and safe in these seats, but I get goosebumps. This is a call to arms of a sort. Representatives from the Norwegian Parliament and the UN rise to remind us how important the arts are to mental health awareness, revealing reality in its grimness and inspiration. They thank the filmmakers for giving visibility to “eyes too often hidden.”


Visibility is the first goal. Decades ago, researchers claimed to have discovered the molecules that caused mental imbalances: depression and psychosis. They deemed their 2nd-generation drugs a cure-all and a win for medical progress. Medical institutions bought this unproven data hook, line, and sinker, and they were off to the races. Until observant journalists and psychiatrists started to notice a disturbing trend: the number of people with “mental illnesses” started increasing. The number of people on disability skyrocketed from 1.2 million to 4 million. The drugs were causing more problems in the long run.


Viewed together,

these films

 covered remarkable ground, moving across countries, treatment models, and deeply personal experiences while returning again and …

title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.


The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.

Date & time:


15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

 Trans communities and activists 


Register here

Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.


The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? title: Le temps des promesses
content:
Alors que la jeunesse française embrase le pays, nous avons interviewé Christian Ingrao pour son nouveau livre

Le Temps des promesses

. La situation présente est le produit d'une lente glaciation de l'espérance qui avait été annoncée non par des prophètes, mais par des historiens, des économistes, des ingénieurs agronomes, et toutes ces littératures grises qui enregistrent, en même temps qu'elles font, l'espérance et ses vacillements. Nous vivons les derniers moments d'une série de promesses nées aux lendemains de la mutation anthropologique des guerres mondiales, et dont la force d'élan et d'entraînement s'est tarie au tournant des années 1980. En réactivant une méthode matérialiste inspirée de Engels et Marx, Ingrao parvient à reconstruire la « sociogenèse de l'espérance », depuis une multitude d'observatoires, dont le temps présent nous dit la fin.

author: Paul Messersmith-Glavin
title: A Lifelong Organizer Shares Lessons on Sustaining Activism for the Long Haul
content:
Organizer Chris Dixon discusses how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Writer and organizer Chris Dixon has his fingers on the pulse of North American grassroots movement. Dixon has extensively and repeatedly traveled throughout North America, talking with people working for social change — engaging with activists concerning their successes and heartbreaks, their frustrations and dreams. His first book, Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements, published in 2014, focused on antiauthoritarian organizers and politics across a range of movements of the 2000s and early 2010s, including migrant justice, prison abolitionism, and Occupy Wall Street. His new book, For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World, focuses on how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Movement elders I am close to — now in their 70s — who maintain radical political commitments developed in their youth, benefitted from both the intense community that formed around movements for Black Power and liberation, the youthful counterculture and the New Left, and anti-war movements, as well as from their own inner convictions that served as an animating passion. For these elders, political engagement is a kind of vocation. Though they continue to maintain relationships with those comrades who are also still alive and committed to political struggle, those vibrant communities they once thrived in are gone. Only their specific commitment to the possibility of freedom and liberation keeps them going.

Coming of age politically in the 1990s, we also had strong bonds of friendship born through relentless organizing meetings, demonstrations, and coalition work. It seemed we could collectively change the world. Thirty years later, only a handful of us remain involved. Why? Why do people stop organizing, beyond and in addition to the realities of acquiring increasing responsibilities as we age? Why do people give up on the possibility of creating fundamental social and structural change together over the long term? How can we cultivate and sustain caring radical communities that support us all, while drawing new people in, or welcoming them back? These are some of the questions Chris Dixon sets out to answer in For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World. The interview that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Paul Messersmith-Glavin: Who should read your book?

Chris Dixon: I wrote For the Long Haul as a practical guide with two main audiences in mind. On the one hand, I wanted to warmly welcome people who have recently become involved in radical political efforts, especially those who have joined movement upsurges since 2020. I’m particularly thinking of the Movement for Black Lives and Palestine solidarity organizing, but also renewed labor militancy and collective defense of queer and trans people. A lot of people I talk to who are newer to movements — many but not all of them younger people — are hungry for conversations about how to sustain lifelong political commitments.

On the other hand, I wanted to speak lovingly to my peers — long-time activists and organizers who have been involved in movements for decades. Many of us talk informally with our friends about the challenges we face in staying actively involved on the left. We’re working a lot to pay our bills, reckoning with disabilities and chronic health conditions, and holding significant care responsibilities for kids, elders, and others in our lives. So many of us are deeply exhausted and hungry for realistic advice about how to stay steady in the fight.

I also wanted to sympathetically address people who participated in movements of the left at one time or another and then moved away from active involvement. I know many people who have followed this trajectory. Rather than being moralistic or dismissive, I wanted to remind them that they’re always welcome back. And I wanted to suggest that perhaps, together, we can build some better structures and practices for helping people stay engaged.

You have spent a tremendous amount of time travelling around the U.S. and Canada, listening to on-the-ground organizers. What have you learned?

title: 'Aile Sağlığı Merkezleri, satılacak bina değil, sağlık merkezidir'
content:
Eylem Nazlıer [email protected]

Türkiye’de koruyucu, birinci basamak sağlık hizmetlerinin yurttaşla buluştuğu en önemli noktalardan biri olan Aile Sağlığı Merkezlerinin (ASM) geleceği, merkezlerin fiziki koşullarından kira giderlerine, deprem güvenliğinden personel eksikliğine kadar risk altında. Kamuya ait binalarda bile kiralarına yüzde 300’e varan zamlar istenen ASM’lerde aile hekimleri zor durumda.

Birlik ve Dayanışma Sendikası Genel Başkanı Dr. Ahmet Mehlepçi, ASM’lerin mümkün olduğunca kamuya ait, depreme dayanıklı ve sağlık hizmetinin gerektirdiği fiziki standartlara uygun binalarda hizmet vermesi gerektiğine vurgu yaparak “ASM’ler yalnızca hekim, ebe ve hemşirelerin görev yaptığı binalar değildi. ASM’ler; koruyucu sağlık hizmetlerinin, gebe, bebek ve çocuk izlemlerinin, bağışıklama hizmetlerinin, kronik hastalık takiplerinin ve vatandaşın sağlık sistemiyle ilk temasının gerçekleştiği temel sağlık kuruluşlarıdır” hatırlatmasını yaptı. Bu nedenle ASM’lerin geleceğine ilişkin kararların yalnızca bina, taşınmaz veya bütçe konusu olarak değerlendirilemeyeceğini dile getiren Mehlepçi, “Konu doğrudan sağlık hizmetine erişim, hizmetin sürekliliği ve kamu yararıdır” diye konuştu.

Sağlık Bakanı Kemal Memişoğlu’nun Kasım 2025’te 1000 yeni ASM yapacaklarını açıklamasından bu yana sadece 278 ASM’nin hizmete girdiğini, 370 ASM’nin inşaatının sürdüğünü ve 352 ASM’nin proje aşamasında olduğu bilgisini veren Mehlepçi, Türkiye genelinde ise yaklaşık 8 bin 300 ASM bulunduğunu söyledi.

Yeni ASM yatırımlarının elbette önemli olduğunu belirten Mehlepçi, mevcut merkezlerin ise kentsel dönüşüm, deprem riski, yüksek kiralar veya taşınmaz satışları nedeniyle hizmet dışı kalmasının önlenmesi gerektiğini vurguladı.

Bir taraftan yeni ASM’ler yapılırken diğer taraftan mevcut merkezlerin kentsel dönüşüm, deprem riski, yüksek kiralar veya taşınmaz satışları nedeniyle hizmet dışı kalma tehlikesiyle karşı karşıya olduğuna dikkati çeken Mehlpeçi “Mart 2026’da TBMM’ye sunulan soru önergesine verilen cevapta İstanbul Kadıköy’deki 33 ASM’den 7’sinin kentsel dönüşüm nedeniyle yıkıldığı ve hizmet veremez hale geldiğini söyledi. Mahlepçi kaç yeni ASM açıldığı kadar, kaç ASM’nin kapandığı, yıkıldığı, tahliye edildiği, taşındığı veya başka bir ASM’nin içine sıkıştırıldığının da kamuoyuyla paylaşılması gerektiğini aktardı.

ASM binalarının deprem güvenliğinin de önemli bir sorun olduğunu belirten Mehlepçi, 2025 yılında yapılan bir çalışmada ASM binalarının yaklaşık üçte birinin 1999 öncesinde inşa edildiğinin ortaya çıktığını söyledi. 6 Şubat 2023 yaşanan depremlerde ortaya çıkan tablonun bu konuda vahim olduğunu hatırlatan Mehlepçi “2026 yılı başında sahadan elde edilen verilere göre Hatay’da 96 ASM konteynerlerde hizmet veriyor. 103 ASM kendi binasında hizmet vermeye devam ediyor ancak bunların bir bölümü deprem güvenliği açısından risk taşıyor. Yaklaşık 56 ASM ise tahliye veya yıkım sürecinde” dedi.

Öte yandan ASM’ler için sorunun yalnızca deprem güvenliğiyle sınırlı olmadığını, ASM’lerdeki sağlık hizmetinin niteliği ve çalışanların koşullarını etkileyen başka fiziki sorunların bulunduğunu da dile getiren Mehlepçi durumu şöyle anlattı: “Penceresi, yeterli mekanik havalandırması bulunmayan kan alma odaları, lavabosu olmayan, iki veya üç sağlık çalışanının aynı odayı kullanmak zorunda kaldığı ASM’ler de var. Hatta bazı çalışma alanları hasta mahremiyetini sağlamaya da elverişli değil.”

Yıkım veya tahliye kararı verilen merkezlerde görev yapan sağlık çalışanlarının başka bir ASM’nin mutfağına, dinlenme odasına veya ortak kullanım alanına yerleştirilerek yeni bir aile hekimliği birimi oluşturulmasının kalıcı bir çözüm olmadığının altını çizen Mehlepçi, “Bir sağlık hizmetinin verilebilmesi için yalnızca bir oda bulunması yeterli değildir. O alanın sağlık hizmetinin niteliğine, çalışan güvenliğine ve hasta mahremiyetine uygun olması gerekir” dedi.

Kamusal sağlık hizmeti sunulan ASM’lerde yükün önemli bir bölümünün aile hekimlerinin üzerine yıkıldığına ve özellikle büyükşehirlerde uygun bina bulmanın giderek zorlaştığına işaret eden Mehlepçi “Kiralar da ASM’lerin sürdürülebilirliğini tehdit eden seviyelere ulaştı. Aylık 100 bin TL ve üzerinde kira ödeyen ASM örnekleri var. Elazığ’da bazı ASM’ler yüzde 350’ye varan kira artış talepleriyle karşılaştı. ASM’ler birer ticarethane değildir. Burada yürütülen faaliyet kamu sağlık hizmetidir” uyarısını yaparak buna rağmen yüksek kira bedellerinin yanı sıra elektrik, su, doğalgaz, temizlik, bakım-onarım …

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.


The root cause


According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.


The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.


“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.


Lives of patients at risk


The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”


The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.


The nurse also told

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.


Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.


It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.


Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Mental Health Reminders
content:
These are dark times. It is, in fact, the world that is crazy – despair and anxiety are natural responses to watching society destroy itself for the wealthy and powerful. But by reaching out to each other, we can find the courage to stay engaged with the world, to survive, and to fight back. Mental health and mental health crises vary a lot between people, and are often intertwined with class, race, gender, and activism. These suggestions are generic, but may be useful for yourself or others. If you find yourself or someone you love having delusional thinking or consider self-harm or other violence, these suggestions probably aren’t enough. Remember that it is okay to reach out for professional help!

• Our brains are connected to our bodies, so physical health can help with mental distress. Eating healthy food on a regular schedule and getting enough sleep are necessary for mental stability and sustained activism. Exercise, dance, and physical movement help, too. So can fresh air and having a stable, calming place to stay. Try to recognize if you’re missing one of these, and if that’s causing distress.

• An important component of mental health is the ability to know ourselves, understand our needs, and be able to talk about them to the other people in our lives. This can be really challenging and can often take guidance from others who have learned how to do it with one another.

• It can help to have language for mental crisis that feels comfortable and makes more sense than the dominant medical language. Transmission of language often happens in groups. Talk to friends about the different ways you can feel “off” and develop your own shorthand to describe them.

• Joining a mutual support group of peers listening to and helping peers as equals can be validating, while not necessarily endorsing your feelings. You can form one yourself or join an ongoing group.

• If possible, find a therapist or counselor who supports your self-determination. Ask about confidentiality if someone else — such as your parents, boss, or governmental program — is paying.

• Drugs and alcohol usually make mental health problems worse.

• Psychiatric drugs such as those for depression or bipolar disorder can help some people reduce distress and maintain stability, while other people with similar symptoms may experience distress or harm from the same drugs. Figuring out what works for you can be a process because people differ.

• Nature and wilderness can be our greatest healers. Spend some time outside the city to get centered. Get away from pollution, which is in itself mind-altering. Look up “Ecopsychology” to learn more.

• Allow social, political, and environmental crises unfolding around you to radicalize you, rather than driving you to despair. Actually articulate the world you would want to be living in; work towards it. Remember change happens collectively – look for ways to plug in. Small acts like talking to neighbors or submitting art to Slingshot can help you feel political agency between larger or more radical actions.

• Many communities have 24 hour a day crisis hotlines or crisis centers. Call 800-SUICIDE if you’re thinking about killing yourself or 800 646-HOPE to reach a rape crisis line for survivors of sexual violence. Warning: if you call and say you want to kill yourself police may arrive at your door.

• Things that can help your mental health day-to-day might not be as effective when you’re in crisis. Review the above reminders, and try to eat, exercise, journal, etc., but it’s okay if that isn’t helping.

• Distracting yourself from depressed or anxious thoughts can help: listening to music, making art, washing dishes, doing a project alone or with others. Embrace sensation: use your hands or massage your fingers. Hold onto an ice cube, or take a hot or cold shower. Give yourself time to gather resources.

• Some current emotional crises may be caused by traumas from the past, which may need to be emotionally and consciously processed in order not to keep recurring; that processing might take time.

• When in crisis, it may help to realize that the feeling will eventually pass and your life will begin to feel manageable and meaningful again later. Depression may feel like lack of feelings and a lack of connection to feeling. Anxiety may feel like rapidly cycling concern for what might happen. Both inhibit your ability to perceive and understand the world correctly. Your perceptions of hopelessness are NOT …

We join women, girls, and human rights defenders across Africa and the globe on this 28th day of September to commemorate the 2026 International Safe Abortion Day, reaffirming a simple truth: safe abortion is essential healthcare.

We are reminded of the transformative power of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), which is lauded as one of the most progressive and comprehensive legal instruments for the promotion and protection of women’s rights globally, particularly in the area of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). Adopted in 2003 by the African Union, the Protocol goes beyond existing international human rights standards by explicitly articulating a wide array of SRHR protections that are often left ambiguous or unstated in other international and regional human rights instruments.

Article 14 of the Maputo Protocol guarantees women’s rights to health and reproductive autonomy, including the right to control their fertility, decide on family size and spacing, and to choose their method of contraception. Most critically, Article 14 makes the Maputo Protocol the first and only binding international human rights treaty to explicitly guarantee access to safe medical abortion in specific circumstances—namely, where the continued pregnancy endangers the mental or physical health of the mother or the life of the mother or the fetus, or in cases of sexual assault, rape, or incest. This Article also mandates access to comprehensive reproductive health services, including antenatal care, safe delivery, family planning, and sexual and reproductive health education. In doing so, the Protocol moves abortion access from a matter left to state discretion to one of binding treaty obligation — a distinction that remains central to the advocacy for its full domestication across the continent.

Currently, 46 of the 55 African states have ratified the Maputo Protocol, while nine – Burundi, Chad, Egypt, Eritrea, Madagascar, Morocco, Niger, Somalia, and Sudan – are yet to ratify it. Bringing these final states on board is vital because over 150 million African women and girls currently live outside the protective legal framework of the Maputo Protocol.

Despite its progressiveness, 9 out of the 46 member states have placed reservations to various provisions of the Maputo Protocol, with Article 14 being the most reserved provision. A reservation lowers the minimum human rights standards contained in a particular treaty for the reserving states and enables the reserving states to escape accountability for human rights violations.

Currently, Africa accounts for 70% of global maternal deaths. These preventable deaths are compounded by persistent gaps in access to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) services, which are essential to safeguarding the lives and dignity of women, children and adolescents. Unsafe abortions continue to claim the lives of thousands of African women and girls, while millions more are left with severe injuries and long-term health complications. According to the World Health Organization, nearly half of all abortions worldwide are unsafe, with Sub-Saharan Africa carrying the highest burden.
